source_description: Pat Summitt's Championing Women in Leadership program. Take your leadership skills to the next level with Championing Women in Leadership. Based on the principles of championship-level leader and coach Pat Summitt, this program is online and self-paced, featuring lessons including video, written and other interactive content such as quizzes and a PDF workbook to accompany the course. Designed to support both current and future leaders, the program is engaging and informative for men and women alike.

Lesson 1 of 4
Introduction

In the world of sports, there are many trailblazers who leave a personal mark on the game—with Pat Summitt at the very top of that list. Her name became synonymous with excellence in women's sports and leadership. Summitt's journey also intersects with a pivotal moment in history known as Title IX—a federal law that transformed the landscape of women's extracurriculars in the U.S.

The impact of Title IX resulted in a cultural shift that exceeded the realm of sports and ushered in a new philosophy of gender equity across the country, just as more and more women began to enter the workforce in the 1980s and 1990s.

video.transcript_text:
Introduction: Pat Summitt's Contributions to Title IX and Gender 
Equality  
 
Robin Roberts 
 
All of us know strong, successful women who have made us who we are today. Whether it 
was a relative, friend or mentor, women have been the backbone of society – and the 
workforce – long before they were officially recognized. 
For me, one of those women was Pat Summitt. I’ve got tell you, I met her for the first time in 
1987. I was a young sports reporter on television and there weren’t a lot of women that 
were doing it at that time. It was very challenging. I had so many conversations with Pat, 
and she was a beacon, a real beacon for me, a real mentor, a real friend. Just a short time 
later, I was at ESPN the worldwide leader in sports.  
Pat wouldn’t have considered herself a feminist – she considered herself a “subversive. ” 
That is, someone immersed in a man’s world at the time, who was slowly re-defining the 
perception of women in her field by her actions. As a woman in a male-dominated industry, 
she smashed the glass ceiling over and over again, paving the way for other women to 
succeed. 
Pat once said, “Here’s how I’m going to beat you. I’m going to outwork you. That’s all there 
is to it. ” That’s so Pat. She was the first female coach to be on the cover of Sports Illustrated 
in 1998. She was the first female coach to negotiate a salary of $1 million and insist that 
she be paid equally with the other male coaches in her profession.  
Pat was also the first person to be an Olympic winner both as a player and a coach. She 
was “Coach of the 20th Century, ” in addition to “NCAA Coach of the Year” seven times. In 
2012, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country’s highest civilian 
honor, alongside other recipients such as Bill and Melinda Gates, John Glenn, and Stephen 
Hawking. 
The road to gender equality in the workplace hasn’t been an easy one. There are still many 
obstacles to women in leadership and making the workplace a more level playing field for 
their bright, talented contributions. 
In this course, you’ll learn more about how we all got here, including some of the specific 
roadblocks for women in leadership. You’ll learn about microaggressions and how they can 
be damaging – to any gender – and about some of the specific strengths of female leaders.

You’ll learn how to “own your game” and be a master of your own destiny, specifically as it 
relates to communication, key conversations and negotiation. 
In Pat’s own words, “Belief in yourself is what happens when you know you’ve done the 
thing things that entitle you to success. ” 
Pat believed women everywhere could be – and already were leaders.  
And you can be too.

steps.source_title: From the Farm to the Basketball Court to Women’s Rights
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 2 of 4
From the Farm to the Basketball Court to Women’s Rights

Pat’s own background was unlikely, in a way— she wasn’t a lawmaker or politician. Pat grew up in the small town of Henrietta, Tennessee, the first girl in the family, with three older brothers. When Pat was born, the family lived in a two-room log cabin, but the family farm eventually grew to a 1,000-acre farm with more than 60 milk cows, in addition to a general store, hardware store, feed mill, gas pump, laundromat, and construction business. Everyone worked on the farm, including Pat, and they lived from crop to crop.

“The best, most valuable thing my father gave me was an equal opportunity,” Pat later recalled of her childhood. “Nobody in the family seemed to regard me as a girl when it came to work or playing basketball. I fought hard and played hard and was expected to hold my own with my brothers, whether we were in the fields or in the hayloft. In most ways I was raised like a fourth son.”¹

“The best, most valuable thing my father gave me was an equal opportunity.” — Pat Summitt

Pat credited her upbringing on the farm with a sense of responsibility and independence at an early age.

“I’ve had more experience with physical pain than most men,” Pat said. “I’ve been paddled and whipped so hard it lifted me off the ground. I’ve had my jaw dislocated, and I’ve blown out my knee and I’ve given birth … Only recently have sports audiences become accustomed to watching women explore their physical limits in competitive arenas, and deal with issues like playing with pain. A tremendous cultural shift has taken place in just the last 25 years, allowing us to run, jump, and throw without being accused of being unfeminine. So don’t tell me what I can and can’t do.”

When Pat neared her high school graduation in 1970, she realized that while her brothers each had athletic scholarships, she wasn’t going to get one, because they weren’t offered to women at the time.

“I was a good enough player that the Cheatham County High School in Ashland City would eventually name the school gym after me,” she said. “But my parents had to scrape to pay my way to the University of Tennessee-Martin. And I thought, this needs to change.”

Three events in 1972 did change everything. Title IX legislation was passed by United States President Nixon. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced women’s basketball would be played for the first time at the 1976 Olympic games, and the Association of Intercollegiate Athletics for Women (AIAW) began to officially oversee women’s sports.

When it was announced that women’s basketball would be played for the first time at the 1976 Olympics, Pat got an invitation to try out for the national team.

“Sports, it struck me, could be a vital avenue to self-worth for women,” she recalls.

Pat would also go on to be a staunch advocate of the new Title IX legislation—Prohibition of Sex Discrimination. Title IX states: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.”²

In the meantime, Pat became the head coach for the University of Tennessee Lady Vols in 1974. During her first two years as head coach she taught PE, coached basketball, attended graduate classes, and trained for the Olympics.

While college athletes were allowed to play full court, at the time, the Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association (TSSAA) felt high school girls were not physically able to play full-court basketball. Girls were limited to a six-player half-court game, with each team comprised of three forwards and three guards. Forwards handled the ball and shot on the other team’s basket on one half court, while guards played defense on the other half court. There were no fast breaks, as players were not allowed to pass the half court line.

Then, in 1976, athlete Victoria Cape sued the TSSAA on grounds that the half-court game constituted discrimination under Title IX and the 14th Amendment. Pat defended Cape’s claim and also argued that the half-court arrangement stifled her college recruiting efforts. The court originally ruled in Cape’s favor, but the decision was later overturned. Frustrated, Pat announced that she would no longer recruit girls from the state of Tennessee to play for the Lady Vols until the TSSAA changed its rule and let Tennessee girls play the full-court game. A month later the TSSAA voted to let the girls play full-court.

Pat’s presence was felt, but a hefty double standard still existed for women and their coaches in the sport. She went on to coach the U.S. women’s basketball team at the 1984 Olympics. The women’s team won the gold medal and hoisted Pat on their shoulders in victory. Legendary Indiana Head Coach Bobby Knight remarked on Pat’s win saying, “You need to retire and start your family.”

Pat’s father agreed with Knight.

“Dad, I can have a family and still coach,” Pat remembers telling him.³

And the rest is history.

“Sports, it struck me, could be a vital avenue to self-worth for women.” — Pat Summitt

Pat went on to be the winningest college basketball coach in American history (men or women) at the time of her retirement. She coached the Lady Vols until 2012, and amassed more than 1,098 wins. During her career, Pat won eight national championships and boasted a 100 percent graduation rate for her student-athletes.

steps.source_title: Cutting the Net … and Smashing the Glass
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 3 of 4
Cutting the Net … and Smashing the Glass

When once asked if she was a feminist, Pat joked, “No, I’m not a sign carrier.” The sign she carried was that of her character, her accomplishments, and an unflinching commitment to equality, which she let stand for itself. Pat’s achievements extend beyond Title IX—and to overall equity for women. As a woman in a male-dominated industry, she smashed the glass ceiling over and over again, paving the way for other women to succeed.

In 1998, Summitt was the first female coach to be on the cover of Sports Illustrated. She was the first female coach to negotiate a salary of $1 million and insist that she be paid equally with men in her field. She was the first person to be an Olympic winner both as a player and a coach (silver medal as a player in 1976 and gold as a coach in 1984). Two college basketball courts were named in her honor—one at UT Martin and one at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville—in addition to two streets. She was the Coach of the 20th Century, in addition to NCAA Coach of the Year seven times. In 2012, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country’s highest civilian honor, alongside other recipients such as Bill and Melinda Gates, John Glenn, and Stephen Hawking.

steps.source_title: Understanding the Playing Field for Female Leaders
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 4
Understanding the Playing Field for Female Leaders

While Title IX was a start, it was only a forerunner of the many gender equality changes that would happen in the U.S. over the next two decades. Discrimination against female employees has taken many forms over the years—most notably, being paid less than male counterparts and/or being subjected to gender stereotypes. Women now make up roughly half the U.S. workforce, but the road to overall equality has been a long one.

This course provides a closer look at the modern obstacles facing women in the workplace, specifically women in leadership. If women start out as half of the workforce, what is impeding their ability to reach the echelons of leadership, bringing gender equality to the decision-making and market success of organizations and businesses? As many researchers point out, the answer may be a “pipeline” problem—the number of qualified women available in all industries is limited, and many opt out of the workforce before leadership is attainable.

So why are women disproportionately spread throughout the workforce, and why are they leaving in higher numbers than men? What are the modern barriers, overt or hidden, that are keeping them from being seen as equal to their male counterparts?

Over the next few lessons, we’ll answer that question and more, including:

The current landscape of women in leadership
The evolution of women in the workforce
The unique obstacles facing women
Gender stereotypes
How to support strong female leaders
The power of female authenticity in the workplace
How to avoid burnout
Communication and negotiation for women
And more...

A Few Important Notes

Before we get into the above, a few notes on what this course is and isn’t:

This course is not an exploration on whether women should be in the workplace or not, because ultimately, the choice is up to the individual female. It solely seeks to explain the obstacles facing women who have decided to have a career, whether by choice or necessity.

It focuses on individuals who identify as a woman. It doesn’t attempt to explore non-binary gender issues in the workplace, as that would be a separate and complex discussion.

It isn’t meant to implicate modern-day men, who aren’t personally responsible for 100 years of U.S. corporate history and economic development and any lingering gender stereotypes. On the contrary, most males we’ve encountered are genuinely curious about how to make the workplace more equal for their female counterparts—they’re just not sure how or even what the exact issues might be. For that reason, we prefer to avoid language like “patriarchy,” “male privilege,” or “man-splaining.”

Finally, this course isn’t meant to imply that men don’t face their own biases or stereotypes in the workplace. This course simply focuses on women, especially as it relates to female leadership development.

As Pat would point out, the men aren’t villains, and women aren’t victims in the story of workplace equality. In her 40-year pursuit for gender equity in her field, she would simply say, “We don’t want special treatment. We just want to have an equal playing field.”

With all that in mind, let’s dive in!

Click to download the Workbook PDF for this course.

Pat Summitt Championing Women In Leadership Workbook.pdf
1.6 MB

Sources:

Unless otherwise noted, all quotes taken from Reach for the Summitt, by Pat Summitt (with Sally Jenkins). Three Rivers Press, Crown Publishing Group. 1998. New York.
U.S. Department of Education. “Sex Discrimination: Overview of the Law.” Washington, D.C. Revised August 2021. Accessed online: https://www2.ed.gov/policy/rights/guid/ocr/sexoverview.html
Title IX, Pat Summitt, and Tennessee's Trailblazers: 50 Years, 50 Stories. Pethel, Mary Ellen. University of Tennessee Press. October 2022.

Lesson 1 of 5
The Current Situation

When Summitt started her career in the 1970s, less than half of women over the age of 16 were working outside the home (43 percent).¹ In today’s workforce, however, women have emerged as a driving force in the global economy. The experiences of women in leadership across various industries are as diverse as they are inspiring, bringing fresh perspectives and new talents to the table.

As the 21st century begins to hit its stride, the contributions of women in the workforce are more important than ever, challenging age-old biases while moving businesses and organizations forward. Yet while great progress has been made over the last 100 years—even the last quarter century—the inclusion of women in the workplace, especially equity among leadership, remains a hotly debated topic. Why? To fully answer that, we have to take a closer look at the status quo.

Lesson 1: Women at Work: The Current Situation

Morgan Vance

When Pat started her career in the 1970s, less than half of women over the age of 16 were working outside the home. In today’s workforce, nearly 50 years later, however, women have emerged as a large part of the U.S. economy.

When it comes to women in the workforce, some may wonder, “What’s the big deal? We’re equal, aren’t we?”

Yes and no.

Women may be equal on paper in certain areas and by certain laws, but a multitude of obstacles still face women trying to succeed in the workforce and advance their career. This includes factors like:

Unequal pay: In her first season, Pat earned a little under $9,000 for her first position as head basketball coach at the University of Tennessee, during a time when many male counterparts were making twice as much.

Unequal representation in certain industries: In Pat’s own field of coaching, today only one-third of all head coaches are women, while two-thirds are men.

Caregiving responsibilities: It’s no secret that working mothers (like Pat) often face additional hurdles. The lack of affordable childcare in addition to domestic duties often forces women to choose between career advancement and family.

Underrepresentation in leadership and gender stereotypes and biases are just a few more ways women lag behind men in advancement opportunities and perceptions in the workforce.

So, what can we do about it? The first step is understanding the current situation and how to navigate the current climate.

What makes things challenge for many female leaders is that many of the complexities of the status quo facing women often feel difficult and hard to prove. After all, it isn’t a standard topic of conversation. Women have learned to persevere in spite of it all. At best…no one talks about it.

That’s what makes the upcoming lessons so valuable! You’ll learn about some of the pitfalls of the current workforce for women and how we got here, shining a light on some of the solutions for women and would-be leaders in their careers.

As a female leader and working mother, I’ve found it’s best to be up front and transparent about our needs so we can perform our roles to the best of our abilities. When one area falls out of balance, other parts of our life do as well, and it impacts our work. What I’ve found helpful during my career is having strong female mentors to help advise on difficult situations while supporting and encouraging my growth as a leader.

In this course you’ll learn to face challenges with strength and resilience like Pat did and specifically how to view some of the unique obstacles facing women in their fields.

Lesson 2 of 5
But We're Equal, Aren't We?

But We're Equal, Aren't We?

Yes…and no. Many people look at three main statistics to prove how far women have come:

Women now make up roughly half the U.S. workforce.
Anti-sexual harassment and discrimination policies are now federal law.
Maternity leave is now required by law, even if unpaid.

“So, what’s the big deal?” you might ask. “Why are women still complaining that things are unequal, or that they face obstacles?”

The truth is, there are several well-documented inequities that continue to face female workers in the modern workplace.

Unequal Pay

The first is the pay gap, which hasn’t changed all that much in the last decade. While the Equal Pay Act of 1963 made it illegal to blatantly discriminate based on gender (up until then, employers could openly advertise “men’s positions” at a higher rate than “women’s positions” in the local advertisements), there is still a way to go to achieve true equity in compensation. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, women continue to earn 82 percent of what their male counterparts make in similar positions.²

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, women continue to earn 82 percent of what their male counterparts make in similar positions.

Unequal Representation in Certain Fields

The second is the underrepresentation of women in certain fields—mostly the more technical and often higher-paying STEM fields (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math). This is coupled with an overrepresentation of women in traditionally lower-paying fields like teaching or administrative assistants.

Even among fields where women are firmly represented overall, like healthcare, disparities exist between men and women in higher-educated roles. For example, dental hygienists are 93 percent female,³ compared to only comprising a little over 37% of dentists. And 86 percent of nurses are female,⁴ compared to only making up 37% of the physician workforce. Even in Pat’s own field of coaching, today only one-third of all head coaches are women, while two-thirds are men.⁵ Similarly, men make up 83 percent of all sports announcers, and only 17 percent of these roles are filled by women.⁶

The imbalance of women across the workforce as a whole leads to its own set of obstacles and challenges. You could argue that it’s hard for women to feel equal when they’re always a minority in an occupation that is two-thirds male. And it’s tough to choose a male-dominated career when women aren’t encouraged to choose a career field that gender biases make unappealing at a young age (e.g., being in the math club is “unfeminine” or makes you “intimidating”).

The imbalance of women across the workforce as a whole leads to its own set of obstacles and challenges.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 3 of 5
Gender Stereotypes and Biases

Caregiving Responsibilities

Next is the challenge women have traditionally faced around caregiving duties. First, balancing the time off women need for maternity and post-maternity, often with multiple children. The Pregnancy and Discrimination Act of 1978 made it illegal to discriminate against female employees due to pregnancy or childbirth, and the 1993 federal Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) now offers women 12 weeks of maternity leave with job protection (although whether the leave is paid or not is still up to the employer). Women have historically been the main caregiver for said children as they grow through the elementary years, often making them the first responder for sick days, sleepless nights, field trips, evening meals, extracurriculars, etc.

In spite of 21st century efforts to balance this caregiving load, modern studies show women work 4 hours and 25 minutes each day domestically outside of their corporate careers, compared with men putting in 1 hour and 23 minutes.⁷ This makes women much more of a candidate for burnout than their male counterparts. All this is coupled with the fact that childcare in most states is expensive, making many women question whether returning to work is advantageous financially.

There’s also what’s known as the motherhood penalty. Studies by organizations such as the Harvard Business Review have shown as much as an $11,000 gap in what mothers were offered in starting salary, as opposed to their childless female counterparts, which just widens the 82 percent female pay gap.⁸

According to one study, women work 4 hours and 25 minutes each day domestically outside of their corporate careers, compared with men putting in 1 hour and 23 minutes.

Underrepresentation in Leadership

One of the more complex issues in today’s workforce is the overall underrepresentation of women in leadership positions. An annual study on women in the workforce by McKinsey and LeanIn found that among C-Suite leadership today, 75 percent are male, while only 25 percent are female. Factoring in racial minorities, only 1 out of 20 C-Suite leaders are women of color.⁹

The reasons for this leadership gap, which we’ll get to in upcoming lessons, are complex. Many have traditionally pointed to childbearing and caregiving as a reason women opt out of the workplace before they reach leadership levels, but 21st century research has started to add more variables to the mix.

Gender Stereotypes and Biases

This brings us to the world of gender biases. Unconscious gender bias still remains a considerable barrier to women’s career advancement, but can be difficult to pinpoint and address.

For example, studies have shown characteristics such as “assertiveness,” “confidence” and “out-spokenness” tended to be viewed positively in men, while carrying a negative connotation among women. Another example, might be a job posting for an administrative assistant requesting candidates be “always smiling and pleasant” or that a leadership position require someone who is “no-nonsense,” “leads with a firm hand,” or is “willing to speak up” (with women displaying such assertive attributes being negatively stereotyped at a higher rate than men).

Unconscious gender bias still remains a considerable barrier to women’s career advancement, but can be difficult to pinpoint and address.

Cracking the Glass and Closing the Gap

In short, we haven’t reached true equality in the modern workplace simply by throwing women into the mix and shuffling the card deck. And the points above haven’t gone unnoticed among top employers and organizations committed to championing women in the workforce and promoting strong female leaders.

So what can employers do specifically to encourage female leadership and support women on their own teams? We’ll discuss that and more in the upcoming lessons.

Lesson 5 of 5
Personal Reflections

Refer to your workbook for the following questions and reflections.

1
Take a minute to reflect on your own thoughts around women in the workplace. How have you viewed equality for women in the workforce in the past?

On a scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being “not equal” and 10 being “totally equal,” how close do you think we are to equality currently? There is no right or wrong answer. This is just a reflective exercise to get you to think about your own perceptions.

2
What are the biggest obstacles women face in your own organization? Why do you think this is?

3
Are there any unique obstacles to female leadership in your organization?

4
If you are a woman, which of these (if any) have you experienced before:

Unequal pay
Unequal representation in certain fields
Caregiving/motherhood penalties
Underrepresentation in leadership
Gender stereotypes and biases

5
If you are male, which of the above inequalities is the most surprising to you, and which one are you the most curious to know more about?

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 2: How Did We Get Here? 
 
Christina Reckard 
So, when it comes to women in the workplace, “How did we get here?”  
That is an excellent question. The last century has seen a remarkable transformation in the 
role of women in the U.S. workforce.  
At the beginning of the 20th century, the role of women in the workforce was largely 
restricted to a handful of careers such as teaching, nursing, and domestic work. Social 
expectations and legal rules limited women’s employment opportunities and rights.  
World War I in the early 20th century marked a pivotal moment. With millions of men 
deployed overseas, women began filling roles in factories, offices, and other industries 
essential to the war effort. This shift demonstrated women's capabilities beyond 
traditional domestic roles and laid the groundwork for change. 
The passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920 granted women the right to vote, symbolizing 
greater political and social empowerment. Women increasingly entered the workforce, 
particularly in clerical positions, thanks to the expanding economy and technological 
advancements like the typewriter. 
However, the Great Depression of the 1930s brought severe economic hardship, leading to 
widespread job losses. During this period, societal attitudes hardened against working 
women, especially married women, who were often seen as taking jobs from men and time 
from their children. Despite this, many women continued to work out of necessity – often in 
poorly paid positions. 
World War II was another turning point. As millions of men went to war, women once again 
stepped into roles traditionally held by men. The image of "Rosie the Riveter" became 
iconic, symbolizing women's contributions to the war effort as factory workers, engineers, 
and in other critical positions. By 1945, women made up nearly 37% of the U.S. workforce, 
a 10% jump in just five years. 
The 1950s saw a return to traditional gender roles, but the 60s brought significant social 
upheaval and the official rise of the women's liberation movement. This decade was 
marked by landmark legislation aimed at reducing gender discrimination, such as The 
Equal Pay Act of 1963 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibited employment 
discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or nationality.

The 1970s – around the time Pat herself first entered the workforce – saw a substantial 
increase in the number of women entering higher education and the professional job 
market. The 1980s continued this trend, with women increasingly entering more advanced 
professions such as law, medicine, and business. However, this decade also highlighted 
ongoing challenges. The term "glass ceiling" was coined – an invisible barrier preventing 
women from reaching top executive positions – and it became a prominent issue. Women 
also faced challenges related to work-life balance as they juggled professional 
responsibilities and family duties. 
The 1990s, around when Pat hit her stride as a coach, was marked by significant growth in 
women's professional achievements. Women began to occupy prominent leadership roles 
in politics, sports, and the decade also saw the implementation of family-friendly policies 
in many workplaces like The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) of 1993. 
Yet in spite of all of this growth, a myriad of stereotypes and biases still plagued women in 
the workforce. While women in were catching up educationally and legally, the old 
attitudes and traditions of corporate America were slow to adjust. The perception of what 
was a “woman’s work” and what was “male work” still persisted. Were women just as 
ambitious as men? Did they have the necessary leadership skills? 
And that brings us to where we are today, examining more of the landscape of the modern 
workplace and the obstacles facing female leaders. As we look to the future, continued 
advocacy, policy changes, and cultural shifts are necessary to ensure women can fully and 
equally participate in and benefit from the workforce. 
Let’s learn more!

Lesson 2 of 8
It [Was] a Man's World

As the familiar song says, it truly was a “man’s world” at the beginning of the last century. In the early 20th century, only 20 percent of women in the U.S. worked outside the home. Secondary education was scarce for everyone in those days, and nearly nonexistent for women. Add to this the facts that women were less likely to do manual labor and that it was socially taboo for married women to work (only 5 percent of married women were gainfully employed).

By 1930, the percentage had grown to 50 percent of single women and 12 percent of married women working outside the home. Forty years later, the number had only slightly climbed to 50 percent of single women and 40 percent of married women. By 1990, however, 74 percent of women had entered the workforce (compared with 93 percent of men). An almost 20 percent gap still persisted, but finally—a mere 30 years ago—women finally entered the workforce in their own right.¹

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in the early 20th century only 20 percent of women in the U.S. worked outside the home.

The point is, the entrance of a majority of U.S. women into the workforce is a relatively new one, having come about largely within the last 50 years. Until then, the overall workforce structure, including rules, social norms, and expectations, had understandably been created by men. This yielded a climate for disparities like the pay gap, caregiving, and other gender biases to emerge and create the landscape we have today.

While college became more of an expectation for men in the 1950s through the 1970s, it wasn’t yet for women, giving them a distinct educational disadvantage when entering the workforce. Furthermore, when women began to enter the workforce en masse toward the second half of the 20th century, their involvement tended towards noncorporate roles, like waitress, secretary, receptionist, bookkeeper, or school teacher.

body_blocks.text: It [Was] a Man's World

As the familiar song says, it truly was a “man’s world” at the beginning of the last century. In the early 20th century, only 20 percent of women in the U.S. worked outside the home. Secondary education was scarce for everyone in those days, and nearly nonexistent for women. Add to this the facts that women were less likely to do manual labor and that it was socially taboo for married women to work (only 5 percent of married women were gainfully employed).

By 1930, the percentage had grown to 50 percent of single women and 12 percent of married women working outside the home. Forty years later, the number had only slightly climbed to 50 percent of single women and 40 percent of married women. By 1990, however, 74 percent of women had entered the workforce (compared with 93 percent of men). An almost 20 percent gap still persisted, but finally—a mere 30 years ago—women finally entered the workforce in their own right.¹
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in the early 20th century only 20 percent of women in the U.S. worked outside the home.

The point is, the entrance of a majority of U.S. women into the workforce is a relatively new one, having come about largely within the last 50 years. Until then, the overall workforce structure, including rules, social norms, and expectations, had understandably been created by men. This yielded a climate for disparities like the pay gap, caregiving, and other gender biases to emerge and create the landscape we have today.

While college became more of an expectation for men in the 1950s through the 1970s, it wasn’t yet for women, giving them a distinct educational disadvantage when entering the workforce. Furthermore, when women began to enter the workforce en masse toward the second half of the 20th century, their involvement tended towards noncorporate roles, like waitress, secretary, receptionist, bookkeeper, or school teacher.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 8
The Present State

2020-Present Day

Fast forward to the present. Higher education for women is no longer an issue—in fact, as of 2019, female college graduates began to outnumber men.² However, many of the traditional issues facing women in the workforce remain due to persistent biases, some of them including:

Women are less qualified than men.
Women are less committed to their careers than men.
Women aren’t as ambitious as men.
Women weren’t designed to do certain jobs, especially in the areas of math and sciences or manual labor.
Women lack inherent leadership qualities such as assertiveness, negotiation, or decision-making skills.

As mentioned, women are relatively new to the workplace. They are new players in a game that has been historically male-dominated, meaning the rules and behavioral rewards are largely established by men. For example, leadership characteristics such as assertiveness and drive are seen as positive qualities in men, but looked on as unfeminine in women, or the fact that the traditionally set U.S. corporate office hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. don’t favor employees who have to pick children up from school. And females aren’t the only players who have workplace culture stacked against them, as there were little traces of minorities or immigrants in corporate America up until the mid-20th century.

Let’s take a closer look at some of these specific biases.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 6 of 8
Biases About the Biases

As mentioned earlier, one of the most long-standing biases is around caregiving and family-rearing. While it’s illegal to discriminate outright, many women carry the silent toll of being working mothers long past their childbearing years.

Myth
Women are less committed to their careers.

Reality
Women have historically displayed a great deal of commitment to their careers, going around, under, and through obstacles like childbearing, prejudices, and the increasing demands of work-life balance.

Myth
Women are less ambitious than men.

Reality
Male-female ambition starts off largely equal.

Myth
Women weren’t designed to do certain jobs.

Reality
Career stereotypes have pushed the perception of acceptable work for women out of bounds farther than any documented biological disadvantages would suggest.

Myth
Women lack corporate qualities.

Reality
The qualities of corporate America were largely decided by males, the founders of U.S. corporate culture. Females do exhibit these qualities, but when they do, they may face more stereotypes and biases.

Many of the women who do choose to remain in the workforce rise before the sun comes up just to be able to juggle childcare duties, transport kids to school, work a job, pick the kids up from school or extracurriculars, help with meal preparation and homework, only to get up and do it all over again. Add to this the stigma of staying home, getting a nanny or au pair (in addition to the financial cost), and women seem to be “darned if they do, darned if they don’t” on this one.

Behind the stereotype of “Women are less committed to their careers” are the biases of “Women would rather be stay-at-home moms” or “Women don’t want to work outside the home.” While this may be true for some women, it certainly isn’t true for all women. Further complicating matters is that some women who have resigned themselves to stay at home, do so because of childcare complications or other logistics—not due to a lack of enthusiasm for an outside career.

Perhaps most notable in all this is the fact that, despite all the progress of the modern century, the division of labor in most U.S. households still remains largely unequal.

“Looking back on it, I don't think anyone in the family worked as hard as my mother or got less credit for it.” — Pat Summitt

“As I got older I understood that women had to fight for respect in more ways than one,” Pat once recalled.

“It seemed to me that my mother worked as hard or harder than my father and my brothers. One impression has stayed with me all these years: at the dinner table when my brothers would finish their tea, they'd hold up their empty glasses and rattle them. They wouldn't say a word; they [would] just lift their glasses and shake them until my mother served them. It was their way of saying, “Come fill my glass.” I can still see those hands holding up those glasses rattling the ice. My mother waited on them and I thought, that isn't right.”

“My dad and my brothers wouldn't do any work around the house, whether it was to make their beds or work in the garden or mow the lawn. They just worked the farm—that was it. But my mother did the cooking and the ironing and the cleaning and the milking and worked the garden and worked in the store and in the dry cleaners. When my dad got into the house-building business, my mother was the one who painted the houses and laid the carpets. Looking back on it, I don't think anyone in the family worked as hard as my mother or got less credit for it.”³

A recent study of more than 200,000 respondents found that women start their careers with just as much ambition as men or more.⁴ That ambition, however, is either encouraged or sabotaged by the opportunities and workplace interactions women face over time. Add to this that women’s ambition has historically been viewed as abnormal, unfeminine, or socially unpopular in previous decades, and it’s a perfect storm for blaming women for being underachievers.

Reality: Women start their careers with just as much ambition as men or more.

While the list of acceptable careers for women has been shattered long ago (thank goodness!), a nagging stereotype still chases women who, even today, choose to be trailblazers in a particular industry: Some jobs weren’t meant for women.

This is usually a result of three categories:

Pat herself was definitely a minority in her field during the peak of her career.

When women are underrepresented, they find themselves in a minority landscape. When they exist in a field but hold subordinate positions, it perpetuates the stereotype that male employees are better leaders/decision-makers.

When women are overrepresented in a field, stereotypes are formed as to what’s woman’s work and what’s man’s work (such as the incorrect but long-held jokes about male nurses or female truck drivers). This is what makes overall workplace equality so important!

The truth is, bias around women lacking corporate qualities isn’t backed by data inasmuch as dogma. As mentioned in previous lessons, when women are graded on leadership qualities, the women generally poll equal in positive feedback to the men. Adding to this is another layer we’ll call the perception gap. There is discussion over whether women genuinely inherently lack certain traits in the workplace, or if it’s the old case of natural vs. learned.

For example, the phrase, “women don’t speak up as much as men,” must mean they are shy, timid, and insecure, right? Well, it depends.

You could also look at it this way:

Pat certainly wasn’t. In short, it’s getting harder and harder to differentiate the chicken from the egg when it comes to decades of workplace stereotypes.

Understanding how we got here helps us understand the landscape of the modern workplace and some of the obstacles female leaders face when navigating the terrain. How do these stereotypes and biases play out in the workplace exactly? Usually in the area of microaggressions, which we’ll discuss in an upcoming lesson.

Women are underrepresented in a field, such as the math and sciences, transportation industry, or roles involving manual labor.
Women do exist in a field, but hold subordinate positions (e.g., a dentist’s office where two dentists are male and 10 dental hygienists are women, or the two airline pilots are male and the flight attendants are mostly women).
Women are overrepresented in a field (e.g., teaching, speech pathology, etc.), sometimes casually dubbed the “pink collar” fields.

Women are more scrutinized in meetings. People who are more scrutinized speak up less.
Women are more likely to have their authority challenged and are frequently talked over in meetings. People who are more likely to be questioned or talked over may naturally hold back for a fear of not getting it just right.
Women are soft-spoken. But anytime women display a so-called unfeminine characteristic, they typically pay the price for it, whether directly or indirectly, raising the question of whether women are any less forthright than men in their natural state.

Lesson 1 of 8
Roadblocks for Women in Leadership

Now that we’ve discussed some of the overall obstacles to women in the workforce, let’s take a look at specific obstacles to women in leadership. If you’re like many organizations, you may have plenty of women leaders at your company. You may even have women at the senior leadership level and think, Hey, two out of our eight board members are women…not bad. The problem is, despite decades of being in the workforce, women are having a much harder time reaching and staying at the upper echelons of leadership, through no lack of qualifications of their own.

According to the LeanIn.org and McKinsey annual survey, 75 percent of C-Suite roles are held by men, compared to 25 percent of women. As the C-Suite generally guides the direction of the business, this means many organizations are being helmed by a female voice of 25 percent, despite women representing half of the actual workforce. When you factor in underrepresentation in certain fields, like technology, this number becomes even more slim at the top. Add diversity to the mix and the situation is even more dire—of that 25 percent, only 1 in 20 is a woman of color.¹

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 3: Roadblocks for Women in Leadership 
 
Joan Cronan 
If you’re like many organizations, you may have several women in key leadership positions 
at your company. You might look at the legacy of female board members or C-suite 
executives and think, “Hey, we’re getting there!”  
The problem is, despite decades of being in the workforce, women are having a much 
harder time reaching and staying at the upper levels of leadership.  
And the problem trickles down to C-Suites and corporate boardrooms all over America. 
Again…why? 
Well, experts have a variety of theories. One is a “leak in the pipeline.” One is expectations 
around traditional gender roles. Women often face stereotypes that label them as “less 
competent” or less suited for leadership roles compared to men – hence the old adage of 
“having to work twice as hard to be thought of as half as good.” 
You know I remember so many times myself as an AD would be sitting in a boardroom and I 
would be the only female in the room. Somebody said, “How do you do it?”  
“One, I was more prepared. Two I wanted to fit in and be part of the discussion, so I just 
didn’t hide at the back of the room.”  
I remember one time we were negotiating television contracts – big money contracts. I was 
the only woman in the room, and a gentleman comes in to do his presentation, and he 
says, “You guys...and Joan.” And then he goes on to give his proposal. I took a deep breath, 
and I said to myself, “OK.”  
Then, a second gentleman comes in the room and says, “You guys...and Joan.” That’s 
when I called timeout, and I said, “Let’s talk about this.”  
I said, “I am here to make a decision just like everybody else. It never bothered me to be 
called ‘you guys’ in a setting like this. I never coached ‘woman-to-woman’ defense, I 
always coached man-to-man. So be sure you don’t try to point out the difference in men 
and women sitting around the board table because you’re all there to do the same job.”  
To be seen as competent, women need to project confidence and assertiveness, but are 
often stereotyped as “unfeminine” or “aggressive” when they do, stereotypes their male 
counterparts don’t encounter when advancing their own careers.

Some include organizational barriers – ingrained practices and policies that inadvertently 
favor men, such as 8-5:00 working hours that weren’t designed for parents who had to pick 
up children from school. Or male-dominated industries where women are constantly 
having to perform as minority players. 
Then, there’s a lack of mentorship – a lack of other females who have been in leadership 
positions to show the way, leaving women to be groomed by men who might have had an 
entirely different set of career struggles than they have along the way. 
In the upcoming lesson, we’ll take a look at some of these examples and more.

Lesson 2 of 8
A Leak in the Pipeline

If women are opting out at a slightly higher rate than men, this begs the question: Why? Historically, many analysts would have pointed to childbearing as the natural culprit. But according to several surveys, surprisingly, the issue isn’t entirely due to childbearing.

A study by Harvard Business Review, for example, found that high-achieving women pursued their careers an average of 11 years, and 60 percent worked well past the birth of their second child.² Most fascinating is the number of women who continue working well beyond their child bearing years and still drop out.

We’ve already discussed gender biases and the isolation of being the only one in the room in certain fields. Like their non-managerial counterparts, future female leaders are often paddling upstream from the start. Then there’s the factor of hidden work, specifically:

Women work more at home after their corporate hours are through.

Women often work more at work, shouldering special projects and initiatives that don’t directly contribute to the bottom line, but contribute to the overall work culture or environment.

Studies show that women are looking for more flexibility in the post-COVID world, and work-life balance is a big reason more women are leaving corporations than men. While both sexes appreciate a healthy work-life balance, women typically have more work at home, making this more of a need than a want.

Lesson 4 of 8
Death by 1,000 Cuts

So what does all this look like in reality? Many women describe their decision to leave the workplace not as something that happened in one fell swoop, but rather death by a thousand cuts. Take these fictitious examples of three women: Lei, Allison, and Felicia.

Scenario 1
Lei

Lei is an associate director of quality assurance in IT. She has held her position for about a year and a half and is finding that she’s questioned more than the male mentor who trained her. She was even asked to provide a weekly report of what she’s working on.

In four of her five standing meetings, she’s the only woman in the room. In one of these meetings, a recurring lunch meeting, the team frequently volunteers her to go pick up lunch—“because no one else knows how to order it the right way,” they say. She begins to wonder if her personal brand is becoming “sandwiches.”

When Lei asks about a raise a year into her role, she’s told raises will be scarce this year and she should be grateful for what she has. Lei is puzzled because her male counterparts didn’t seem to have issues getting a raise six months earlier. She debates taking it up, but worried she might look like she’s playing the minority flag, or worse, complaining. After all, she might not have all the facts, and discussing salary is taboo. Lei continues to work, but feels like a sparrow in a hen house.

Scenario 2
Allison

Then there’s Allison, a newly hired VP of product with 20 years of experience at an organization with all its VPs at the senior board level: the VP of finance, VP of marketing, VP of human resources, VP of operations and VP of creative.

The company hires two new male VPs, the VP of technology and the VP of sales at the same time they hire Allison. The two new VPs are placed on the board immediately, but Allison is told she needs to “prove her worth” before she can be considered. Right away this puts Allison at a disadvantage—because the VPs of sales, technology, and marketing, whom she needs to collaborate with regularly, are all on the board and she isn’t.

In addition, whenever she tries to present the new product line, the male VP of Sales constantly interrupts Allison, making it difficult to get through her slideshow. When Allison mentions this to her leader, she’s told she’s “probably being too sensitive about it.”

The company is preparing for a major conference, with Allison’s team putting in extra work in the office to revamp conference room space. While her male counterparts stay till 7 p.m., Allison has to leave at 5 p.m. to pick her kids up from the after-school program, driving back to work at 6:30 p.m.and working until 8:30 p.m.

The conference networking event is a golfing tournament hosted by the company’s CEO, followed by a bourbon tasting at a local distillery. Allison attends, but is relegated to the sidelines, as she doesn’t know how to play golf and doesn’t particularly care for bourbon. While Allison went to school to be a product manager and loves her job, she wonders if she’s ever going to fit in at this new company and secretly dreams of going into real estate, like her sister-in-law.

Scenario 3
Felicia

Lastly, there’s Felicia, a 35-year-old associate creative manager with a degree from a highly respected private college. Felicia worked for eight years before having her first child. Eager to continue her career, she puts the child in daycare at $800 per month. Two years later when she has her second child, she puts that child in daycare as well, for a total of $1600 a month. Felicia’s bi-monthly take-home pay is only $2,100 per paycheck.

Her company is bought out, and Felicia is hopeful for more flexibility with the new leadership, but they reduce the number of work-from-home days from eight days a month to two. A male counterpart from another division is then promoted to creative director over Felicia, in spite of having four and a half less years of experience. Felicia is crushed. She then learns that her first child has been diagnosed with hearing loss and will require special attention and additional therapy appointments. She decides to opt out of the corporate workforce and become a freelancer, hoping to replace 60 to 70 percent of her corporate paycheck, but on her own terms.

Summary

While these are fictitious examples, they represent the myriad of nuanced challenges women face in their careers. Have you ever known someone like a Lei, Allison, or Felicia?

Lesson 5 of 8
The Confidence Gap

Because of having to face more resistance in their careers than men, women sometimes run into the “confidence gap.” While some might attribute this lack of confidence to their sensitive and perceptive social nature (aka picking up on nonverbal clues and slights others might miss), studies point out that it may also be learned due to an accumulation of years of gender biases in the workplace.

PERSON A
Take Person A, whose input in meetings is often received well and rarely questioned.

PERSON B
Take Person B, who is interrupted twice as much as Person A and often has their statements questioned in front of everyone, in addition to being lectured (however innocently) on basic principles. Through no lack of confidence, Person B would naturally learn to be more hesitant in speaking up and would question their capabilities, especially if everyone else in the room accepts this behavior as normal.

To add insult to injury, Person B is told they need to “speak up more” to be thought of as leadership material.

The same goes for assertiveness: Person A is socially rewarded for their candor, frankness, and overall drive. Yet when Person B exhibits the same characteristics, they are told they sound bossy or aggressive.

If you’ve always been in the role of Person A, it may be hard to identify the life of Person B, yet these are the types of interactions women repeatedly observe and report.

Because of having to face more resistance in their careers than men, women sometimes run into the “confidence gap.”

Lesson 6 of 8
The Leadership Trap

The Leadership Trap: He’s a Baller, She’s Scary.

This leads us to one of the next hurdles for women, the “leadership trap.” When it comes to being potential candidates for leadership, oftentimes women report:

Having to be assertive enough to be thought of as a leader, yet when exhibiting assertive qualities, you run the risk of being stereotyped as bossy.

Being a team player, only to find you’re seen as too much of a team player to be thought of as a leader.

Taking advantage of work-life balance policies to achieve caregiving needs, only to be labeled as not as committed.

Being told you are greedy or unrealistic when trying to negotiate salary, despite a 12 percent pay gap, and the fact that men negotiate salary more often than women.

Attempting to be likable, but not too likable, or they’ll think you’re not leadership material.

On top of it all, there exists a smaller margin of error for women. Men in leadership roles are historically forgiven for domineering personalities and social faux pas as long as they get the job done (even being praised as a good leader in spite of it all), whereas women are penalized for similar behavior.

On top of it all, there exists a smaller margin of error for women.

So, given all the above, what can an organization do to support and nurture strong female leaders at their organization? The good news is, the answer may not be as hard as you think. We’ll discuss that specifically in upcoming lessons.

Remembering Pat: Pat’s Legacy 
 
 
Sue Nokes 
 
Pat Summitt was probably the most incredible woman or person I ever met. Pat Summitt 
was everything you ever dreamed she would be and thought a role model or an example 
should be.  
 
She tried to live it every day to the fullness of who she was. She was a great mother. She 
was a great wife. She was a great leader. She was a wonderful friend, and she was as 
competitive as heck, but she had such integrity and you would have never outworked her. I 
mean, she would work you to death, but she never asked you to do anything that she wasn't 
willing to do herself. And again, her integrity and her honesty was just exceptional, and she 
just was everything I hoped she would be.  
 
During my time at T Mobile, I had the great privilege to work with a lot of the NBA players 
and the WNBA players. And I did a lot with Magic Johnson, and Magic Johnson would keep 
saying, “Could you get Pat to come out to LA? Could you get Pat?” They respected her.  She 
was so respected in the industry, in the profession and in the game. That it was amazing to 
me to see.  
 
The other thing I would tell you, is that Pat readily shared just as she went to others to learn. 
And she's infamous for who she went and learned about their offense or their defense, or 
she was always that student that was always trying to learn and evolve and develop her 
game and her coaching ability and her leadership so that she could deliver better for the 
girls and the girls had more success, whereas most people are afraid and we don't want to 
share because we're afraid they'll use it and then use it against us and they'll get the 
promotion or whatever and we won't. 
 
She wasn't like that at all. She would tell you, she'd say, “Well, here's what I found works. 
Here's what doesn't work. Do this. Don't do that.”  
 
She shared, just as much as she asked others to share with her.

The Glass Cubicle

The first step in making the playing field more even for women was making it legally equal. The second step is making sure women are treated without bias in the workplace—that both sexes are treated without bias for that matter. video.transcript_text:
Lesson 4: The Glass Cubicle: Gender Microaggressions  
 
Patty Hoppenstedt 
 
"You’re very articulate for a woman." 
"You don’t look like an engineer." 
"Who babysits your kids while you’re at work?" 
"I didn't expect you to be so assertive!" 
"You’re the office mom." 
"Why aren’t you smiling?" 
Any of these sound familiar? 
Chances are if you’re a woman that you’ve heard your fair share of these over the years! 
A microaggression is an everyday verbal or behavioral action that communicates subtle, 
negative, messages toward an individual or group.  
These are different than macroaggressions, which is discrimination on a much larger scale. 
This is important, because we often tend to measure the progress towards gender equality 
with the progress in the lane of macroaggressions or large-scale discrimination without 
realizing and addressing the everyday wear and tear microaggressions take on women in 
leadership. 
Microaggressions aren’t exclusive to women – men get them too. 
“Real men don’t cry.” 
“You should know how to fix this.” 
“You know men aren’t good at multitasking.” 
“You’re really sensitive for a guy.” 
“You like to cook? Don’t tell anyone!” 
Did some of these irritate you? The truth is…no one likes microaggressions! 
There are three types of microaggressions – verbal, non-verbal, and institutional.

We’ve covered some examples of verbal. Non-verbal might be something like, looking for 
approval from one gender in a business meeting while ignoring the other gender, or paying 
attention when men are speaking but goofing off while a woman in presenting in a 
conference.  
Again, it goes both ways! 
And this is important, because the daily battle for equality in the workplace is often won or 
lost in the area of microaggressions and how prevalent they are in your own workplace 
culture. 
The first step is being aware of what microaggressions are and how to spot them at work. 
You want to make sure both men and women are aware of what microaggressions are, and 
how not to perpetuate unfair stereotypes with everyday comments or behavior. 
In the upcoming lesson, we’ll discuss more of how to handle microaggressions and steps 
you can take to eliminating them in your workplace.

Lesson 2 of 9
What Is a Microaggression?

The term microaggression refers to everyday verbal, behavioral, or environmental actions that communicate subtle messages toward an individual or groups.

Microaggressions are different from macroaggressions. A macroaggression might look like a female leader being blatantly turned down for a job, denied a promotion, sexually harassed, passed over for an assignment, or paid less than a man despite having the same qualifications. Many of these actions are now illegal, making these biases rarer than in previous decades.

We typically measure society’s progress toward diversity at the macroaggression level, because there are generally more statistics available to measure macroaggressions. But refusing to acknowledge unhealthy microaggressions can be just as damaging to the overall progress of gender equality.

Microaggression refers to everyday verbal, behavioral, or environmental actions that communicate subtle messages toward an individual or groups.

So what exactly are some examples of microaggressions? A few practical examples might include:

Using masculine language or job titles by default, such as using "guys" to refer to everyone instead of “team,” or saying "salesman" instead of "salesperson."

Expecting women to organize the office housekeeping tasks, like planning birthday parties or cleaning the communal kitchen.

Praising a man running late for a meeting due to having to drop off the kids at school for being a good dad, while a female was scolded for tardiness in the same circumstance a week earlier.

Asking a female colleague to take notes or to write notes on a whiteboard, because “she would have the best handwriting.”

Automatically assuming women are weaker in math and science than men and need help.

Explaining something publicly to a woman that she didn’t ask to be enlightened on.

Telling a woman she is too sensitive or overreacting when she raises concerns about discrimination or equality.

Privately making fun of a male colleague for getting emotional in a meeting and tearing up.

Joking about a man’s testosterone levels after he brings homemade banana bread to the office.

Expecting a man to assemble an office bookshelf and then joking that his “man card” is on the line for doing it right.

Expecting the only man in the room to squash a bug.

Assuming a man likes to watch sports and if he doesn’t want to go to a professional sporting event mixer after hours, there’s something wrong with him.

All these behaviors are rooted in stereotypes and microaggressions that arise from gender bias. But it’s important to note, microaggressions aren’t exclusive to women—they can be directed at any group, at any time.

The truth is, no one likes microaggressions! And because they are more subtle, harder to prove, and generally more frequent than macroaggressions, they often fly under the radar.

Oftentimes the people reporting microaggressions are told they’re being too sensitive or can’t take a joke. But it’s not a joke if it makes someone uncomfortable in the workplace— regardless of gender.

Because they are more subtle, harder to prove, and generally more frequent than macroaggressions, microaggressions often fly under the radar.

Lesson 4 of 9
Eliminating Microaggressions

There are several kinds of microaggressions: verbal, nonverbal, and institutional. An example of a nonverbal microaggression might be mimicking a female coworker’s mannerisms to make her look unprofessional. Or seating women in the back of the room in chairs, balancing their work materials in their laps, while allowing men a seat at the board table so they can participate better. An institutional microaggression might be having a cigar night or traditionally male event as a sales reward for high achievers.
It’s important to note that half or more of all microaggressions may be completely unintentional! Many times the colleague who committed the infraction isn’t even aware of it … and would be embarrassed if they were. Left unchecked, however, microaggressions can create a culture that is alienating to the minority gender, and the more normal it becomes, the harder it is to eliminate from an organization’s culture.

There are several kinds of microaggressions: verbal, nonverbal, and institutional.

Verbal
Let’s take a look at some tips for dealing with microaggressions and how to begin to create a gender-neutral environment, starting with verbal microaggressions. A good rule of thumb when it comes to eliminating verbal microaggressions is to flip the script—meaning, if you couldn’t easily say it to both genders, don’t say it to women.
For example:

It’s hard to imagine saying this to a man, as it implies a parent-child-like relationship. The same critique to a man would probably be delivered as “let’s work on your communication,” or “your communication is coming off as forceful, etc.”

"I don't like your tone."

"You should smile more."

A man might get a critique on his presentation, but probably wouldn’t be told it looks too manly. He would get specific feedback like “the PowerPoint fonts are too boxy,” or “you need more graphics,” etc.

"Your presentation is too girly."

"Don't be so emotional."

Avoid terms of endearment.

Avoid terms of endearment (honey, sweetie, darling) the same way you would avoid similar terms for men (like junior or buddy).

Stay away from anything with sexual undertones.

Stay away from anything with sexual undertones, such as commenting on appearance. When in doubt, avoid commenting. The latter merely indicates someone looks professional.  Or “Dig the new haircut!” (acknowledging someone’s drastic new do) instead of “That haircut brings out your eyes” or “You have such pretty hair.”

Don't reference hormones.

Talking in a huddle, stopping abruptly when someone of the opposite gender walks up, excluding them from the conversation.

Job postings listed with gender-biased language like “able to have direct, man-to-man conversations” or “must be pleasant and friendly” or “you’re a sales superman.”

Example 2

Bias seen in the dress code, such as women can have earrings, but men can’t, or men can wear comfortable shoes like sneakers while women must wear heels, etc.

Example 3

The company sends men to sexual harassment training, but not women.

Example 4

Team-building events like hockey games or ax-throwing that lean toward one gender (ask yourself: How might men respond to a pedicure afternoon or jewelry-making class?).

Example 5

Keeping the thermostat on an extreme setting that caters to one gender, such as men in suits or women in short sleeves.

Lesson 6 of 9
Handling Microaggressions

Heading

With a little intentionality, you can take a step toward eliminating unchecked microaggressions from your organization’s culture. Here’s how:

Educate your team thoroughly on what microaggressions are...

...and why they are undesirable (for either sex). Remember, people come from a variety of backgrounds, and you can’t expect modified behavior if you haven’t clarified what the desired behavior is.

When microaggressions occur, call them out and move on.

This is an open-opportunity call-out policy—not just for one gender or just for leaders, etc. Take a quick moment to acknowledge what was said or done (“Aaron, you said ‘guys’ just now, and we happen to have six females in the room.”), then apply gentle correction (“We know what you meant, but next time let’s just say team.”), and move on.

Assume innocent intent, especially on the first few infractions.

Most people aren’t aware of some of the nuances of microaggressions and genuinely didn’t intend to offend. No one needs to be publicly shamed or embarrassed. Just call it out, keep it matter-of-fact, and move on.

We recommend instituting the Rule of Three: If something happens once, assume innocent intent. Someone could be oblivious or just having a bad day. If it happens again, assume the same thing. Someone could be in a rush and not have a filter on their speech. But if it happens three times, it’s hard to argue that there isn’t a pattern developing, and it may warrant a private conversation with the individual.

Over-exaggerating the issue

Politely correct the behavior and move on. It shouldn’t be a showstopper or something the office talks about for days. Try to avoid giving someone an in-depth rebuke in front of other employees. If it warrants further conversation, do it one-on-one away from the rest of the group.

Name-calling.

Avoid saying things like, “That’s a sexist remark,” “You’re behaving like a chauvinist,” or “Were you raised in a barn?”

Excusing certain employees/groups based on age, industry etc.

For example, ignoring microaggressions from a baby boomer because they grew up in a different time or implementing gender-neutral policies at the corporate headquarters, but not the trucking division because there aren’t that many females.

Two-Way Street

Now, aren’t you taking it a little too far?, you may be thinking. In a word, no. A culture war on microaggressions in the workplace has to be just that—for the whole workplace and all genders. It doesn’t matter if “no one in the room was offended.” They weren’t this time, but someone could be next time. And one microaggression or bias usually leads to another.
Remember, microaggressions go both ways! Women don’t want to be volunteered to clean out the office refrigerator because they’re women any more than men want to stand out in a 90-degree parking lot directing traffic at a corporate event just because they’re men. Women don’t want to always write on the whiteboard because “their handwriting probably looks better” any more than men want to always speak in public “because their voice is louder and can be heard better.” Hire a cleaning service. Get a microphone.
There are always ways to be more gender-neutral than you think.

states_text.text: Educate your team thoroughly on what microaggressions are...
...and why they are undesirable (for either sex). Remember, people come from a variety of backgrounds, and you can’t expect modified behavior if you haven’t clarified what the desired behavior is.
When microaggressions occur, call them out and move on.

This is an open-opportunity call-out policy—not just for one gender or just for leaders, etc. Take a quick moment to acknowledge what was said or done (“Aaron, you said ‘guys’ just now, and we happen to have six females in the room.”), then apply gentle correction (“We know what you meant, but next time let’s just say team.”), and move on.
Assume innocent intent, especially on the first few infractions.

Most people aren’t aware of some of the nuances of microaggressions and genuinely didn’t intend to offend. No one needs to be publicly shamed or embarrassed. Just call it out, keep it matter-of-fact, and move on.
Over-exaggerating the issue

Politely correct the behavior and move on. It shouldn’t be a showstopper or something the office talks about for days. Try to avoid giving someone an in-depth rebuke in front of other employees. If it warrants further conversation, do it one-on-one away from the rest of the group.
Name-calling.
Avoid saying things like, “That’s a sexist remark,” “You’re behaving like a chauvinist,” or “Were you raised in a barn?”
Excusing certain employees/groups based on age, industry etc.

For example, ignoring microaggressions from a baby boomer because they grew up in a different time or implementing gender-neutral policies at the corporate headquarters, but not the trucking division because there aren’t that many females.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: With a little intentionality, you can take a step toward eliminating unchecked microaggressions from your organization’s culture. Here’s how:

items.title: Educate your team thoroughly on what microaggressions are...
items.description: ...and why they are undesirable (for either sex). Remember, people come from a variety of backgrounds, and you can’t expect modified behavior if you haven’t clarified what the desired behavior is.

items.title: When microaggressions occur, call them out and move on.
items.description: This is an open-opportunity call-out policy—not just for one gender or just for leaders, etc. Take a quick moment to acknowledge what was said or done (“Aaron, you said ‘guys’ just now, and we happen to have six females in the room.”), then apply gentle correction (“We know what you meant, but next time let’s just say team.”), and move on.

items.title: Assume innocent intent, especially on the first few infractions.
items.description: Most people aren’t aware of some of the nuances of microaggressions and genuinely didn’t intend to offend. No one needs to be publicly shamed or embarrassed. Just call it out, keep it matter-of-fact, and move on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: We recommend instituting the Rule of Three: If something happens once, assume innocent intent. Someone could be oblivious or just having a bad day. If it happens again, assume the same thing. Someone could be in a rush and not have a filter on their speech. But if it happens three times, it’s hard to argue that there isn’t a pattern developing, and it may warrant a private conversation with the individual.

items.title: Over-exaggerating the issue
items.description: Politely correct the behavior and move on. It shouldn’t be a showstopper or something the office talks about for days. Try to avoid giving someone an in-depth rebuke in front of other employees. If it warrants further conversation, do it one-on-one away from the rest of the group.

items.title: Name-calling.
items.description: Avoid saying things like, “That’s a sexist remark,” “You’re behaving like a chauvinist,” or “Were you raised in a barn?”

items.title: Excusing certain employees/groups based on age, industry etc.
items.description: For example, ignoring microaggressions from a baby boomer because they grew up in a different time or implementing gender-neutral policies at the corporate headquarters, but not the trucking division because there aren’t that many females.

items.heading: Two-Way Street
items.paragraph:
Now, aren’t you taking it a little too far?, you may be thinking. In a word, no. A culture war on microaggressions in the workplace has to be just that—for the whole workplace and all genders. It doesn’t matter if “no one in the room was offended.” They weren’t this time, but someone could be next time. And one microaggression or bias usually leads to another.

Remember, microaggressions go both ways! Women don’t want to be volunteered to clean out the office refrigerator because they’re women any more than men want to stand out in a 90-degree parking lot directing traffic at a corporate event just because they’re men. Women don’t want to always write on the whiteboard because “their handwriting probably looks better” any more than men want to always speak in public “because their voice is louder and can be heard better.” Hire a cleaning service. Get a microphone.

There are always ways to be more gender-neutral than you think.

Lesson 1 of 5
The Strength of Female Leadership

Now that we’ve talked about biases and roadblocks for women, let’s talk about their strengths.
While it’s important to avoid automatic biases about either sex, the journey to workplace equality doesn’t mean ignoring some of the unique attributes and characteristics that women typically bring to the workforce.
First, a few ways in which men and women are the same—a myriad of studies show both sexes have similar levels of education, ambition, and drive/work ethic. Yet there are some biological nuances between men and women that employers can use to their advantage when building teams and encouraging female leaders. In other words, being equal doesn’t necessarily mean the same.

Heading

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 5: The Strength of Female Leadership  
 
Alexis Hornbuckle 
OK, we’ve discussed biases and obstacles. Now let’s talk strengths! 
The truth is, if you’re not utilizing the unique strengths of women on your leadership team, 
you’re missing out! While it’s important to avoid biases about either sex, this doesn’t mean 
ignoring some of the unique characteristics and perceptions that women bring to the 
leadership roundtable.  
How many times have you stepped into a man’s office, and it was apparent that no woman 
had ever set foot there. At least, no woman had had a say in the decorating!  By contrast, 
how many times have you visited a woman’s office, and it was obvious no man visited it 
frequently – pastels, flowers, you name it. This is what your leadership team looks like, 
metaphorically speaking, when it’s all one-sided. You need both genders contributing to 
the overall landscape of your leadership team to bring balance. 
While every woman is different, women are traditionally known for: 
• Emotional intelligence 
• Empathy 
• Collaboration 
• Communication 
• Attention to detail 
• Strategic thinking 
• Risk aversion 
• Resilience and adaptability, just to name a few. 
How many times have you had a one-sided hiring committee who picked a job candidate 
and then discovered there were major red flags when they started the job that were 
missed? How many times have you had a team of “idea people” in a room and made a 
decision without thoroughly assessing the details? Have you ever encountered a brilliant 
manager who was a visionary thinker, but couldn’t communicate well? 
Again, leadership teams need balance – both males and females – to bring an equilibrium 
to corporate leadership and decision-making. Each gender has its own strengths and 
weaknesses.

Oprah Winfrey, Ruth Bader Ginsberg, Queen Elizabeth II, Sheryl Sandberg, Mary Kay Ash, 
Melinda Gates – you may be familiar with these names, but there are many more.  
How about, Mary Barra, CEO of General Motors and the first woman to lead a major global 
automaker. Marillyn Hewson, the former CEO of Lockheed Martin, known for her leadership 
in aerospace and defense. Beth Ford, CEO of Land O'Lakes, or Ursula Burns the former 
CEO of Xerox Corporation, and the first African American woman to lead a Fortune 500 
company, just to name a few! 
The reality is women bring a certain depth, strength, and strategic advantage to every 
organization. 
Let’s find out more.
