Lesson 2 of 5
A Balance to the Force

Heading

Other than diversity (and fairness), let’s look at some specific reasons you should want women on your team.
Each gender has its super-skills—or traits that come more naturally to one gender than the other.

Attention to Detail

On the whole, women remember details easily. Biologically, females have a larger hippocampus, which is where the memory part of the brain is stored, allowing them to bring complex bits of detailed information to mind quickly and readily. This can be an invaluable skill in just about any workplace. Women demand perfection and generally hold their work to high standards.

Emotional Intelligence

Traditionally, women excel in the soft skills, meaning they readily pick up on environment, verbal and body language cues (EQ). They have a natural gift for empathy, intuition, and are in tune with the overall dynamic of the team, all of which are key leadership skills. Their capacity to understand and respond to the emotions of others can lead to improved conflict resolution, reduced workplace stress, and increased employee engagement.

Heightened Intuition in Decision-Making

Studies show men often take a fact-based approach to their environment, categorizing and sorting things based on data. Women lead with intuition and feeling, partially because of their heightened social perceptions around communication and conflict. While men tend to sort things into black and white, women often tend to involve more details in their decision-making processes. Why does this matter? For optimal decision-making, you need both—not just facts, but data plus supporting details and EQ.

More Verbally Communicative

Because men compartmentalize things more readily, they often prefer solitude or low-energy distractions after an especially eventful day. The female brain is more active at rest, which is why women tend to want to process things verbally or socially in times of stress. Women are more likely to speak up in the workplace and not bottle things up—if they feel safe doing so—which can be an invaluable  leadership skill.

Risk-Averse, Multi-tasking and Resiliency

Women are often more risk-averse than men. Their caution is an important balance to workplace decisions and long-term planning.
Women often juggle multiple responsibilities in both their personal and professional lives. In a fast-paced work environment, these skills are invaluable for meeting deadlines, managing projects efficiently, and maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Women are also highly adaptable, a key quality in the face of adversity.

Analytical

Women have also been known to excel in the following areas: multitasking, problem-solving, organization, and planning. They are keenly analytical, but in a different way than men—always analyzing personal interplay, like a computer program running in the background of their mind. Female receptors can sometimes be more heightened to hidden body language or communication nuances, allowing them to synthesize and process large amounts of information.

Collaborative

As team members, women often prove to be highly collaborative. They are also more likely to take on unspoken work that contributes to the team dynamic. This is important because a team that is highly skilled but can’t get along is a poorly functioning team. Women realize this, and have a natural tendency to seek conflict resolution. Women often display less ego, as they have less of the innately wired Alpha-male signaling than their testosterone-bearing counterparts. On the contrary, many women feel the need to qualify or soften their statements to make them more humble, and therefore more socially acceptable:
“I could be wrong, but…”
“I just wanted to ask…”
“This may be a dumb question, but…”

They are keenly analytical, but in a different way than men—always analyzing personal interplay, like a computer program running in the background of their mind. Female receptors can sometimes be more heightened to hidden body language or communication nuances, allowing them to synthesize and process large amounts of information.
Collaborative

As team members, women often prove to be highly collaborative. They are also more likely to take on unspoken work that contributes to the team dynamic. This is important because a team that is highly skilled but can’t get along is a poorly functioning team. Women realize this, and have a natural tendency to seek conflict resolution. Women often display less ego, as they have less of the innately wired Alpha-male signaling than their testosterone-bearing counterparts. On the contrary, many women feel the need to qualify or soften their statements to make them more humble, and therefore more socially acceptable:
“I could be wrong, but…”
“I just wanted to ask…”
“This may be a dumb question, but…”

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 5
A Word on Female Strengths

It’s important to note that while there are certain attributes or characteristic patterns that lend themselves more readily to one gender, blatant stereotyping eliminates the uniqueness of each individual and the potential contributions. Just as it would be incorrect to assume all men want to dress up in suits and charge corporate America or spend time in the wild wearing camouflage and a shotgun, it would be incorrect to assume that all women have a higher EQ or are better at multitasking than a man in the next cubicle.

This simply isn’t true. Humans are multi-faceted, and the extent to which an individual displays certain characteristics might lie just as equally with personal development as it does with psychological wiring. Summitt herself, known for skirts and heels on the sidelines, could fix a tractor, mow hay, plow a field, “fire a barn,” and call cows, in addition to being a devoted mother and coaching championship-level NCAA teams.

While experts agree women display patterns of high competence in these areas, they aren’t the only skills women bring to the table. It should be noted that in addition to the characteristics already mentioned, women have been proven to display an equal level of general leadership characteristics to men. For example, according to one study from the Harvard Business Review, which analyzed thousands of 360-degree reviews, women outscored men on 17 of the 19 capabilities that differentiate excellent leaders from average, such as initiative, self-development, speed, being results-driven, integrity, mentorship, motivation, and bold leadership.1

Heading

Therefore, while it’s definitely worth taking note of natural gifts, we don’t prescribe turning these into biases toward females or males in the workplace, as this can cause harm.

Deep Dive: Having Diversity on Your Team

In today’s rapidly evolving business landscape, the importance of diversity cannot be overstated. Among the various dimensions of diversity, women in leadership stand out as an indispensable part of driving innovation, improving decision-making, and creating a more inclusive culture for everyone.
Simply put, the female perspective represents half of society. This is invaluable in many different fields: marketing, product research, advertising, human resources, finances, customer service, etc. You wouldn’t want only the male perspective marketing to the general population, treating patients, or developing groundbreaking research any more than you would want a female only perspective.

Deep Dive: Having Diversity on Your Team 
 
 
Sue Nokes 
 
I think it's important for any organization to build a culture and our ideal culture would be to 
be a place where all people are valued. And that of course has to do with race, creed, color, 
religion. But it also sometimes is making sure that you have representation from the 
markets and the communities that you're trying to serve. 
 
Sometimes we will build a team. I've walked into product development teams that are 50 
guys. And you say, well, where are the phones for the girls? Because they're silver and 
black. There's no pink and girls may want a pink phone.  
 
So what are you doing to understand the markets that you serve and have somebody in the 
room that can tell you a little bit about where they come from and help you understand who 
you're trying to serve and the employees that you're trying to hire to serve those markets so 
that you develop a better product and service and the entire organization wins. 
 
The company wins, the employees win because they're contributing to something they 
believe in and their customers are loving the product.

Remembering Pat: Being a Leader at All Times 
 
 
Alexis Hornbuckle 
 
Coach Summit was a stickler for leadership, teaching it, challenging you as a leader and 
definitely holding you accountable for moments that you weren't. I remember a time when 
Coach Summit was on me about leadership. She was an advocate about leadership and 
how you lead and when you lead, which was all the time. 
 
I didn't think it was all the time. So, I recall in South Carolina at South Carolina as a point 
guard, not performing well, particularly that day. And Pat was on me. About not calling the 
right plays, not communicating well, you know, the little things, attention to detail. And 
when she asked me, actually, she said, “You look like you've never touched a basketball 
day in your life.” 
 
I whipped my head around as a nice young, hardheaded rookie and said, “Well, you 
recruited me.” 
 
That got me all types of time on the bench guys. She basically let me know this is not what 
leadership looks like. I learned that lesson. Took me one time. From then on out, I knew 
how serious she was about communicating, attention to detail, being resilient in tough 
times, and leading, no matter what the circumstances.

Lesson 1 of 7
Climbing With Confidence

Click play to hear the quote above.

Heading

Now it’s time to take a look at some special areas of growth or opportunity for female leaders. We just outlined several of the challenges facing women in the workplace, so don’t let them take you by surprise! As Pat would say, knowing the opposition you are going to face in any situation never hurts. Rather, take things in stride, and learn how to navigate the workplace as it is, even as we all strive for improvement
This is important because when attempting to understand some of the hurdles facing women in leadership, many women get frustrated and simply give up. This may come in the form of career changes, opting out of the workforce, or simply quiet quitting.
A key aspect to thriving in corporate leadership, for both men and women, but especially for women, is attitude. As mentioned in previous lessons, historically, women have lower levels of confidence based on the additional challenges they may face. And the key to boosting that confidence to a healthy level is attitude.

Embrace Challenges as Opportunities

To start, attitude involves viewing challenges not as insurmountable obstacles but as opportunities. Instead of shying away from difficulties, learn to embrace them with curiosity. Setbacks are a natural part of any career and can be viewed as stepping stones rather than stumbling blocks. By reframing challenges as chances to grow, as a woman, you can approach your career with a fresh sense of professionalism and optimism.

Lesson 6: Climbing With Confidence  
 
Nikki Anosike 
Raise your hand if you’ve ever felt out of your depth at work? OK, I see you! I see some men’s 
hands up too! Confidence is a crucial asset for success in any professional environment. 
However, for many women, maintaining and bolstering their confidence can be challenging.  
Why? Well, workplace stereotypes that portray women as less competent, assertive, or capable 
of leadership can undermine anyone’s confidence. The underrepresentation of women in senior 
leadership positions can also erode female confidence. Many times, the culprit is simply our 
own perfectionism and a fear of failure.  
That’s why, in this lesson, you’ll learn how to view challenges as opportunities. You see, our 
interpretation of events significantly influences our reactions and decisions. When faced with a 
difficult situation, we have two primary choices: we can see it as a threat or as a chance to learn 
and grow.  
Viewing challenges as opportunities requires a deliberate shift in mindset. It involves 
recognizing that every setback carries the potential for a valuable lesson, a new skill, or a 
chance to build resilience. Failure is often seen as the opposite of success, but in reality, it is a 
key component of the learning process. Each failure highlights areas for improvement and 
making us better. Pat was a big believer in learning from failure. In the business world, this 
concept is known as "failing forward."  
For individuals like you and me, adopting a “fail-forward” mindset can lead to immense personal 
growth. When we stop fearing failure, we become more willing to step out of our comfort zones 
and take on new challenges. This openness to new experiences can lead to unexpected 
opportunities and achievements that we might have otherwise missed. Challenges also test our 
resilience, the ability to bounce back from adversity. 
Instead of thinking, "Why is this happening to me?" ask, "What can I learn from this?" or "How 
can this situation make me stronger?"

Now it’s time to take a look at some special areas of growth or opportunity for female leaders. We just outlined several of the challenges facing women in the workplace, so don’t let them take you by surprise! As Pat would say, knowing the opposition you are going to face in any situation never hurts. Rather, take things in stride, and learn how to navigate the workplace as it is, even as we all strive for improvement

This is important because when attempting to understand some of the hurdles facing women in leadership, many women get frustrated and simply give up. This may come in the form of career changes, opting out of the workforce, or simply quiet quitting.     

A key aspect to thriving in corporate leadership, for both men and women, but especially for women, is attitude. As mentioned in previous lessons, historically, women have lower levels of confidence based on the additional challenges they may face. And the key to boosting that confidence to a healthy level is attitude.

items.heading: Embrace Challenges as Opportunities
items.paragraph: To start, attitude involves viewing challenges not as insurmountable obstacles but as opportunities. Instead of shying away from difficulties, learn to embrace them with curiosity. Setbacks are a natural part of any career and can be viewed as stepping stones rather than stumbling blocks. By reframing challenges as chances to grow, as a woman, you can approach your career with a fresh sense of professionalism and optimism.

Lesson 2 of 7
Have a Growth Mindset

Heading

The foundation of a positive attitude also begins with adopting a growth mindset. What do we mean by that? A growth mindset is the belief that abilities or intelligence can be developed through hard work. It’s understanding that our careers aren’t a byproduct of our circumstances or predetermined by external factors, but instead depends on our willingness to be challenged and grow. Some individuals may have to work harder to have a growth mindset in certain circumstances than others, but growth at its core is a resource available to everyone.

Pat firmly believed in a growth mindset, so much so that it was a prerequisite of everyone who played under her leadership. She famously said:
"How can you grow, if you never change? Without changing something almost every year, Tennessee never would have won five national championships…And without accepting some pretty dramatic changes in my own life, I wouldn’t be the head coach of the Lady Vols."

"There is nothing wrong with personal or professional growth, as long as you are strong in who you are and don’t lose sight of where you came from. Self-improvement doesn’t mean abandoning your old identity…Today, if someone tells me I’ve changed, I take it as a compliment. The plain fact is, without change, the game of women’s basketball would never have grown, nor I with it."

So what does a "growth mindset" involve? Click on the icons to expand & view.

Viewing Setbacks as Learning Experiences

As mentioned, setbacks are an inevitable part of any journey, but the key lies in how you respond to them. Instead of dwelling on failures, leaders with a growth mindset see setbacks as valuable experiences. Analyze what went wrong, extract lessons, and use the newfound knowledge to pivot and move forward. You can’t grow if you’re not learning, even if that learning sometimes manifests itself as mistakes.

Listening to Criticism

Constructive criticism is one of the most valuable tools for personal growth. The key is knowing how to seek it out and learn from it. Successful women leaders have mastered both. Instead of seeing feedback as a personal attack, strong women leaders view it as an opportunity to refine their skills. They have learned not to run from or avoid criticism, and know when it has helpful intentions behind it.
“The older I get, the more flexible I’d like to be,” Pat said. “Change is a force of nature; the truth is that nothing, good or bad, lasts forever. There will be setbacks, injuries, and adverse circumstances, and the person who deals best with them will win out.”

Setting Goals Regularly and Adapting

One fundamental part of any career is setting career-related goals. Setting goals is essential for growth, but a growth mindset also requires flexibility when going after those goals. This means regularly examining your objectives and taking into account new information and changing circumstances. Think of it as a game plan that has to be continually re-evaluated at the end of each season. Visualize yourself achieving your career goals and imagine the steps it takes to get there.

Surrounding Yourself With a Growth-Minded Community

It’s no secret that the company we keep plays a huge role in shaping our mindset. Surround yourself with individuals who share a growth mindset and encourage personal development. Engage in positive, growth-minded conversations and avoid relationships built on negativity.

Continuous Learning

The most obvious part of a growth mindset is continuous learning and skill development. The professional landscape is constantly changing, and staying ahead requires continual effort. Seek opportunities to enhance your skills, whether through formal education, workshops, or on-the-job training. Embrace a love of lifelong learning, new technologies, and industry trends. This can include formal education like conferences, workshops or online courses, or informal learning like reading and networking.

Committing to an Attitude of Resilience

Women are historically resilient, and the workplace is no exception. Men and women both have to be resilient at work, but often in different ways. Make it your mission to have an attitude of resilience in your career.  This includes positive self-talk, an attitude of gratefulness, and the willingness to pivot when needed.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 4 of 7
Confidence and Self-Talk

Cultivating Confidence
Confidence is a necessary quality for both men and women in leadership. Yet due to the confidence gap, some women may have to work harder than their male counterparts to develop confidence in their careers. So how do we do that?

Recognize Negative Patterns and Challenge Them

The first step is becoming aware of negative thought patterns. Examples of these include:

Seeing situations in black-and-white terms, without acknowledging the gray areas or nuances.

All-or-Nothing Thinking

Expecting the worst possible outcome, even when evidence suggests otherwise.

Catastrophizing

Drawing broad conclusions based on limited evidence, often leading to negative self-assessment.

Overgeneralization

Taking responsibility for events or outcomes that are beyond your control.

Personalization

Focusing solely on the negative aspects of a situation while ignoring the positive elements.

Filtering

Assuming you know what others are thinking, often attributing negative thoughts to them without evidence.

Assumptions

Setting rigid, unrealistic expectations for oneself and others, leading to constant feelings of inadequacy (e.g., “I should have finished that report sooner!”).

"Should" Statements

Heading

Once you’ve learned how to limit negative thought patterns, the next step is replacing the negative thoughts with positive self-talk.

Become a Master of Self-Talk

Pat practiced self-talk with her players, especially in tight, important games. “Our attitude [was] ‘You couldn’t be better prepared. You know exactly what to do. So go do it,’” she recalls.

The power of self-talk is undeniable, influencing our thoughts, emotions, and ultimately, our actions. One key to being a master of positive self-talk is to practice affirmations regularly.

Daily Affirmations

Affirmations are powerful statements that reinforce positive beliefs about oneself. To do this, create a list of affirmations tailored to your professional goals and repeat them regularly. For example:
I am right where I need to be in this moment.
I have enough time to do everything that is important to me.
I am strong, I am powerful, and I have everything I need.
I greet this day with gratitude.
I am more than up to the challenge.
I am at the peak of my career—and the best is yet to come!

Replace "I Can't" with "I Can"

The language we use internally shapes our mindset and influences our actions. Swap limiting phrases like "I can't" with empowering alternatives like "I can" or "I will."
Instead of: “I can’t master pivot tables.”
Reframe: “I will master pivot tables in Excel!”
Instead of: “I can’t lead a meeting that confidently.”
Reframe: “I can lead a meeting that confidently, with some practice.”

Constructive Self-Criticism vs. Destructive Self-Talk

There's a fine line between constructive self-criticism and destructive self-talk. Instead of dwelling on mistakes with statements like, "I always mess up," or “I should have known better,” reframe your self-talk to focus on improvement: "I can learn from this and do better next time."

Celebrate Your Strengths

Women often downplay their achievements or attribute success to external factors. Shift your self-talk by consciously focusing on your strengths and celebrating your accomplishments. (“I know how to rock a speech and can do it again!”) Acknowledge the unique skills, talents, and value you bring to your team.

Surround Yourself With Positive Influences

Finally, the people we surround ourselves with significantly impact our mindset! Seek out positive influences and build a supportive network for your leadership career. Engage with colleagues, mentors, or friends specifically who uplift and encourage you. Share your goals and aspirations with those who genuinely celebrate your successes. By surrounding yourself with positivity, you create an environment that automatically reinforces constructive self-talk and bolsters your confidence.

Click play to hear the quote above.

Deep Dive: The Three Types of Confidence

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

OK, so we all know confidence is important to having success as a leader. But did you know that not all confidence is the same? There are three main types of confidence that you will encounter in your career:

Often characterized as "fake it till you make it,” isn’t all bad – it can be somewhat useful when starting a new challenge or career role. It involves leaning heavily on your past successes to navigate the unfamiliar territory until you can build confidence of your own in that area.

False Confidence

Conditional confidence means confidence that fluctuates based on external outcomes. When things are going well, you’re confident in that area! When things aren’t going well, doubt tends to creep in, and you feel insecure about your abilities. This type of confidence is a trap many people fall into during their careers.

Conditional Confidence

Unconditional confidence is the end goal, where your confidence and overall self-assurance is largely rooted in the things you can control—your habits, effort, and attitude—rather than external factors. This stable, more resilient form of confidence is key to thriving as a leader in your career.

Unconditional Confidence

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Self-Talk and Affirmations 
 
Nikki Anosike 
The second bookend to having confidence is learning to use affirmations and confidence 
anchors. Affirmations are positive, specific statements that help individuals overcome 
negative thoughts and self-sabotage.  
The science behind affirmations lies in their ability to influence our subconscious mind. 
When we consistently repeat positive statements, we create new neural pathways that 
strengthen our positive self-beliefs. This process is known as neuroplasticity, where the 
brain adapts and reorganizes itself by forming new connections. In other words, by 
repeating certain affirmations every day, you can actually rewire your brain to think more 
constructively and have more confidence! 
For example, someone struggling with self-esteem issues might use affirmations like, "I am 
worthy of love and respect, " or "I am capable and confident. " The effectiveness of 
affirmations depends on how they are phrased and used. Here are some key principles to 
consider: 
Be Positive. Fame affirmations in a positive manner. Instead of saying, "I am not a failure, " 
say, "I am successful in almost everything I do. ” 
Be Present. Use the present tense to create a sense of immediacy. Affirmations should 
reflect the present moment, such as, "I am strong and resilient. " 
Be Specific. Tailor affirmations to address specific areas of concern or goals. For instance, 
if you want to boost your public speaking skills, an affirmation could be, "I am working 
every day to being more confident and well- spoken when speaking in public. " 
Be Personal. Make affirmations personal and meaningful to you. They should resonate with 
your values and aspirations, not someone else’s. 
Be Repetitive. Finally, consistency is key! Repeat your affirmations daily, ideally multiple 
times a day, to reinforce the positive messages. 
The goal of an affirmation isn’t to repeat something that is false – for example, if you are 
struggling with a health issue, you wouldn’t say, “I am in perfect health!” You might say 
something like “I am getting better and better every day!” or “I don’t need to feel perfect – I 
have all the energy I need to make this day a great one. ” An affirmation is simply phrased

around the end goal, the part of your mind that you can control, reminding yourself that you 
are making progress. 
For example, when I was a player, I needed to hear I wasn’t alone, so I would always repeat to 
myself “You’re not alone. You’ve got great coaches and teammates that are working towards the 
goal with you.”  
You also want to take advantage of confidence anchors. Confidence anchors are simply visual 
reminders of confident feelings. Maybe it’s a medal from the last time you ran a half-marathon, 
to remind you can do challenging things. Maybe it’s a coffee mug someone gave you the last 
time you crushed a key project that makes you feel like a boss whenever you look at it! Think 
about a time when you felt exceptionally confident and empowered and select a physical object 
or image that you can associate with the positive experience. 
Confidence – and learning how to actively grow your confidence – is key to anyone climbing 
with success, male or female. So, let’s learn more.

items.paragraph:
Cultivating Confidence
Confidence is a necessary quality for both men and women in leadership. Yet due to the confidence gap, some women may have to work harder than their male counterparts to develop confidence in their careers. So how do we do that?

items.heading: Recognize Negative Patterns and Challenge Them
items.paragraph: The first step is becoming aware of negative thought patterns. Examples of these include:

back.description: Seeing situations in black-and-white terms, without acknowledging the gray areas or nuances.
Expecting the worst possible outcome, even when evidence suggests otherwise.
Drawing broad conclusions based on limited evidence, often leading to negative self-assessment.
Taking responsibility for events or outcomes that are beyond your control.
Focusing solely on the negative aspects of a situation while ignoring the positive elements.
Assuming you know what others are thinking, often attributing negative thoughts to them without evidence.
Setting rigid, unrealistic expectations for oneself and others, leading to constant feelings of inadequacy (e.g., “I should have finished that report sooner!”).

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Once you’ve learned how to limit negative thought patterns, the next step is replacing the negative thoughts with positive self-talk.

items.heading: Become a Master of Self-Talk
items.paragraph: Pat practiced self-talk with her players, especially in tight, important games. “Our attitude [was] ‘You couldn’t be better prepared. You know exactly what to do. So go do it,’” she recalls.
The power of self-talk is undeniable, influencing our thoughts, emotions, and ultimately, our actions. One key to being a master of positive self-talk is to practice affirmations regularly.

items.title: Daily Affirmations
items.description:
Affirmations are powerful statements that reinforce positive beliefs about oneself. To do this, create a list of affirmations tailored to your professional goals and repeat them regularly. For example:

 

I am right where I need to be in this moment.

I have enough time to do everything that is important to me.

I am strong, I am powerful, and I have everything I need.

I greet this day with gratitude.

I am more than up to the challenge.

I am at the peak of my career—and the best is yet to come!

items.title: Replace "I Can't" with "I Can"
items.description:
The language we use internally shapes our mindset and influences our actions. Swap limiting phrases like "I can't" with empowering alternatives like "I can" or "I will."

 

Instead of: “I can’t master pivot tables.”

Reframe: “I will master pivot tables in Excel!”

 

Instead of: “I can’t lead a meeting that confidently.”

Reframe: “I can lead a meeting that confidently, with some practice.”

items.title: Constructive Self-Criticism vs. Destructive Self-Talk
items.description: There's a fine line between constructive self-criticism and destructive self-talk. Instead of dwelling on mistakes with statements like, "I always mess up," or “I should have known better,” reframe your self-talk to focus on improvement: "I can learn from this and do better next time."

items.title: Celebrate Your Strengths
items.description: Women often downplay their achievements or attribute success to external factors. Shift your self-talk by consciously focusing on your strengths and celebrating your accomplishments. (“I know how to rock a speech and can do it again!”) Acknowledge the unique skills, talents, and value you bring to your team.

items.heading: Surround Yourself With Positive Influences
items.paragraph: Finally, the people we surround ourselves with significantly impact our mindset! Seek out positive influences and build a supportive network for your leadership career. Engage with colleagues, mentors, or friends specifically who uplift and encourage you. Share your goals and aspirations with those who genuinely celebrate your successes. By surrounding yourself with positivity, you create an environment that automatically reinforces constructive self-talk and bolsters your confidence.

items.heading: Deep Dive: The Three Types of Confidence
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: OK, so we all know confidence is important to having success as a leader. But did you know that not all confidence is the same? There are three main types of confidence that you will encounter in your career:

back.description: Often characterized as "fake it till you make it,” isn’t all bad – it can be somewhat useful when starting a new challenge or career role. It involves leaning heavily on your past successes to navigate the unfamiliar territory until you can build confidence of your own in that area.

Conditional confidence means confidence that fluctuates based on external outcomes. When things are going well, you’re confident in that area! When things aren’t going well, doubt tends to creep in, and you feel insecure about your abilities. This type of confidence is a trap many people fall into during their careers.

Unconditional confidence is the end goal, where your confidence and overall self-assurance is largely rooted in the things you can control—your habits, effort, and attitude—rather than external factors. This stable, more resilient form of confidence is key to thriving as a leader in your career.

Deep Dive: Self-Talk and Affirmations 
 
Nikki Anosike 
The second bookend to having confidence is learning to use affirmations and confidence 
anchors. Affirmations are positive, specific statements that help individuals overcome 
negative thoughts and self-sabotage.  
The science behind affirmations lies in their ability to influence our subconscious mind. 
When we consistently repeat positive statements, we create new neural pathways that 
strengthen our positive self-beliefs. This process is known as neuroplasticity, where the 
brain adapts and reorganizes itself by forming new connections. In other words, by 
repeating certain affirmations every day, you can actually rewire your brain to think more 
constructively and have more confidence! 
For example, someone struggling with self-esteem issues might use affirmations like, "I am 
worthy of love and respect, " or "I am capable and confident. " The effectiveness of 
affirmations depends on how they are phrased and used. Here are some key principles to 
consider: 
Be Positive. Fame affirmations in a positive manner. Instead of saying, "I am not a failure, " 
say, "I am successful in almost everything I do. ” 
Be Present. Use the present tense to create a sense of immediacy. Affirmations should 
reflect the present moment, such as, "I am strong and resilient. " 
Be Specific. Tailor affirmations to address specific areas of concern or goals. For instance, 
if you want to boost your public speaking skills, an affirmation could be, "I am working 
every day to being more confident and well- spoken when speaking in public. " 
Be Personal. Make affirmations personal and meaningful to you. They should resonate with 
your values and aspirations, not someone else’s. 
Be Repetitive. Finally, consistency is key! Repeat your affirmations daily, ideally multiple 
times a day, to reinforce the positive messages. 
The goal of an affirmation isn’t to repeat something that is false – for example, if you are 
struggling with a health issue, you wouldn’t say, “I am in perfect health!” You might say 
something like “I am getting better and better every day!” or “I don’t need to feel perfect – I 
have all the energy I need to make this day a great one. ” An affirmation is simply phrased

around the end goal, the part of your mind that you can control, reminding yourself that you 
are making progress. 
For example, when I was a player, I needed to hear I wasn’t alone, so I would always repeat to 
myself “You’re not alone. You’ve got great coaches and teammates that are working towards the 
goal with you.”  
You also want to take advantage of confidence anchors. Confidence anchors are simply visual 
reminders of confident feelings. Maybe it’s a medal from the last time you ran a half-marathon, 
to remind you can do challenging things. Maybe it’s a coffee mug someone gave you the last 
time you crushed a key project that makes you feel like a boss whenever you look at it! Think 
about a time when you felt exceptionally confident and empowered and select a physical object 
or image that you can associate with the positive experience. 
Confidence – and learning how to actively grow your confidence – is key to anyone climbing 
with success, male or female. So, let’s learn more.

videos.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: The Three Types of Confidence 
 
 
Christina Gradillas 
 
OK, so we’ve talked a little about affirmations and self-talk and the role they play. Now let’s 
talk a little about the three types of confidence.  
 
Knowing about the three types of confidence is important in progressing through your 
career and having belief in yourself.  
 
The first is false confidence. This is being confident you can do something with no evidence 
to back it up. You might call this “fake it till you make it,” and you just sort of hope it works 
out. Maybe you know some people in your own life who are notorious for false confidence – 
they are convinced things will work out, or they can deliver, but with little to base those 
claims on! Some people stay in this phase for a long time, but these are the “talkers,” not 
the “doers” of the world. 
 
False confidence isn’t all bad. The truth is, sometimes you need a little false confidence to 
get yourself started when you’re tackling something new. You may be in a new field or a 
new industry, maybe you’ve taken on a new promotion and you’re doing something you’ve 
never done before. You have no clue what you’re doing. What you want to do in this phase 
is lean on your self-talk and confidence anchors to get you through. These are areas where 
you have succeeded in the past, and you’re leaning on the confidence from that anchor 
and applying it to a new area. 
 
Let’s say you’ve run a marathon before, but your spouse wants you to train to go rock 
climbing with them and you’ve never climbed anything before. Or maybe you’re used to 
leading a large marketing team, but you have a new role in TV and film where you’re now 
managing a production crew. It’s easy to feel a little intimidated when you have to do 
something you haven’t done before, but the proper self-talk can get you through this phase 
as quickly as possible. You don’t want to hang out in this phase for long. 
 
I remember when I was first starting out as a speaker and trainer, and I remember I had no 
clue what I was doing. I was so, so nervous, sweating, you know one of those things. And I 
just remember putting myself in the shoes of my leader for that one hour. I was not 
Christina, I was Dave, and I put on the mask and I put on the face, and I just went out there 
and I just went out there and faked it and it end up being OK, but I was very, very conscious 
in making sure I got through that phase really well. 
 
So, the next kind of confidence is conditional confidence. Conditional confidence is 
attaching your confidence to results.  This is a trap most women fall into. It’s the ups and

downs of confidence. If you have a big day or a big month then your confidence is high. If 
you have a bad week or bad month in terms of your career or results, your confidence is 
low. 
 
If you just crushed a major project or got a big promotion, you’re feeling great. If you’re 
having difficulty with a co-worker or you just got passed over for a role you really wanted, 
your confidence takes a nose-dive. Or, if things are going well at home, you feel like a 
rockstar, as a mom you’re crushing it! If you find things getting out of balance, you’re a “bad 
mom, ” what am I doing? 
 
Sound familiar? Conditional confidence causes a lot of stress and can cause you to 
question everything. 
 
You want to move as quickly as you can from conditional confidence to the third type of 
confidence, unconditional confidence.  
 
Unconditional confidence is where we all want to get to. Your confidence isn’t based on 
whether or not you’re doing a good job or what’s happening in the moment. Unconditional 
confidence is based on your habits and the things you can control. You can’t control 
results sometimes – whether or not you get promoted, whether or not you’re picked to be 
on a certain work committee or land that big account – but you CAN control your effort, 
your attitude and, to a certain degree, your skillset.  
 
This is the type of confidence that we want to strive to have most consistently. Because 
unconditional confidence takes you to the next level. 
 
So, take a minute to think about where you are in your life today. Are you operating in false 
confidence, conditional confidence or unconditional confidence? And it may not be one 
zone – it may look different for different parts of your life, right? 
 
But now that you know what to do, go out and make today a great one, one where you can 
be your BEST, most confident self.

Lesson 1 of 6
The Power of Unapologetic Authenticity

Heading

With lingering gender bias in the workplace, it can be tempting for women to curb their behavior or personal brand at work to fit in. This can manifest itself in a lot of ways:

Not speaking up when you have a solution.

Not developing your skills in a particular area that could be perceived as “unladylike.”

Not asking for a promotion, for fear of looking too bold or greedy.

Underplaying your accomplishments or achievements for fear it might come across as bragging.

Volunteering to plan an office lunch or outing you really don’t have time to plan.

Downplaying your personal brand to look “nicer” or “friendlier.”

Pretending to be interested in sporting events or other traditionally male events in order to fit in.

The truth is, the workplace is filled with complex and unique personalities. No one has every skill or talent—we fill in the gaps for each other to form completeness as a team.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 7: Owning Your Game 
 
Christina Gradillas 
Take a moment to stop and think. Is there any area this past month in which you’ve haven’t 
been true to your authentic self at work? C’mon…you know what I’m talking about! That 
time when you knew a solution but didn’t want to look rude. Maybe you downplayed a skill 
you have in order to fit in with the workgroup you were on. Or that time you know you should 
have spoken up in a meeting…but didn’t and the opportunity passed. 
Whatever it was, you didn’t “own it. ”  
It’s OK – we all do this! We’re wired to “fit in” and “go with the flow” and for women 
sometimes that means accidentally fitting into stereotypes other people have created for 
our gender. 
But as strong, powerful women, we can’t afford to think like this anymore. The workplace 
needs your contribution. I’ll say it again – Your workplace needs you! 
As with any team, the corporate workplace is filled with unique personalities. No one has it 
all – we fill in the gaps for each other and all work together towards a common goal. 
There are several parts to “owning your own game, ” beginning with:  
#1 – Knowing yourself. You’ve got to know your own strengths. What are you good at? What 
are you great at? What can you help your team or your leadership team with right now? 
#2 – Knowing your brand. What image do you currently project, and what image do you 
want to project. What do you want people to think about when your name comes to mind? 
Reliable? Sharp? Focused? Collaborative? Innovative? You get the idea. 
#3 – Knowing your boundaries. An important part of owning your game is knowing your 
boundaries at work. Where are you prepared to go beyond for the team, and where are 
areas you need to rein it in to guard your priorities? 
Finally, knowing when to speak up. The art of knowing when to speak up and when to be 
silent is truly an art. And many women simply default to not speaking up in order to 
“maintain an even strain. ” This doesn’t mean you need to speak up on or challenge 
everything. It means knowing the right time to weigh in, and not putting yourself on 
autopilot. 
And it goes without saying that you want to be a “go-to player” in your field.

I actually know of a woman who was very quiet, very reserved, always sat in the back of the 
room, and she actually didn’t do very well in her position. It was the moment she started to 
speak up. It was the moment that she stood up for herself, created her own boundaries, 
and stayed in her own lane. When you can stay in your own lane, there’s no one else who 
can compete with you. She ended up being one of the top producers in our company once 
she broke her own mold.  
We’ll go over all of this in the upcoming lesson.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: With lingering gender bias in the workplace, it can be tempting for women to curb their behavior or personal brand at work to fit in. This can manifest itself in a lot of ways:
Not speaking up when you have a solution.
Not developing your skills in a particular area that could be perceived as “unladylike.”
Not asking for a promotion, for fear of looking too bold or greedy.
Underplaying your accomplishments or achievements for fear it might come across as bragging.
Volunteering to plan an office lunch or outing you really don’t have time to plan.
Downplaying your personal brand to look “nicer” or “friendlier.”
Pretending to be interested in sporting events or other traditionally male events in order to fit in.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 2 of 6
Be Your Authentic Self

If Pat were here, she might say, “Own your own game.” Don’t hold back who you are and what you can contribute to your team or as a leader in your workplace. In other words, be your authentic self. So what does it mean to be your authentic self?

Click on the buttons below to expand the full text.

Know Yourself

Know your strengths and don’t hide them. What are you good at? What are you great at? How can you help your team or your leadership team right now? What problems are you uniquely positioned to solve? Whose permission are you waiting for? Step into your own shoes, and be comfortable in your own skin! Know your weaknesses and work on them… but don’t apologize for them.

Know Your Brand

Your personal style is an extension of your authenticity. While it’s important to always be professional, authenticity is often expressed in attire or personal brand. When you see someone wearing pearls and heels, you have one perception of that person. When you see someone wearing slacks and sneakers, you make another perception about their personality. What do you want to project?
Aside from people’s outward perceptions, dressing authentically allows you to feel confident and comfortable in your professional skin. Do you prefer heels and tights? Do blazers make you feel like a rock star? Maybe you prefer sweaters and slacks. Think about how you want to be perceived and craft your professional image from there.
On an internal note, reflect on what aspects of your personal life you want to include as part of your image or personal brand and what you want to keep private.
Overall, a good question to ask yourself is: What words do I want people to associate with me when they think of my personal brand?

Set Boundaries

Similar to knowing your nonnegotiables, setting boundaries means knowing lines you will and won’t cross—here you’re willing to fake it till you make it and where you won’t (although no one is suggesting anyone be fake!). Think about what you’ll speak up about and what you won’t, when you’ll stay late and when you won’t.
Consider these your core values. Nothing is less authentic than allowing yourself to be pushed around outside of your boundaries at work.

Speak Up

Finally, express your voice. You don’t have to speak up on everything, but offer your opinions and expertise on the things that matter. No one will ever know the authentic you if you don’t let them! Sometimes we are our own worst censor.

Deep Dive: Finding the Right Fit

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Finding the right fit at work is a must for both personal satisfaction and career satisfaction. When it comes to being unapologetically authentic, the concept of "fit" goes beyond just matching your skills with the job description; it involves aligning your talents, values, and work style with the broader team and company culture.

The first step is ensuring that your unique talents complement the needs of the overall team and ultimately, the organization. Every work team is a unique blend of individuals with diverse strengths, and the most effective teams are those where members’ skills are complementary.

Beyond the technical skills, cultural fit is equally important. Every organization and team has its own culture, which is shaped by shared behaviors, norms, and values. Finding a workplace where your personal values align with the company’s culture is essential for long-term success and happiness. For example, if you thrive in a collaborative environment but find yourself in a company that values competition over cooperation, or a remote, independent producer type of career, you may struggle to feel comfortable and perform at your best. Or if you have a more informal approach to your work and your company has a highly corporate, more formal environment (or vice versa), you’ll spend a large part of your time simply trying to “fit in,” rather than playing to your strengths.

Heading

To sum it up, finding the right fit at work is important for your long-term career development! When your talents are aligned with your role and the organizational culture, you’re more likely to receive opportunities for growth, whether through promotions or new responsibilities. A good fit means that you’re not just performing a job, but actively contributing to and growing with the organization.

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Finding the Right Fit 
 
Sue Nokes  
 
So, Pat always said to own your game. And that's very, very true, and I don't disagree with 
her, obviously. But your game has to fit in the broader team.  
 
Charles Barkley taught me about “fit.” Charles, when I worked at T Mobile, Charles and I 
had an opportunity to work several times together and he was harassing me one day, and I 
looked at him and I said, well, what about you and all that money you spent to get a title 
before you left the NBA? 
 
And Charles had given up like 10 million dollars of his own money to go get the final piece 
because they were trying to get him an NBA title before he hung up his sneakers. And he 
did, and he went and got a big-name guy who I won't mention, but I said, so how did that 
spin go for you, buddy? Where's that ring? 
 
And he looked at me and he said, I didn't know. He couldn't play without so-and-so. And 
the deal is, do you fit in the system? You see it all the time in sports that one team will 
purchase a great reliever pitcher and send them to another team and they don't turn out to 
do as well in their new home. It's about fit, and fit is important for you to be and own your 
own game. 
 
When you go look for jobs and you're assessing where you want to go or where your next job 
is going to be or what your next move is going to be, what's very important is – yep -- you 
need to know the official rules and regulations and what are their aspirations and what are 
their values and how do they say they want to run the joint. But there's always an unofficial 
set of rules. 
 
And what you have to figure out is, “Is it a good fit for me?” Because if it's not a good fit for 
me, I will never be all I can be in that environment, and I will never give them the best I can 
be in their environment. This was made very clear to me early on in my career when I was 
offered a COO job and a major healthcare company. 
 
And at the time I was an SVP , and I thought, “Oh my.” You know, women, glass ceilings. And 
for me, it was always about making a difference. Could I go someplace and make a 
difference? Would they know that I've been there? And so, I thought, “Well, healthcare. 
Who loves their healthcare provider?” So, here I go, and I go for the interview. 
 
I interviewed with the CEO. And the CEO was new to that role. And I came back, got my 
feedback, and my feedback was, “They love you. They like you, et cetera, et cetera. When 
can you go?”

And my answer was, “I can't.” Because I knew that that CEO and my values were not in 
harmony. That we would cause each other to stroke within the next 12-18 months. 
 
Because my focus was more on the customer and the frontline employee and theirs was 
not. Doesn't make that CEO wrong and me right, but it does alter where you will be more 
effective. So, I always tell people, don't chase the title. Don't try to take a job to just get your 
foot in the door. Really look around and say, “Do I fit?” 
 
One of the things that I found is most effective -- the most effective tool for a leader and 
your career is a mirror, because when things aren't going well, you need to pick it up and 
kind of look at it and say, “What is it that I know about myself that I'm not using, or what is it 
that I know about myself that I'm suppressing?” 
 
Because it's not everybody else. It's about 80/20 proposition. 80 percent of your career is 
your responsibility. What job is it you want? Have you told anybody you want it? But at first, 
when you'd ask women what they want to be when they grow up, they may sometimes say, 
“Well, you know, I might be able to be... ” and it would be the next level in the organization, 
because you didn't want to seem too aggressive and all those other negative words that 
come along with knowing what you want. 
 
Today, I have those conversations with women that say, “Well, I'm going to be a COO and if 
it's not here, it'll be someplace else.”  
 
I like it. Because it's okay to know what you want. And what are you willing to do that's not 
illegal, immoral, or indecent? And what are your values? And how are you going to use and 
maximize the skills you have and build a team that gets you where you want, and everybody 
can come with you. 
 
If you build the right team and you give them the proper training and tools and information, 
they need to do their job, and you are aligned around a goal...There is no better example 
than Pat Summit.  
 
So, when you go into that organization, again, profit, for-profit, non-profit, academia. What 
is it that you're aspiring to? And have you communicated that vision and are you all aligned 
on the goals? And this is what, what we're going to achieve together. And here are the rules 
by which we're going to play together. And when you're not, you hold each other 
accountable to that and amazing things can happen. But you got to know where you're 
going. 
 
Because good old Alice in Wonderland says, “If you don't know where you're going, any 
road will take you there.”

It's about, do you fit? And can you be you as a part of that team and be your true self and 
give it all you got.

Lesson 4 of 6
The Inner Struggle

What are some of the ways women suppress their authentic self? (Click on the icons to expand the text.)

Fear of Judgement

The fear of judgment, especially in male-dominated industries, can stifle authenticity. Women may hesitate to express their true opinions, showcase their skills, or even take on a leadership role to begin with out of fear of being judged or not taken seriously.

Conforming to Gender Norms

Many of us grew up with gender norms we tried to fit into and it’s hard to erase decades of learned behavior, and it can be doubly hard to put that aside when it comes to expectations in the workplace.

An Endless Balancing Act

Juggling multiple roles and responsibilities, particularly for working mothers, can lead to the pressure of a constant balancing act while striving to appear composed and unflustered, resulting in a polished facade.

Avoiding Conflict

Conditioned to prioritize harmony and avoid confrontation, women often suppress their authentic views to maintain a semblance of peace.

Over-apologizing

Women often have a tendency to over-apologize, even when not at fault. This habit may stem from a desire to avoid being perceived as demanding, leading to a less assertive presence in the workplace.

Downplaying Achievements

A reluctance to highlight personal achievements is a common phenomenon among women. The fear of being perceived as boastful or arrogant may result in downplaying accomplishments and suppressing the authentic acknowledgment of their contributions.

Of the examples listed above, which do you find yourself guilty of, and why?

Conclusion

In short, stay true to your vision. Take calculated risks. No one benefits when you curb your talents and skills, especially to fit inside a preconceived mold that was created decades ago. Let the best parts of yourself shine. Know how to navigate office etiquette, but also how to be real and valuable to your team.

A reluctance to highlight personal achievements is a common phenomenon among women. The fear of being perceived as boastful or arrogant may result in downplaying accomplishments and suppressing the authentic acknowledgment of their contributions.

video.transcript_text:
Remembering Pat: Going into Labor on a Recruiting Visit 
 
 
Michelle Marciniak 
 
So, in 1991, I was a high school senior, and I was the National High School Player of the  
Year, heavily recruited by all the schools in the country. Pat Summit and the University of 
Tennessee was on their way to a home visit in Allentown, Pennsylvania, which is where I 
went to high school, where I lived. 
 
I was coming home a little bit late. Once I got home, I just noticed that Pat was just a little 
bit hurried, kind of in an odd, sort of in a rushed way. We sat down and Pat was nice, but 
she was preoccupied and a little bit distracted. Everything seemed rushed. Pat kept getting 
up, going to the bathroom, coming back, getting up, going to the bathroom, coming back. 
 
Finally, on Pat's like fourth or fifth trip to the bathroom, she came back and said, “Michelle, 
I'm afraid I'm going to have to cut this visit short.”  
 
She said, “My water broke getting off the plane. The baby is on its way.”  
 
And I just looked at her, and I said, “Like...now?”  
 
And she was like, “Uh, yeah, so we have to go.” 
 
My dad knew about this. He said “OK, let's get you to the hospital.” It was about three 
minutes away. She could go there, have a baby. Tyler would have been born in Allentown, 
Pennsylvania.  
 
But she said, no. In true Pat Summit fashion, she said, “I want to go home, I want to have 
this baby in Knoxville.” 
 
My brother and I hopped in the car, we got there, we got to the plane, all we could do was 
get them out of their car and try to get Pat and Mickie on the right planes.  
 
Well, they went through the gates, but the pilots wanted to make an emergency landing in 
Charlottesville, Virginia, where the University of Virginia is.  
 
Pat would not let them land the plane because Tennessee had just lost to Virginia when 
Knoxville was hosting the Final Four. 
 
So, Tennessee didn't get to the final four because they lost to Virginia. Pat said, “I'm not 
having this baby in Virginia. We're going to keep flying.”

So, they’re in the air, in the midst of, I think Mickie trying to take a whiskey shot because she 
had to calm her nerves. Pat was probably the calmer one to be really honest. But they flew 
the plane into Knoxville to an ambulance who took her into the airport, and they had a baby, 
Tyler. So that's how Tyler was born.

Lesson 1 of 6
In It for the Long Haul

Heading

Ever know an individual who tried to fight every battle? Maybe you’re thinking of someone in your office right now. You may even be thinking of yourself!
As a woman, there are a few strategic principles to staying in it for the long haul and making your career go the distance when others before you have flamed out.

Become a Go-To Team Player
The first is, become a go-to team member. Remember the previous lesson about being your authentic self? Don’t wait for recognition or a promotion to become an ideal team player. As a coach, Pat intentionally looked for players who wanted the ball—those who had declared themselves competitors and felt confident enough in their skills to request the ball when the game was on the line. Their team knew they could count on them to perform so they became the go-to.
This takes intentionality and sometimes going above and beyond in strategic areas. The key word is strategic. Learn how to best add value to your team without automatically accepting every assignment that comes your way.

Click play to hear the quote above.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 8: In It for the Long-Haul  
 
Michelle Marciniak 
How many times have you heard it said before, “It’s a marathon, not a sprint!” or “Slow and 
steady wins the race?”  
Too many?  
Well, in the case of the workplace it couldn’t be more true. When it comes to your career, 
you have to pace yourself for “the long haul, ” as they say. 
A lot of people don’t think of it this way – they dive in straight out of college – or maybe 
you’ve just started a new career and a new chapter and you’re rearing to go. Long nights, 
stolen weekends, a little here and a little there. No detail is too small, no work trip 
unimportant. 
This works for a while. Maybe it even works for years. But it does catch up with you. It 
catches up to all of us! 
The fact is, there are a few strategic principles to staying in it for the long haul and making 
your career go the distance. This involves picking your battles and avoiding burnout. 
First, picking your battles. You have to know which battles to fight, and which to leave to 
someone else. Which projects need 100% of your time and energy, and how to move on or 
delegate. There is an art to this – it does not come naturally. 
Second, avoiding burnout. According to research, women are statistically more likely to 
report burnout than men – nearly half of all women surveyed by some reports. And 
according to the American Psychological Association, 76% of adults said they have 
experienced health impacts due to stress in the prior month.  
76 percent! 
Women are at a higher risk than men for several reasons – one is the headwinds they face 
in their careers, which we’ve already outlined here. The second is the fact that women are 
more likely to take on “hidden work” – work that is prep work or behind the scenes, work 
that contributes to the office culture but not the bottom line. And the third is the simple fact 
that women face more caregiving responsibilities at home than men – traditionally, that is. 
When you go home and your work doesn’t “stop” and you keep running until bedtime, it’s 
no wonder you’re at a higher risk.

So, what can you do to avoid burnout and stay in it for the long haul? An ounce of 
prevention is worth a pound of cure here. 
The first is being aware of the stages of burnout and know that it has the tendency to creep 
up. Stress manifests itself in three categories: 
Acute stress is short-term, like a stressful month or two buying a house or working on a 
one-time project. 
Episodic stress is short term, but frequent, like a tax accountant during busy season or 
realtor during the peak summer months. 
Finally, chronic stress is long-term or ongoing stress that lasts longer than 6 months.  
You do not want to live in the chronic stress zone, especially as mother, wife, or simply as a 
human being prioritizing their health and well-being. 
So, what can you do to avoid burnout? 
Be mindful of stress and how it manifests itself in your life and your workday. All types of 
stress are not the same, some are good, some are bad, but too much of any of it will affect 
your health and ultimately your career. 
Next, identify triggers. The farther you go in your career, the better you’ll be able to 
recognize your own personal triggers and how to avoid them. 
Speak up about the stress. Know when to speak up and when to power through. Don’t be 
afraid to stand up for the boundaries you need to keep things on the rails in your career. 
Remember – marathon, not a sprint! 
And finally, make de-stressing an intentional part of your workday and work week. You 
heard me – it’s not going to come naturally! Our human instinct is to either be “on, ” running 
around, multi-tasking, trying to do all the things, or “off, ” where we are in front of the TV at a 
long hard day, making poor diet choices, or worse – too tired to leave the house or engage 
in time with family.  
De-stressing can look like several different things to different people, and we won’t get in to 
them all in this video – sometimes it’s intentional breaks during the day. Sometimes it’s a 
20 min walk after work to reset your mind. Sometimes it’s a hot shower with some 
aromatherapy, time at the gym, happy hour with friends, spending time in the evening 
reading to your son or daughter. Whatever it is for you, these things are natural speed 
bumps in your day for a reason to slow things down and calm you down to keep you 
optimized and ready for the next workday.

So, with that in mind, let’s learn more about how we can win the marathon, or in Pat’s case, 
the championship, without sacrificing the things we enjoy and the unique things that make 
you, YOU. 
You’ve got this! Let’s take a closer look.

Lesson 2 of 6
Pick Your Battles

Heading

You can’t fight every battle. You just cannot. When it comes to women in the workplace overall, and your career specifically, know which battles to fight and which to leave alone. Grow your long-term perspective. This has several advantages as you progress as a female leader.

Strategic Decision-Making

Knowing when to pick your battles involves assessing the importance of an issue, understanding the potential impact on your career, and considering the long-term consequences of engaging in a particular issue.

Preserving Energy and Focus

Engaging in every battle can be exhausting and detract from your overall focus and productivity. Knowing when to pick your battles allows you to preserve your energy for the issues that truly matter.

Demonstrating Emotional Intelligence

Emotional intelligence plays a big role in workplace dynamics. Choosing battles requires recognizing and managing emotions effectively, leading to more constructive interactions between you and your peers.

Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Issues

Not every workplace issue requires the same level of your attention. Period. Major issues that align with your core values or significantly impact your work should be prioritized.

Assessing the Long-Term Impact

Consider the long-term impact of a potential conflict. Will the issue at hand have lasting consequences on your career, relationships, or the overall work environment?

Evaluating Personal Investment

If the matter directly affects your responsibilities, well-being, or professional growth, it may be worth addressing. However, for issues that are more peripheral to your role, choosing to step back might be the wiser option.

Lesson 4 of 6
Handling Burnout

Deep Dive: Guardrails for Burnout

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

When it comes to being “in it for the long haul,” one classic challenge female leaders face is a greater susceptibility to burnout. Burnout can look quite different for each individual, and a lot of it can be prevented on the front end with a little intentionality. First, you want to stop and think about your overall career goals and where your career “guardrails” are, what you will and won’t do. This is important, because it’s easy to eagerly accept long hours, salary changes, or a change in commute in the wake of an exciting new promotion. But without an honest assessment of your personal guardrails, women often find themselves landing squarely in the burnout zone. Don’t let this be you!

Your guardrails may change over the course of your career, and that’s OK! The important thing is to stop and think about where you are now and where you want to be. If, 10 years from now, you’re doing exactly the same thing as you are now, is that OK? What are the “non-negotiables” in your career when it comes to salary, work hours, long weekends, travel, location, commute, flexibility, etc.?
Some things are OK for a season, but you want to make sure you understand where your personal boundaries are as your career progresses.

Deep Dive: Recognizing Burnout

Because of caregiving duties and other factors we mentioned earlier, women are often more susceptible to burnout than men. The signs are subtle and easy to miss, but if you learn to course-correct before hitting the ditch, you’ll go farther and be able to perform better in your career.

Heading

Burnout is more than just feeling stressed or tired. It's a state where you feel constantly emotionally and physically exhausted. You might become cynical, detached from work, and feel like you're not accomplishing anything. Potential causes include:

Excessive workload

Lack of control

Unclear expectations

Lack of recognition

Poor work-life balance

Inadequate resources

The best way to stop burnout is before it starts. This involves keeping a close eye on yourself and your emotions when you start feeling the first signs of stress.

Sort the cards below into their proper categories.

Procrastination

Time-blocking

Heavy  workloads

Ample training

Unrealistic targets

Lack of support

Workplace conflicts

Open communication

Streamlining tasks

Establishing a sense of purpose

Setting realistic goals and targets

Burnout

Balance

Deep Dive: Guardrails For Burnout 
 
Patty Hoppenstedt 
Okay, we’ve touched on things you need to keep in mind in order to be “in it for the long 
haul. ” Now let’s take a closer look at burnout. 
When it comes to being in it for the long haul, first, begin with the end in mind. What do 
YOU need to “go the distance?” 
Stop and think about that for a second. Is it a certain salary level? Maybe it’s earning 
enough to afford childcare, or a job that offers remote options for work-life balance? I 
s it a position located within a certain area of your home, or are you willing to move? How 
much are you willing to commute? What about retirement options, like a 401K plan? 
Start by making a list of where you want to be in 10 years. What does that job look like?  
You may want to split things into two categories, what the “dream version” of that job looks 
like and what are non-negotiables for you to be working in 10 years. 
The dream version can include things like a certain title, or the goal of having a certain 
position in a certain industry. The non-negotiable side may include things like a minimum 
salary or how much travel the job involves. 
There are things we do when we’re starting off in our careers that we won’t do when we’re 
older. In your 20s you may not have kids, so working unconventional hours or traveling on a 
moment’s notice doesn’t matter. You may not be married or have a house so you might be 
willing to move for that big opportunity.  
 
Things usually change the further we get into our career. You learn what’s important to you, 
and what you will and don’t compromise on. Even if a spouse or kids aren’t a consideration, 
you usually have other obligations or interests that influence your deal-breakers in the 
workplace.  
Maybe you’re an adrenaline junkie who thrives in an unexpected, fast-paced environment 
and you know you like the element of excitement in your career. Maybe you’re the opposite 
– you prefer professional but predictable, with a steady course. 
When you know where you’re going – the end result – and you know your boundaries, 
navigating your career options as they present themselves becomes a little clearer.

This is important, because to avoid burnout you need to know where your boundaries are 
and how to safeguard them when you find yourself getting pushed close to the line.
