videos.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Preventing Burnout: Know the Signs 
 
Patty Hoppenstedt 
 
There is no “one thing” or magic tip for avoiding burnout, despite what all the articles and 
tabloids may tell you. There aren’t any shortcuts. You have to prevent it holistically. There 
are two basic parts to burnout: physical and mental, and both are important. 
We’ve already talked a little about the mental – slowing down and taking breaks during the 
day. Having strategies to “de-stress” like mindfulness or meditation, knowing what you 
need specifically at the end of a day or in any given work week to recharge. Knowing how to 
distance yourself from issues at work and setting boundaries. But the physical is just as 
important as the mental.  
Having a career is a lot of stress – it doesn’t matter which industry you’re in, and you have 
to make sure your body is set up appropriately to handle it. This includes three basic areas 
of preventative care: 
First exercise – one of the most common effects of stress on our body can be mitigated by 
exercise. Psychologists will tell you when you’re experiencing stress, one of the best things 
you can do is to get moving -- even if it’s just 20-30 min a day. When your body is wound up, 
it produces a lot of stress hormones and adrenaline that have nowhere to go unless you 
release it.  
The key is finding the type of exercise that fits the best in your schedule, that is the most fun 
for you. For some people it’s walking, for some people it may be the gym. Others take a 
weekly class or enjoy yoga – whatever it is, find what works for you so you can keep your 
body in shape to go the long haul. 
Next is sleep – Making sure you’re getting 7-8 hours of sleep each night and not skipping on 
shuteye, in addition to getting quality sleep. Tossing and turning till 11:30 pm and waking up 
at 5:00 am is not quality sleep!  
Finally, you know what I’m going to say – eating habits. You don’t have to exist on carrot 
sticks and tofu, but you really want to be mindful of what you’re putting into your body. How 
much fast food, how much processed food, what your first meal of the day looks like, right 
down to the shakes and supplements you take.

These three things work together to keep your body functioning at a healthy, optimal level to 
handle the amount of stress you’re going to put on it. 
So the third step to avoid burnout is to know the signs. Let’s say you’re doing all of the 
above, but you still feel off, like something isn’t right. It’s going to happen.  
Many people, sometimes the best and brightest of us – or the toughest – blow right past this 
one and wind up driving themselves into a wall. Many people see the signs, but they feel 
trapped and just don’t know what to do. So, what are some specific signs you may be 
experiencing burnout? 
The first is usually fatigue. A nagging, chronic fatigue that doesn’t go away with rest. When 
you experience chronic fatigue it’s your body’s way of telling you that something is off. 
Something in your life is causing more fatigue than your body can handle, and work is often 
times the culprit. The extreme version of this is full-blown insomnia, finding it hard to wind 
down or go so sleep because your body is so wound up or jacked up during the day. 
You might find yourself overly dependent on stimulants like caffeine, energy drinks or tea 
just to make it through the day. Having 2-3 cups of coffee a day doesn’t always mean you’re 
burnt out, but you want to be careful about how much you’re “overriding” your body’s 
natural responses and rhythms with chemicals. 
Next, you may have difficulty concentrating, you feel overwhelmed, like it’s hard to stay on 
top of all the details. Like you’ve been behind – for months – and you can’t seem to catch 
up. You may have increased irritability and find yourself on a shorter fuse than normal. 
Many psychologists point to an increase in cynicism and unplugging yourself from your job 
– a lack of enthusiasm about the things you used to care about. You may feel like you’re just 
“mailing it in. ” There’s a lack of motivation or you feel overwhelmed. The extreme version of 
this, of course, is depression and isolation, where you physically withdraw to protect 
yourself from the burnout or stress. 
And the truth is, there is a wide variety of health symptoms that accompany burnout – we 
don’t have time to list them all here, but these are just a few: headaches, unexplained 
stomach issues, non-cardiac chest pain, muscle pain, blood sugar issues or getting sick 
every other month – all this plays into how your body feels and how it’s trying to handle the 
stress. Remember the old saying, “The body keeps the score. ” 
OK, so how do we avoid getting there? If we know some of the signs, how can we avoid 
getting to the point where burnout controls our lives or worse, causes you to have to quit a 
job you love?

It comes down to two main things -- Read the writing on the wall, and always have a backup 
plan. 
First, once you spot the signs of burnout and you’ve done all you can to address the 
burnout in the role you’re in, you’ve got to “read the writing on the wall. ” You’ve got to see 
things for what they are. Are they going to get better? Not just wishes and hopes -- have 
they gotten any better in the last year or two? Do you have the power to affect the change in 
this situation, or is it in the hands of another person? 
It goes without saying that before you read the writing on the wall, it may mean an honest 
conversation with your employer about what’s going on and seeing about any adjustments 
that can be made to the situation you’re in. How many times have you seen an otherwise 
great team member who was struggling with burnout, and they didn’t say anything until 
they just gave up and crashed? That’s not what we’re saying here. The writing may not be 
“on the wall” yet. You don’t want to hit the eject button too early. 
Many times, there’s adjustments that can be made before it gets to that point, and 
sometimes you don’t know what they are until you speak up. There may be things you can 
delegate, even if it requires more training for a team member. It may mean setting more 
realistic goals, or re-setting expectations with your team. You may need to set boundaries 
at work or around certain projects. All of these things can help.  
But let’s say that you’ve done these things, and you still find yourself at a dead end. Or 
maybe there’s something that just can’t be changed about the situation you’re in. Reading 
the writing on the wall and not being afraid to do so – being honest about where you are – 
puts the power back in YOUR hands to be able to honestly assess the situation and make 
any changes you need to make. The mistake most people make it letting things go too far 
and they don’t read the writing on the wall until they crash or hit empty, and they don’t wind 
up making the best decision about what comes next. At that point things usually can’t be 
saved and it’s “any port in a storm. ”  
When your entire world, your livelihood, your worth, isn’t attached to whatever drama or 
stress may be going on at the moment, you can see things a lot clearer.   
Early on in my career, I was a mom, had my first big promotion, and I couldn’t handle it all. I 
felt guilty not being there for my child and my husband. I wanted to show the world that I 
was a rockstar professional, that I can handle anything that was thrown my way, but I 
couldn’t. So, I ended up seeking external help from a mentor. Please make sure you know 
the signs as stated. I avoided the signs, and I wish I would’ve caught it much sooner, but I 
did reach out for help. Reaching out for help can look like many things depending on what 
you need at the moment. Regardless, just stop, take a deep breath. Don’t be so hard on

yourself. Know that you can’t always do it all for everyone, and don’t let yourself get to 
burnout. Remember, be in it for the long haul.  
We want you to be the best version of you at work. And that requires being able to handle 
burnout like a boss.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 9: Communicating for Success: Getting the Message 
Across 
 
Danni Varlan 
 
Pat believed in communication so much that it is Definite Dozen Principle #4: Learn to be a 
Great Communicator. 
As women in in the workplace, good communication is key to getting your ideas across, 
networking with colleagues and communicating with upper leadership. Male OR female, 
the art of mastering communication is a lifetime goal.  
There are several parts to great communication – Pat liked to focus on three in particular: 
tone, situation, and nonverbal communication. Another area that can be challenging for 
women in particular is avoiding the use of qualifying or filler words. 
Filler words are words like kind of, sort of, really, very, little, pretty that diminish the power 
of what you’re trying to say.  
Which sounds more confident: 
“I could be wrong, but I sort of think we should pick the first option.” 
or simply: 
“I would choose the first option. ” 
Do you see the difference? There were three qualifying words in that first statement! 
Qualifying phrases are words like “I’m not sure but… ” or “If I’m not mistaken… ” or “Correct 
me if I’m wrong, but… ” Women are more prone to these words than men in their 
communication.  
Another key component of communication for both genders to master is the art of brevity. 
Men typically use less words than women, but this is a skill for both genders to take into 
consideration – the art of communicating succinctly…and powerfully.  
How are your voice mails? Are you able to state the message in 30 seconds or less, or do 
you find yourself getting cut off at the beep? What about text messages and emails? More 
than 2-3 paragraphs in an email may come across a little differently than intended, if this is 
your normal habit.

Whether we’re talking about body language, active listening or the timing of a message, 
there is so much to learn here, it would be impossible to cover it all. The point is being 
open-minded and self-aware of how you’re communicating in the workplace – which areas 
are your strengths, and which areas you can improve on. Ask a colleague for a second 
opinion if you’re not sure! 
Now that we know more of what to look for, let’s take a closer look.

Lesson 2 of 7
Communicating for Success

Tone

Pat was famous for her authoritative presence on the sidelines, but would be the first to clarify that it wasn’t the only communication style she employed as a leader:

"I employ three completely different modes of communication as a coach,” she once said. “Off the court, I am a confidante and substitute mother. In that situation, my chief role is to listen, advise, and comfort. In practice, I speak as a teacher who sometimes needs to employ severe methods in order to maintain the attention of the students.
In a game, I issue blunt commands and motivate our players to endure adverse situations. It’s a competitive situation with no time for politeness or misunderstanding. My different tones, taken out of context, would be counterproductive or even downright offensive in any other situation."

Knowing how and when to use different tones appropriately can be the difference between coming off as authoritative in a situation or weak, sensitive or insensitive, excited or unenthusiastic.

Situation

The second component of personal communication is being able to appropriately assess each unique situation to determine the right level of communication.
“Frequently, knowing what to say to someone is all about time and location,” Pat once said. “You don’t always make the right call. There’s a judgment involved. You have to ask yourself, ‘What does this person need today?’ And you have to watch his or her body language.”
As Pat used to say, part of knowing how to communicate successfully is knowing what each person needs at the moment: “Do they need a pat on the back, or a kick in the rear?”
Context, she believed, was important. “Circumstances dictate how you need to speak or whether you need to just shut up and listen,” she said. “You don’t holler at a golf tournament. You don’t whisper in a forest fire.”

Nonverbal Communication

Nonverbal communication plays a significant role in conveying messages, feelings, and intentions. Mastering the art of nonverbal communication can enhance your professional and personal interactions. Here are a few tips for doing just that:

Summary

To summarize, nonverbal communication plays a significant role in conveying messages, feelings, and intentions. Mastering the art of nonverbal communication can enhance your professional and personal interactions.

Maintain Eye Contact

Eye contact is a large part of nonverbal communication. It signifies confidence, attentiveness, and sincerity. However, it's essential to strike a balance. Too much eye contact may come across as intimidating, while too little might suggest disinterest. A powerful gaze like Pat Summitt’s “Summitt Stare,” for example, communicated strength and assertiveness as part of her personal brand.

Confident Posture

A strong and confident posture can significantly impact how others perceive you. A straight posture exudes self-assurance and professionalism. Stand tall with your shoulders back and head held high. Avoid slouching or crossing your arms, as these gestures may convey insecurity. It can be helpful in this area to film yourself or get feedback from friends. Plus, there are all types of devices on the market nowadays to help you work on your posture.

Gesture with Purpose

Gestures can enhance verbal communication, but they should be purposeful and not distracting. Use gestures that complement your speech, emphasizing key points. Avoid excessive or erratic movements, as they can be distracting or detract from your message.
Use your hands purposefully to enhance your verbal communication. Some individuals have nervous habits that can detract from their nonverbal communication. Whether it's playing with hair, tapping fingers, or fidgeting, being aware of and minimizing these habits is crucial for professionalism.

Facial Expressions

Pay attention to your facial expressions, ensuring they align with the context of the conversation. A genuine smile or look of interested attention in what is happening at the moment can instantly create a positive atmosphere.

Active Listening

Nonverbal cues are equally essential in demonstrating active listening. Nodding, maintaining eye contact, and mirroring the speaker's expressions show that you are fully engaged. Avoid distractions and give your full attention to the person speaking.

Lesson 5 of 7
Brevity

Heading

Finally, one of the last components to stellar communications as a leader is brevity. Men typically use fewer words than women, but brevity is an underrated skill almost everyone can benefit from.
Brevity is most essential in your day-to-day communications for voice mails, emails, texts, or phone calls. Here are a few simple recommendations:

Voicemails

Keep voicemails 30 seconds or less. The point of a voicemail should be to leave one or two sentences with enough information to solicit a callback, not leave an entire monologue with all the details in someone’s voice inbox.

Texts

Because texts are already supposed to be short and sweet, anything over two or three sentences can come across as hitting your point too hard or warranting a phone call instead.

Emails

For emails, two to three short paragraphs should suffice. More than three paragraphs may come across differently than intended and may warrant a phone call or meeting to clear up the issue instead.
Be direct—clearly state the purpose of the email in the opening lines, and once you’ve typed a draft, review your emails to eliminate redundant phrases and information. Resist the urge to provide excessive background information in the email, and use special punctuation sparingly, such as exclamation points or too many question marks.

In the spirit of brevity, we’ll stop there, but to determine where you fall on the scale of brevity, consider getting some peer feedback on your communications. Ask a colleague or trusted friend to show you where you can improve if this area of communication is a challenge for you.

Deep Dive: Tone and Non-Verbals

Tone of voice and body language are often overlooked parts of effective communication, especially when you're in a leadership role. Think about how many times a situation has gone from “eh” to “Oh no!” just because someone’s tone was off. We’ve all been there—raising our voice when we’re excited or letting emotions like frustration or anger sneak into our words. But here’s the thing: mastering your tone can make a world of difference.

Similarly, body language plays an underrecognized role in communicating in the workplace. The way you carry yourself can scream confidence—or not—even before you say a word. Ever noticed how some people just command the room? It’s not magic; it’s body language. Good posture, eye contact, and not jiggling your leg like you’ve had too much coffee can make a huge impact in how you’re perceived.

And then there’s your face. Yep, that expressive mug of yours can either be your best friend or your worst enemy in communication. Ever been on a Zoom call and realized your facial expressions were betraying your inner thoughts? Maybe you have the kind of face that shows every emotion, or maybe you’ve got a poker face that makes you look like you’re plotting something. Either way, it’s worth getting some feedback—ask a trusted colleague to let you know if your face is sending mixed signals.

Sure, nobody’s perfect—we all have our quirks—but with a little practice, you can take your communication skills from good to great. And who knows? You might just surprise yourself with how much you can grow.

Conclusion

In summary, communication is a skill you practice continually. Great leaders never arrive, and are frequently revisiting the components above to see where they can improve. Make it a part of your own leadership toolkit to get regular feedback in these areas so you’re continually taking your game to the next level.

body_blocks.text: Brevity
Heading
items:
Finally, one of the last components to stellar communications as a leader is brevity. Men typically use fewer words than women, but brevity is an underrated skill almost everyone can benefit from.
Brevity is most essential in your day-to-day communications for voice mails, emails, texts, or phone calls. Here are a few simple recommendations:

body_blocks.text: Voicemails
items: Keep voicemails 30 seconds or less. The point of a voicemail should be to leave one or two sentences with enough information to solicit a callback, not leave an entire monologue with all the details in someone’s voice inbox.
Texts
Because texts are already supposed to be short and sweet, anything over two or three sentences can come across as hitting your point too hard or warranting a phone call instead.
Emails

For emails, two to three short paragraphs should suffice. More than three paragraphs may come across differently than intended and may warrant a phone call or meeting to clear up the issue instead.
Be direct—clearly state the purpose of the email in the opening lines, and once you’ve typed a draft, review your emails to eliminate redundant phrases and information. Resist the urge to provide excessive background information in the email, and use special punctuation sparingly, such as exclamation points or too many question marks.

body_blocks.text: Heading
items: In the spirit of brevity, we’ll stop there, but to determine where you fall on the scale of brevity, consider getting some peer feedback on your communications. Ask a colleague or trusted friend to show you where you can improve if this area of communication is a challenge for you.

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Tone and Non-Verbals 
 
 
Christina Gradillas 
 
OK. We’ve talked a little about certain words, what to say and not say when communicating, and 
how to be concise. Let’s talk a little more about tone of voice. 
 
Tone of voice is powerful when it comes to mastering the art of communication. How many times 
has a situation escalated simply because of the tone of voice? We all – male or female – fall 
prone to this…betraying our emotions when speaking, or raising our voice when we don’t mean to, 
when we get excited.  
 
There are several ways to work on your tone, but we’ll start with one simple one. This is a little 
exercise we like to call “Bring it down.” Meaning, bring down the tone.  
 
To do this, look for situations in your everyday life where something has a strong emotion 
attached to it and “bring it down” with your communication. 
 
Maybe it’s an irate customer on the phone that you can’t get to calm down who is taking the 
opportunity to cuss you out. Instead of hanging up the phone and telling a colleague, “Oh my 
goodness…that was the worst call ever!” Afterwards you might say something calmly to a co-
worker like, “The client was visibly upset.” 
 
Your toddler just spilled cereal all over the floor 10 minutes before visitors are arriving at your 
house? Maybe you calmly state “This is an opportunity for us to clean the floor.” 
 
Make it a game! Did the car go out on the side of the road? Instead of “ I AM SO LATE. I JUST 
SPENT 45 MINUTES ON THE SIDE OF THE ROAD!” surprise everyone by re-telling it in a cool, 
calm, collected way. “It wasn’t ideal, but we worked out the problem.”  
 
You get the point. When you get used to describing the frustrating, unexpected or the latest 
catastrophe in an even, collected way – even if it doesn’t deserve to be…maybe it was a disaster 
– when facing a business situation where you need to dial it back and explain something in a 
professional tone, you’ll have plenty of practice. 
 
There’s nothing wrong with emotion, don’t get me wrong, but good leaders – skilled 
communicators, know how to master their emotion and be mindful of their tone. Pat Summitt 
knew when to raise her voice during a game, but she also knew when to “bring it down” and 
remain calm.  
 
Next, where are you in the area of body language?

Pat once said, “There is more to being vocal than simply being audible. Especially if you are in a 
leadership role. You communicate with gestures and body language all the time without realizing 
it. How you sit in a meeting may send a message. Which chair you choose to sit in might send one 
also. You can unconsciously project confidence or uncertainty.”  
 
“Generally, I don’t sit on the sidelines. I stand because I feel closer to game. Also, I am aware that 
my body sends a message from 90 feet away. Good eye contact, a straight posture and a 
thumbs-up can impart conviction.  It's not enough to say, ‘I’m confident.’ You can say those 
words one hundred times over and over, but no one will buy it if your shoulders are slumped and 
your voice cracks.” 
 
It turns out, when it comes to success with professional body language, your mother was right: 
Stand up straight. Don’t fidget. Smile. Give a firm handshake.  
 
One way you can start to learn this is simply by observing others. Have you ever intentionally 
noticed this before. Who in your office has great body language?  
 
Take some time after this video to jot down a few people who come to mind. 
 
Now, why is this? What are they doing that sets them apart? 
 
Maybe they always appear cheerful and confident. Maybe it’s the way they give you their full 
attention when someone is talking. Maybe they mimic your expressions to show they’re with you 
when you’re explaining something. It could be a variety of different things. But be intentional. Be 
on the lookout this week in your office. 
 
There are several books or videos out there that can help you work on your body language, but 
there are just a few techniques: 
 
• Good posture – not slouching 
• Not crossing your arms and looking closed off 
• Avoiding any nervous gestures like jiggling your leg, or playing with your jewelry 
• Face the person talking to you or lean in when they’re speaking to show interest 
• Proper use of your hands – not overdoing it or underdoing it with hand motions 
 
It’s hard to find someone who is a master at body language – we all have our unique quirks and 
traits, so it’s important to figure out what yours are. And to do this, you may need a little bit of 
help. Have you ever watched yourself on a home movie and been horrified? “Do I talk like that? 
Do I sound like that?” You know who you are. 
 
OK, I thought so!

So you want to do an audit, where you are in the realm of body language. What are your strengths, 
and what are your weaknesses.  
 
You also want to do the same for your facial expressions. It’s easier than ever to see this now in 
the world of Zoom calls, but you may want to call in a friend or colleague you trust for backup. Tell 
them you’re working on your body language, and would they give you an honest opinion on two 
things you can improve, or to let you know when your face is betraying you. Ladies, we all know 
what that face can look like.  
 
And you’d be surprised at how many times our face is communicating something entirely 
different than what we think it is! 
 
You may have an expressive face, in which case every emotion – concern, frustration, anger, 
disappointment – is visible on your face. Or you may have the opposite problem – a poker face 
where there’s little to no expression on your face and your co-workers can’t read you that well. 
They may think you’re displeased when you’re not, or unfriendly when you’re not. So, start with 
your face.  
 
You also want to be mindful of your eye contact. This may come very naturally to you, but 
sometimes women can be naturally shy, perceived as less confident. If you’re an introvert – male 
or female – good eye contact may not come naturally.  
 
A good rule of thumb is to make eye contact 50% of the time when speaking and 70% when 
listening. That’s right – 70% when listening! If you find yourself struggling with eye contact at first, 
practice noticing the color of people’s eyes. Hold eye contact for several seconds, as long as it 
takes to determine the color of their eyes, then look away if you need to. If looking people in the 
eyes is too stressful, look at the spot right between their eyes, or their nose. Whatever it takes to 
start building the habit. 
 
Another technique is trying to read people’s expression by looking only at their eyes. You’d be 
surprised at what someone’s eyes can tell you. Do the eyes look sad, tired, excited, nervous? 
There’s a reason they say the eyes are the window to the soul. You’ll find that in the process of 
trying to read people’s eyes, you’re working two skills – holding eye contact and learning to read 
other people’s body language, which is a key part of emotional intelligence. 
 
So that’s several things to work on, but it’s worth it. And even the greats still have to work on their 
body language and overall communication. In her memoir, Pat once wrote that she didn’t 
consider herself starting off to be a very good communicator. “I was pretty hopeless. It’s a change 
I’m proud to have made, and it’s the way in which I’ve grown the most as a coach.” 
 
With all that in mind, how will you grow?

Michelle Marciniak

Lesson 1 of 6
Powerful Conversations

Heading

When it comes to being a female leader, nothing can make or break your career quite like communication, especially communication with your leader. Many times a female leader is reporting to a supervisor of the opposite sex—or maybe you’re managing team members of the opposite sex, making the communication gap even trickier.
While we won’t go into all the nuances of male-female communications here, there are a few practical things you can do to make sure your communication is received in the best possible light, especially when it comes to communicating with your leader, having difficult conversations, and negotiating successfully, which we’ll cover in the following lesson.

Lesson 10: Powerful Conversations  
 
Alexis Hornbuckle 
When it comes to communication, there are two areas that can make or break your career: 
how well you communicate with your leader (or upper management), and how well you 
handle conflict – that is to say, how you handle difficult conversations with a colleague or 
team member. 
Ever been around someone who didn’t handle difficult conversations well? Anything that 
had the slightest bit of emotion around it, and within five minutes it was like a bomb went 
off in the conversation? Maybe this is you – does just the thought of having a difficult 
conversation make your heart race? 
How about those you know who couldn’t communicate well with their leaders? Their leader 
never knew what they were working on, or they felt conversations with this person were 
always negative, a never-ending string of problems.  
How far do any of these people go in their careers?  
Not as far as those who master the art of powerful conversations! 
Let’s start with your leader. Think about your current leader. On a scale of 1-10, how well do 
you feel you communicate with them currently? Do you know your current leader’s 
communication style? 
There are three keys to remember when communicating with your leader: right channel, 
right timing, right message. 
In addition, there are a few best practices to keep in mind with your leader. 
Be positive! This one is important. Leaders quickly learn which team members are solution-
oriented who are looking for the positive in each situation, as opposed to those who are a 
Negative Nancy. 
Be prepared. Always be prepared when you take your leader’s time. Do you know what you 
plan to discuss? Is there something important you need to show them? Plan this out in 
advance, so your meetings are well-organized and productive. 
Bring solutions. Problems are real, but whenever bringing an issue to your leader, also 
present some options for solving the problem if you’re able. Your leader may have thoughts 
of her/his own, but they will appreciate you bringing options to the table.

Be open to feedback. Be coachable! This one is a must for any growth in your career. 
Sound doable? Let’s learn!

Many times a female leader is reporting to a supervisor of the opposite sex—or maybe you’re managing team members of the opposite sex, making the communication gap even trickier.

While we won’t go into all the nuances of male-female communications here, there are a few practical things you can do to make sure your communication is received in the best possible light, especially when it comes to communicating with your leader, having difficult conversations, and negotiating successfully, which we’ll cover in the following lesson.

Lesson 2 of 6
Communicating with Your Leader

Sometimes great communication with your leader may come naturally (if it does, great!). Other times it may be a challenge, especially if your leader has a different personality type or communication style than you do. As a female leader, there are a few things you can do to optimize interactions with your leader.

Know your leader's communication style. This can be summed up in three parts:

Right channel

What medium do they prefer most (email, phone, text, Teams or Slack chats, etc.)?

Right timing

How often do they prefer communications? Leaders are busy, and some managers prefer frequent updates, while some prefer consolidated updates. Some prefer to receive news/information as it happens in real time, while some prefer to hold items to be discussed in a one-on-one or meeting. Take a minute to think about your leader’s overall preferences. (When in doubt, just ask them!)

Right message

Make sure your communication is professional, concise, and free from frustration. More on this later.

Optimizing & Sustaining Communication

Let's review some ways to optimize your communication with your leader.

In Conclusion

In review, here are some of the ways we've suggested to sustain an open and communicative environment with your leader:
Optimize Your 1:1s
Be positive
Be prepared
Bring solutions
Be open to feedback

Optimize your 1:1s with your leader.

Don’t overlook the rapport that can be formed in regular one-on-ones with your leader. Many times this is the foundation for trust that will help your career sink or swim.

Be Positive

This should be a given, but it’s not. Employees who bring a sense of positivity to work are rarer than you think, and in the world of leadership it can be a breath of fresh air. It doesn’t matter how talented you are—if your attitude is negative (or perceived as negative), your relationship with your leader will eventually suffer. Make positivity a part of your personal brand. Not all conversations will be positive in themselves, but when faced with something negative to communicate, try your best to frame it in a positive way.
“No one ever got anywhere, accomplished anything, or survived any amount of ill luck by being negative… With attitude you can determine your own performance.”
– Pat Summitt

Be Prepared

A little preparation goes a long way. Whenever you take up your leader’s time, even in a standing meeting or one-on-one, come prepared with a list of items to discuss or an agenda for the meeting, in addition to any information or data that may be needed.

Bring Solutions

This one is important! Leaders often feel like their office is a revolving door of problems to solve. Whenever bringing an issue to your leader, also present some options for solving the problem. Your leader may have thoughts of their own on the matter, but the fact that you took the time to think through solutions will go a long way in displaying your own leadership abilities. Depending on the issue and vantage point, sometimes you may be even more qualified to solve the problem than your leader.

Be Open to Feedback

Finally, be open to feedback and take any constructive criticism with an open mind. Remember, there’s usually a grain of truth in every bit of feedback, even if the feedback seems severe at the time.
Giving feedback is a sign of respect and care. Your leader cares enough to offer it to you and believes you have the maturity to receive it. Try not to get defensive about critiques or criticism, but instead use it to propel your best work forward.

Lesson 4 of 6
Having Hard Conversations

Deep Dive: Having Hard Conversations

As a female leader, there are going to be times when hard conversations are necessary, whether with a leader, colleague, or other business associates on the team. As humans, we all tend to naturally shy away from hard conversations, which can be harder for females due to fear of stereotypes or biases and how they might be perceived.

Have the conversation privately!

When defenses are high, they will be even higher in a public setting. It can be intimidating to have a private conversation when conflict needs to be resolved or negative feedback given, but hard conversations are almost always best relayed in private.

Pick the right time.

As Pat noted, timing is everything in communication, especially when having sensitive conversations. Is first thing in the morning or the very first day someone is back from PTO the best time to have a difficult talk? How about late on a Friday, when everyone is tired and 20 minutes away from the weekend? Pick a time that is not only best for you, but also conducive to your message being received.

Is this a repeat occurrence or a one-time offense?

Whether it’s happened once (e.g., an insensitive comment) or two or three times, it will still need to be addressed. But acknowledging the frequency of occurrence will be key in how you address it. Was someone having a bad day and speaking thoughtlessly, or is this a repeat behavior?

Begin by asking the person how they’re doing and if anything is going on outside of work.

Here’s where emotional intelligence comes into play for savvy leaders. You think you know your colleagues, but you never really know what may be going on, and it helps to know the context for the conversation you’re about to have. If someone just had a miscarriage a few days earlier or is upset because a close friend passed away, it’s probably not the best time to scold them for parking in the wrong parking space, even if it does need to be addressed eventually. And you won’t know unless you ask. Context is key.

Try to keep it objective and leave out other co-workers.

Instead of saying something like, “People have noticed that you’re late…” or “Your tone in the last meeting made people feel uncomfortable,” stick to the facts. “You’ve been running behind to the last four team meetings,” or “In the last meeting, you sounded defensive and frustrated” will suffice.
Don’t quote other people who haven’t agreed to be quoted in the conversation, unless you get their permission. (“Javier said your tardiness was affecting his meetings as well.”) It would be up to them to have a conversation with that person.

Be mindful of your tone; keep it low and slow.

Do your best to keep frustration and anger out of your voice, even if these are emotions you may be feeling at the time.

Don’t beat a dead horse.

Once the point has been made, leave it. Emphasizing someone’s shortcomings over and over will start to erode the conversation and make them defensive

Finally, listen to what the other person has to say.

Nothing is more frustrating than being criticized and being kept from being able to say anything. Give them a chance to process what has been said, and listen thoroughly to their response.
With a little intentionality, you can become the master of having hard conversations when needed.

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: How to Have Difficult Conversations 
 
Christina Reckard 
The second part of communicating at work is knowing how to have difficult conversations. 
That’s right – conversations that make your heart race a little faster, the ones that you might 
be dreading. You might be thinking of some examples right now.  
I know in my own career, I have had to have some very difficult conversations. At one point, 
I even had to dismiss an underperforming team member that had helped to hire and train 
me, and who I considered a friend. Talk about a difficult conversation.  
As a woman in leadership or a future leader, difficult conversations come with the territory. 
The key is to learn how to master them, or at least not be afraid of them. Because when we 
put off the thing that needs to be said, or the conversation that should have been had with a 
team member four weeks ago, everyone loses. So here are some things to keep in mind. 
First, don’t put it off. The harder the conversation is, the less you want to put it off. Hard 
things only get more difficult with time, not easier. Pat once said “When something 
unpleasant happens between two members of our team, I don’t believe in burying it. I ask 
the two players to confront each other and settle it. ” 
Before initiating the conversation, make sure you can clearly articulate the main issue. 
There may be several details or general things to address, but what are the 2-3 main things, 
“We can’t leave this room until this is squared away. ”  
You also want to keep the discussion rooted in the facts. Instead of “You’re 
underperforming, ” which could be seen as subjective, try “Our revenue numbers are down 
due to lack of sales, ” or “The new product isn’t doing as well as we need it to, ” instead of 
“You rolled this product out too quickly. ”  
Facts help ground the conversation in reality and reduce emotional responses. If you’re 
having a conversation with your leader about a new role with new job duties, for example, 
what are the 2-3 main things you need to make sure they understand? 
 
Before having the conversation, make sure you pick the right time and place. This usually 
means in private, not public, and at a time when it’s convenient for both parties. Ever had 
someone who gave you some difficult news at 8 a.m. in the morning and you had to walk 
back to your desk and pretend nothing had happened? How about a Friday afternoon at 5 
p.m., right when you were about to walk out the door for the weekend? Having a

conversation with the finance team about hiring more people on the last week of the month 
when they’re trying to reconcile the numbers probably isn’t the best timing. Nor is having an 
important conversation in the middle of a crowded place, or within earshot of others. 
 
You also want to approach the conversation with a constructive mindset. Aim for a 
collaborative discussion, not a confrontational one. If there is a desired outcome or change 
that needs to happen from the conversation, you want to disarm the other person as much 
as possible from putting up their defenses or thinking their beliefs are under attack. 
That being said, be specific and direct. There’s an old saying “To be unclear is to be unkind. ” 
You want to clearly articulate the issue without beating around the bush. Don’t retreat to 
the safety of generalizations. 
Remember, this is a conversation. You want to make sure that you listen and leave time for 
the other person to share their perspective. Listen without interrupting and try to 
acknowledge their feelings and viewpoints. “I know you really like Sheila, but the fact is, her 
work is below the standard of what we usually accept. ” Or “I can see where you feel the 
new department merger is unfair. But we’re counting on you to help make this work. ” 
 
Do your best to stay calm and composed throughout the conversation. If emotions run 
high, take a break. Try to avoid escalating any emotions that may be present. 
 
After everything has been discussed and you’ve listened to the other person’s perspective, 
you want to shift the focus from the problem to finding solutions. Collaborate with the 
other person to identify steps to address the issue. At the end of the conversation, 
summarize the key points discussed and the agreed-upon action items. This ensures that 
both parties have a clear understanding of the outcomes and next steps. 
Now, those are some principles to consider in general for difficult conversations. If you’re 
going to be delivering feedback as part this conversation, maybe as in a 1:1 with a team 
member, here are some things to keep in mind. 
Slow down. Let them know your heart. Provide feedback in context of your belief in that 
person. “I know you’re capable of more than this, ” or “I’ve seen you perform better than this 
in the past. ” Frame your concerns from your own perspective using “I” statements. For 
example, say “I’ve noticed that deadlines are often missed, and I’m concerned about the 
impact on our projects” instead of “You always miss deadlines. ”  
Don’t speak for people who aren’t in the conversation, unless you have their permission. 
That isn’t fair to the other person and robs them of the opportunity to communicate in their

own way, in addition to making the person on the other end of the conversation feel like 
they are being ganged up on. You’re sharing other people’s opinions and feelings, but the 
only person they have to discuss them with is you.  
Finally, go slow, and give them time to process. Have them repeat back to you what they’ve 
heard, in order to make sure both of you are on the same page with what the next steps 
need to be. 
Now, I know that’s a lot, but with some time and practice, difficult conversations won’t be 
so difficult. As a leader or future leader, you want to know how to communicate in the best 
way, even in the worst of times or circumstances.

Pick the right time. | As Pat noted, timing is everything in communication, especially when having sensitive conversations. Is first thing in the morning or the very first day someone is back from PTO the best time to have a difficult talk? How about late on a Friday, when everyone is tired and 20 minutes away from the weekend? Pick a time that is not only best for you, but also conducive to your message being received.

Is this a repeat occurrence or a one-time offense? | Whether it’s happened once (e.g., an insensitive comment) or two or three times, it will still need to be addressed. But acknowledging the frequency of occurrence will be key in how you address it. Was someone having a bad day and speaking thoughtlessly, or is this a repeat behavior?

Begin by asking the person how they’re doing and if anything is going on outside of work. | Here’s where emotional intelligence comes into play for savvy leaders. You think you know your colleagues, but you never really know what may be going on, and it helps to know the context for the conversation you’re about to have. If someone just had a miscarriage a few days earlier or is upset because a close friend passed away, it’s probably not the best time to scold them for parking in the wrong parking space, even if it does need to be addressed eventually. And you won’t know unless you ask. Context is key.

Try to keep it objective and leave out other co-workers. | Instead of saying something like, “People have noticed that you’re late…” or “Your tone in the last meeting made people feel uncomfortable,” stick to the facts. “You’ve been running behind to the last four team meetings,” or “In the last meeting, you sounded defensive and frustrated” will suffice.
Don’t quote other people who haven’t agreed to be quoted in the conversation, unless you get their permission. (“Javier said your tardiness was affecting his meetings as well.”) It would be up to them to have a conversation with that person.
Be mindful of your tone; keep it low and slow. | Do your best to keep frustration and anger out of your voice, even if these are emotions you may be feeling at the time.
Don’t beat a dead horse. | Once the point has been made, leave it. Emphasizing someone’s shortcomings over and over will start to erode the conversation and make them defensive

Finally, listen to what the other person has to say. | Nothing is more frustrating than being criticized and being kept from being able to say anything. Give them a chance to process what has been said, and listen thoroughly to their response.
With a little intentionality, you can become the master of having hard conversations when needed.

Lesson 1 of 6
Negotiation for Women

Negotiation is a life skill. Whether you are in business, sales, or any other profession, you will need negotiation at some point in your life. Maybe you already use it regularly. The point is, don’t be afraid of it, and don’t take it personally.
Unfortunately, gender expectations can impact how women in particular approach negotiation. Many women feel intimidated by the very thought of having to negotiate, or being labeled as "difficult" or "pushy."

Rachel

Take, for example, Rachel who has an upcoming annual review. She feels strongly that she is underpaid in her position, but is afraid to negotiate a salary increase beyond the standard 3 to 5 percent; what if it doesn’t go over well?

Jayla

And then there’s Jayla, who has been in her position for two years and has consistently delivered exceptional results in her role, but has a hard time approaching the subject of promotion with her managing director. Leadership roles are limited at her organization, and who is she to imply that she is more qualified than some of her peers?

Lynn

Elsewhere, Lynn is starting to notice that certain projects aligning with her specific expertise are often assigned to other team members. She wants to advocate for a different set of job duties but is afraid to be perceived as rocking the boat.

Carmen

Finally there’s Carmen, a dedicated professional and new mom who loves her job, but wants to negotiate for a more flexible work schedule.
Any of these sound familiar?

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 11: Negotiation for Women 
 
Nikki Caldwell Fargas 
Who’s ready for a fun one – negotiation! Who doesn’t want to be a better negotiator…am I 
right? 
The truth is, negotiating can be intimidating for a lot of reasons. You’re communicating with 
someone – usually in a power position of some sort – trying to come to a mutual 
agreement. They have power over an outcome you want…or vice versa. 
You may be negotiating something you care deeply about, like your salary, a new job role, or 
the hire of a new team member, and it’s hard to keep emotions out of the way.  
Negotiating may be challenging, but that’s part of the fun of it. You can rise to this 
challenge!  And the results are usually worth the effort. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.  
And negotiation doesn’t always have to be in a board room. The truth is, we negotiate every 
day in ways we don’t even realize. 
There was this one time I was an assistant coach for Pat Summitt. We had a player that was 
late for curfew and Pat runs a very disciplined program. So if you miss curfew, that meant 
an automatic suspension for the next game. Well, this player in her entire career had never 
missed anything. And so Pat was very disappointed as we all were, and she was going to 
suspend the player for the next game.  
Now, mind you, we scheduled this game because we enjoyed taking players back to their 
hometown or near where they grew up, and we would play the closest university. So when 
Pat was alerted that this player had missed curfew, I was torn, because I knew that this 
person had made a mistake. So at that time, I felt the need to step in and negotiate on 
behalf of the player with Coach Summitt. 
 So, through the negotiation, we were able to arrive at a mutual agreement. The negotiation 
ended with the player only missing half of the game. I felt that was a win for both sides. So, 
in negotiation, it is important to come to a mutually agreed upon decision that serves both 
sides. And I’m so glad we went on to win the game.  
Pat herself negotiated her salary from a little less than $9,000 when she first started out, to 
more than $1 million by the time she finished her career. And she would be the first to tell 
you she grew up as a farm-girl from Henrietta, Tennessee!

This lesson will cover some basics and help make sure you know a few tips you can 
practice to take your negotiating tips to the next level, wherever you are today. 
First, you want to make sure you approach any negotiation with the right attitude.  
Remember, you are trying to come to a mutual agreement that meets your needs, but 
without alienating the other party – especially in the business world. You don’t want to take 
the approach of “my way or the highway, ” but you don’t want to cave in either. Don’t view it 
as something to be “won” or “lost. That can be intimidating in itself. You’re there to 
participate in the negotiation and go as far as you can towards an outcome everyone is 
happy with. 
Use silences to your advantage in a negotiation. Give the other time to process and think. 
Listen for their “no, ” or any objections…those aren’t blockers or dealbreakers. Those are 
only the starting point in a real negotiation. If they don’t give you their objections, you can’t 
find a way around those objections and it’s hard to continue the conversation. 
You want to clarify what you’re hearing at each step of the negotiating so you can isolate 
exactly what any objection points may be. 
“So, it sounds like you’re saying you’d be willing to change the venue if we could come down 
on price, is that right?” 
“So, you’re saying you would be open to giving me a salary increase around the first of year 
if I’m able to demonstrate the value I’ve added to the team by Q4, is that correct?” 
Finally, don’t expect the other side to be won over purely by your logic. If logic was the sole 
determining factor in a negotiation, we probably wouldn’t be having a negotiation. There are 
usually variables or details people are emotionally invested in. Sometimes it comes down 
to pure old-fashioned pride and not wanting look weak or that you “lost” an argument. 
There are also special points to consider when negotiating your salary. We’ll go over all this 
and more in the upcoming lesson.

Lesson 2 of 6
Negotiation Tips & Techniques

Negotiation Tips and Techniques

Maybe the thought of negotiation intimidates you, and you see yourself in one of the four examples in the previous lesson. Or maybe you work in sales, event planning, or use negotiation regularly in your role. Either way, here are a few negotiation practices and strategies for women specifically so you can take your skills to the next level.

In Conclusion

Utilize these tips & techniques to elevate your negotiation skills.

Silence is key in a negotiation.

Only talk as much as you need to! Pause. Don’t rush. Give the other person time to process your offer. People don’t think at lightning speed, especially when they’re trying to negotiate. It’s fine for there to be silences and long pauses while they process what’s being said. Don’t assume silence is disapproval and cut yourself off trying to fill in the gaps with a better offer.

Don’t underestimate the art of congeniality.

Even if things are tense with the other party or you feel like you hold most of the cards, you never want to walk into a negotiation with a closed perception, or like The Godfather: “I’m going to make him an offer he can’t refuse.”The more likable you are, the more likely the other person will be disarmed and come around to your side. Or if you are negotiating for three to five weeks of PTO in a new position instead of two, don’t say, “I was hoping for at least three weeks.” Explain your reason for needing more PTO in the package and listen to what the other side says. They may surprise you with more than what you are asking.

Know the range you are willing to negotiate in, but don’t give the other person your range.

For example, if you are negotiating salary or cost, don’t say “I’d be willing to accept $7,000 to $10,000.” All the other person will hear is $7,000. Say $10,000, and go from there. Give yourself room! Don’t start negotiating at $7,500 if $7,000 is the lowest you’ll take, even if the initial offer seems high to you. That’s why it’s called a negotiation.

Use specific numbers, if possible.

When it comes to business negotiations or even personal negotiations like the price of a used car, saying that it’s valued at $4,588 sounds more precise and leaves less room for grandiose negotiation than round numbers like $5,000 or $7,000. Similarly, $1,852,245 sounds more precise with less wiggle room than simply tossing out $1.8 million.

Listen for their “no.”

Listen for their no. In a negotiation, the no is the starting point. Specifically, why are they saying no? Is it the cost? Is it the timeline? Is it convenience? Many times we assume they don’t like one part of the bargain. They may even pretend they don’t like one part of the bargain, but upon listening further you realize the hang-up is actually another factor entirely.

Avoid black-and-white “yes” or “no” questions.

For example, rather than saying, “Is this the best you can do?” or “Is this the highest you can go?” leave room for the other side to be creative by saying things like, “What if I told you I just can’t make that number work with my manager?” or, “If we had to come up with another option, what would you suggest?” Then listen to what they say. Again, they just may surprise you.

Give (concise) reasons for your offers.

You don’t want to give too much information, but in general, giving the other person a reason for your proposition shows you care enough to treat them like a person and provide context, rather than simply stonewalling or saying, “That’s the best I can do,” or “That’s just what I need.” The key word here is concise. Simply saying, “We don’t have enough floor space at my facility to bring on any more people,” will suffice, rather than “It’s not happening” or “That’s a nonstarter.”

Don’t expect the other person to be won over by your logic.

Ever have the most logical argument in the world but still couldn’t get the other side to come to an agreement? Negotiations aren’t 100 percent logical. They’re emotional, just like any other form of communication. You can have the most rational argument in the negotiation, but that doesn’t mean the other side is going to automatically agree. You have to keep the mood light and emotions managed enough for the negotiation to continue in a productive way, and reach a settlement that both parties agree on.

Clarify what you’re hearing from the other side at each step of the negotiation.

“It sounds like I’m hearing you say you want more travel days worked into the package, right?” or “It seems like you are OK with the venue, but have concerns about the entertainment being offered, is that right?” Doing this frequently eliminates the chance for misunderstandings, and makes it less likely the other side will do an about-face later and try to renege on their deal.

Avoid tossing a “bomb” or ultimatum into the negotiation.

If things are going slow, resist the urge to shake things up or get their attention. The minute one party says, “That’s it, I’m out,” or “I’m going to get management on the phone,” the conversation ceases to be a negotiation.

Get the terms of the arrangement in writing.

Once an agreement is reached, even if the situation doesn’t warrant a contract, do your best to get the outcome in writing, even if it’s an email recap of what was discussed. Having it in writing eliminates the chance that one party can renege on what was decided upon later.

Give yourself room! Don’t start negotiating at $7,500 if $7,000 is the lowest you’ll take, even if the initial offer seems high to you. That’s why it’s called a negotiation.
Use specific numbers, if possible.

When it comes to business negotiations or even personal negotiations like the price of a used car, saying that it’s valued at $4,588 sounds more precise and leaves less room for grandiose negotiation than round numbers like $5,000 or $7,000. Similarly, $1,852,245 sounds more precise with less wiggle room than simply tossing out $1.8 million.
Listen for their “no.”

Listen for their no. In a negotiation, the no is the starting point. Specifically, why are they saying no? Is it the cost? Is it the timeline? Is it convenience? Many times we assume they don’t like one part of the bargain. They may even pretend they don’t like one part of the bargain, but upon listening further you realize the hang-up is actually another factor entirely.
Avoid black-and-white “yes” or “no” questions.

For example, rather than saying, “Is this the best you can do?” or “Is this the highest you can go?” leave room for the other side to be creative by saying things like, “What if I told you I just can’t make that number work with my manager?” or, “If we had to come up with another option, what would you suggest?” Then listen to what they say. Again, they just may surprise you.
Give (concise) reasons for your offers.

You don’t want to give too much information, but in general, giving the other person a reason for your proposition shows you care enough to treat them like a person and provide context, rather than simply stonewalling or saying, “That’s the best I can do,” or “That’s just what I need.” The key word here is concise. Simply saying, “We don’t have enough floor space at my facility to bring on any more people,” will suffice, rather than “It’s not happening” or “That’s a nonstarter.”
Don’t expect the other person to be won over by your logic.

Ever have the most logical argument in the world but still couldn’t get the other side to come to an agreement? Negotiations aren’t 100 percent logical. They’re emotional, just like any other form of communication. You can have the most rational argument in the negotiation, but that doesn’t mean the other side is going to automatically agree. You have to keep the mood light and emotions managed enough for the negotiation to continue in a productive way, and reach a settlement that both parties agree on.
Clarify what you’re hearing from the other side at each step of the negotiation.

“It sounds like I’m hearing you say you want more travel days worked into the package, right?” or “It seems like you are OK with the venue, but have concerns about the entertainment being offered, is that right?” Doing this frequently eliminates the chance for misunderstandings, and makes it less likely the other side will do an about-face later and try to renege on their deal.
Avoid tossing a “bomb” or ultimatum into the negotiation.

If things are going slow, resist the urge to shake things up or get their attention. The minute one party says, “That’s it, I’m out,” or “I’m going to get management on the phone,” the conversation ceases to be a negotiation.
Get the terms of the arrangement in writing.

Once an agreement is reached, even if the situation doesn’t warrant a contract, do your best to get the outcome in writing, even if it’s an email recap of what was discussed. Having it in writing eliminates the chance that one party can renege on what was decided upon later.

Lesson 4 of 6
Negotiating Salary

Deep Dive: Negotiating Salary

Negotiating Salary

When it comes to negotiating, salary is one of the most common negotiations women leaders face. Negotiating your salary is more than just a financial discussion; it's a reflection of your value, skills, and contributions to the organization, which makes it feel very personal.

Review

In short, with a little practice, negotiation won’t seem so foreign. If you’re able, practice some of these guidelines on smaller negotiations where the stakes aren’t so high. Every female leader needs negotiation at some point in her career (if not regularly) and practice makes perfect!

Know your worth.

The first step in successful salary negotiation is understanding your market value. Studies show that women routinely dismiss or undervalue their own skills in the workplace, which is problematic when advocating for pay increases. Arm yourself with data by researching industry standards. Consider your qualifications, experience, and the responsibilities of the role. Many times the first number in a salary negotiation is based on what the previous person was paid or what the department can afford for the role, and may not be based on market value or your skills specifically. Confidence stems from preparation.

Be armed with a range, not a finite number.

What’s the lowest you would accept, and what is your ideal range? Your dream number? The three might be very different, but it’s important to think about where the bottom is and what you’re working toward in advance of the negotiation. As stated earlier, don’t give out your range.

Be open and flexible.

Negotiation is a two-way street. Be open to discussion and compromise. If the employer can't meet your salary expectations, explore other areas such as additional benefits, flexible work arrangements, or performance-based bonuses. You don’t have to automatically accept, but it’s important to be open-minded.

Maintain a positive tone.

To keep the negotiation positive, emphasize your enthusiasm for the role and the company while discussing compensation. Let them know that you’re coming from a place of excitement about the role, not implying that you need to be compensated for the grunt work, stress, or long hours involved. Frame your negotiation in positive terms. Instead of saying, "I can't accept this offer," try, "I’m excited about the opportunity and my role here, and I believe a slight adjustment in the salary would better align with my skills and experience."

Quantify your achievements.

Provide concrete examples of your accomplishments and their impact on the company (or for previous employers). Salary shouldn’t be a hypothetical number. Use metrics and specific examples to demonstrate the value you bring to the table.

Don’t expect an answer on the spot.

Don’t be too frustrated if the other party needs to review your salary offer. There may be other implications to consider, such as salary increases given within 90 days of your professional review or salary constraints for a particular position. Many times your direct leader or supervisor isn’t the only person who has to sign off, so be prepared for a slight delay. But be prepared with an acceptable time frame: “I know my annual review isn’t for eight months, but I’ve taken on a new role with increased work. What can you do in the next 90 days?”
In short, with a little practice, negotiation won’t seem so foreign. If you’re able, practice some of these guidelines on smaller negotiations where the stakes aren’t so high. Every female leader needs negotiation at some point in her career (if not regularly) and practice makes perfect!

Lesson 11: Negotiating Salary  
 
Nikki Caldwell Fargas 
One of the most common negotiations you’ll face in your career is how to successfully 
negotiate your salary. Whether it’s negotiating at the onset of a job or during your position in 
a certain role, how you negotiate your salary is key.  
For women, mastering this skill is especially important in addressing the gender pay gap 
and ensuring fair compensation. By doing thorough research, knowing your worth, and 
approaching the negotiation with confidence and professionalism, YOU can make sure you 
get paid the salary you deserve.  
We’ll go over a few things to Do and Don’t here. 
First off, a few things to Do:  
Research your market value. The first step in salary negotiation is understanding your 
worth. Consider your qualifications, experience, and the responsibilities of the role. 
Studies show that women routinely dismiss or undervalue their skills, which can be an 
issue when negotiating salary. Arm yourself with data by researching industry standards.   
Be armed with a range, not a number. When accepting a new position, know your range. 
What is your ideal salary? The lowest you would accept? Think about what you’re working 
toward before the negotiation. Don’t give out your range – that’s just for your own guardrails. 
Pick the right timing. Timing can significantly influence the outcome of a salary negotiation. 
Ideally, try to negotiate after a successful project or a performance review when your 
contributions are fresh in your employer’s mind. Avoid negotiating during stressful periods 
for your company or immediately after a budget cut.  
Get everything in writing. Sometimes a salary increase is promised after the first 90 days, or 
they may communicate that you just had a raise and need to wait six months before they 
can get another approved. That’s fine, but ask if you can have that in writing from your 
supervisor. Tell them you understand, but want to make sure that the promise is 
documented, so there won’t be confusion later. Remember the saying, “If it’s not in writing, 
it’s not real.” 
Keep emotions out of it. OK, this is easier said than done. We’re talking about your salary 
after all – your bread and butter! – but try to stay focused on the facts and avoid getting 
emotional during the discussion. Remember, you are a highly talented, competent

individual, and this is not your only option in the workforce (even if it’s a job you love and 
don’t want to leave). Putting too much pressure on the discussion will only make you 
emotional, which can come off as desperate. Do your best to keep emotions out of it and 
pick a time that you can calmly and rationally make your pitch – not immediately following 
a downsizing to a single-household income or right after bad financial news. That in itself 
shouldn’t be the motivating factor for a raise.  
All this being said, the art of negotiating salary is as much about knowing what not to do as 
it is what to do. 
Here are some things you want to avoid: 
Don’t focus on the negative: “I need to be paid more for what I put up with. ”  or “I’ve taken 
on more work in the last year and my salary hasn’t gone up. ” A salary increase should be 
based on the value you provide the company, not simply the hours you work. It may be true, 
but it’s not helpful in a salary negotiation. Don’t mention grunt work, stress or long hours. 
You want to focus on the positive – how you are adding value to the company. You want to 
show so much ROI that you make them think they are practically saving money by keeping 
you on and giving you a raise! 
Don’t compare yourself to others: “I don’t get paid nearly as much as [fill-in-the-blank.]” 
Leave other people out of it! Their salary is their business and your salary is yours. Plus, it 
won’t help your case. It will only make your employer defensive. 
Don’t wait until you are actually in your annual review with your supervisor to talk about 
salary. Most salary increases have to be approved months in advance. Go on the offense 
here – 90 days out is a good window. If you need a salary increase, let your supervisor know 
a few months in advance of your annual review: “My annual review is coming up in January. 
I’d like to sit down before then to go over some of my recent contributions and discuss 
some future topics. ” This gives you an opportunity to go on the offense outlining the value 
you provide, backed up by any data, and let your supervisor know that you think a raise of X 
amount would be fair. It then gives them time to work on the request prior to your review. 
Don’t be inflexible. Negotiation is a two-way street. Be open to discussion and 
compromise. Be prepared for counter offers. If the employer can't meet your salary 
expectations, explore other areas such as additional benefits, flexible work arrangements, 
or performance-based bonuses. You don’t have to automatically accept, but it’s important 
to be open-minded. 
Don’t expect an answer on the spot. Don’t be too frustrated if the other party needs to 
review your salary offer. Many times your direct leader isn’t the only person who has to sign 
off, so be prepared for a slight delay. But be prepared with an acceptable time frame: “I

know my annual review isn’t for eight months, but I’ve taken on a new role and added a lot 
of new value to the company. What can you do in the next 90 days?”      
Finally, don’t throw down an ultimatum: “If I’m going to stay here long term, I need a salary 
increase. ” This starts the negotiation out on the wrong foot. This should only be used if you 
are truly prepared to walk out the door that moment, as in, you have another job lined up. 
Don’t let it get to this point! With successful salary negotiating, you can head off the need 
for any ultimatums at the pass. 
In a nutshell, negotiating salary is a skill that can significantly impact your career trajectory. 
Just like any skill, it has to be developed – and it can be learned!  
Remember, negotiation is not just about the money – it’s about recognizing your value and 
taking control of your career. 
You’ve got this!

items.title: Negotiating Salary
items.description: When it comes to negotiating, salary is one of the most common negotiations women leaders face. Negotiating your salary is more than just a financial discussion; it's a reflection of your value, skills, and contributions to the organization, which makes it feel very personal.

items.title: Review
items.description: In short, with a little practice, negotiation won’t seem so foreign. If you’re able, practice some of these guidelines on smaller negotiations where the stakes aren’t so high. Every female leader needs negotiation at some point in her career (if not regularly) and practice makes perfect!

items.title: Know your worth.
items.description: The first step in successful salary negotiation is understanding your market value. Studies show that women routinely dismiss or undervalue their own skills in the workplace, which is problematic when advocating for pay increases. Arm yourself with data by researching industry standards. Consider your qualifications, experience, and the responsibilities of the role. Many times the first number in a salary negotiation is based on what the previous person was paid or what the department can afford for the role, and may not be based on market value or your skills specifically. Confidence stems from preparation.

items.title: Be armed with a range, not a finite number.
items.description: What’s the lowest you would accept, and what is your ideal range? Your dream number? The three might be very different, but it’s important to think about where the bottom is and what you’re working toward in advance of the negotiation. As stated earlier, don’t give out your range.

items.title: Be open and flexible.
items.description: Negotiation is a two-way street. Be open to discussion and compromise. If the employer can't meet your salary expectations, explore other areas such as additional benefits, flexible work arrangements, or performance-based bonuses. You don’t have to automatically accept, but it’s important to be open-minded.

items.title: Maintain a positive tone.
items.description: To keep the negotiation positive, emphasize your enthusiasm for the role and the company while discussing compensation. Let them know that you’re coming from a place of excitement about the role, not implying that you need to be compensated for the grunt work, stress, or long hours involved. Frame your negotiation in positive terms. Instead of saying, "I can't accept this offer," try, "I’m excited about the opportunity and my role here, and I believe a slight adjustment in the salary would better align with my skills and experience."

items.title: Quantify your achievements.
items.description: Provide concrete examples of your accomplishments and their impact on the company (or for previous employers). Salary shouldn’t be a hypothetical number. Use metrics and specific examples to demonstrate the value you bring to the table.

items.title: Don’t expect an answer on the spot.
items.description:
Don’t be too frustrated if the other party needs to review your salary offer. There may be other implications to consider, such as salary increases given within 90 days of your professional review or salary constraints for a particular position. Many times your direct leader or supervisor isn’t the only person who has to sign off, so be prepared for a slight delay. But be prepared with an acceptable time frame: “I know my annual review isn’t for eight months, but I’ve taken on a new role with increased work. What can you do in the next 90 days?”

In short, with a little practice, negotiation won’t seem so foreign. If you’re able, practice some of these guidelines on smaller negotiations where the stakes aren’t so high. Every female leader needs negotiation at some point in her career (if not regularly) and practice makes perfect!

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 12: Thriving Together: Women Supporting Women  
 
Petra Dunn 
What would the world be like if we all supported each other? If we saw our colleagues as 
comrades-in-arms and not competition or obstacles in our way? 
Maybe you’ve had these thoughts before too. How can women do a better job of 
championing and supporting other women, especially in leadership roles? 
Pat would be the first to tell us all to intentionally celebrate the victories of other women in 
the workplace and have an “abundance” mindset. Eliminate any trace of a “scarcity” 
mindset that might propel you to view other co-workers – male or female – as competition 
in your own organization. What a joy it is to celebrate others who are navigating the same 
twists and turns of leadership and doing it well. Adopt a “You Win, I Win, ” mindset! 
You also want to ensure that you include strong female leaders on your support team…and 
we all need a support team! This means intentionally creating your own championship 
team with its own set of players to help you in your own career journey.  
There are a few people you want to include: 
First, “Work BFFs” – these are the people who are with you in the daily grind, who bring a 
smile to your face and make work a pleasure. Or maybe they provide a much-needed 
comic relief when you need to unwind, reminding you everything is going to be OK. These 
types of team members are everywhere and may not share your exact title or status and 
that’s OK.  
Next are Comrades-in-Arms – these are colleagues who are “in the trenches” with you. 
They may share a similar job description or be in a partnership role. 
Coaches are those who may or may not work at your business but have worked in your 
industry or in the workplace for many years and can offer encouragement. 
Finally, mentors. Everyone needs mentors! A mentor isn’t a peer or a “coach. ” Their job isn’t 
to make you feel good, but rather to give you insight and pass on experience. Mentors can 
be male or female and are usually a little older than you are. They might have experience in 
an industry you are trying to break into or a skill you can learn to acquire.  
We all know what it feels like to have someone who believes in us, someone who is on your 
side.  I was fortunate to have some really strong mentors along my career path.  Women

that showed me by their own example that success is more than just my career, that I need 
to use my visibility to lead in the community beyond the workplace.  
You might ask a mentor certain questions like:  
How did you get to where you are today? 
Are there specific skills or experiences you recommend I focus on? or 
What strategies do you recommend for professional development? 
We’ll go over all this in the upcoming lesson.
