Lesson 2 of 7
Creating Your Championship Team

There are several types of players you want on your support team, and we’ll go over a few below.

The Support Team

There are several types of players you want on your support team. Here's a few:
Work BFFs
Comrade-in-arms
Coaches
Mentors

Summary

These are just a few examples of the great foundations to build your Championing Team.

Work BFFs

Work BFFs, if you will, are the unsung heroes of the daily grind. They're the ones who understand your coffee addiction and can read your facial expressions during meetings. These people simply make you feel better! They can be a refreshing break in your weekly routine, giving you the energy to keep going. So don’t skip out on making friends or lunch buddies at work—just make sure they are the type of positive and professional friend who will keep you moving forward.

Comrade-in-arms

Comrade-in-arms are important peers who share similar professional goals or who are your partners on particular projects. Whether you're planning an ambitious marketing campaign, rolling out a new product, or doing something you’ve never done before, having this type of peer in your tribe makes the journey more enjoyable. Comrade-in-arms help keep you accountable and can offer much-needed support in the trenches. Plus, success is sweeter when celebrated with those who truly get the hustle.
Pat’s comrade-in-arms were undoubtedly two of her assistant coaches Mickie DeMoss and Holly Warlick, whom she considered as good friends. The three were inseparable, and Pat often relied upon them to keep her grounded and in check.

Coaches

Coaches are just that—those who may or may not work for your organization, but have a history in the workplace and can offer encouragement. A coach is there to offer support and point out potential potholes in the career road to avoid, which a work BFF or comrade-in-arms may not necessarily see from their vantage point. Think of them as an encourager or cheerleader with an eye for critical thinking.

Mentors

Last, but certainly not least, are mentors. A mentor isn’t a peer or a coach, they’re someone who has gone before you in your industry—maybe even at your own organization or one similar. They’re not here to be a cheerleader, but rather to pass on experience. Imagine you're facing a workplace decision that feels impossible. Or you’re wondering how to navigate a new technology rollout you haven’t used before, and the team isn’t on board. This is where mentors come in. They've been there, done that, and can help you navigate the twists and turns.
Mentors can be male or female, and balanced leaders usually have both on their support team. Cross-generational mentors in particular bring a unique perspective that younger generations might readily miss. A mentor might have prior experience in a role or a particular skill set to teach that will help move you forward in your career path. It's not about finding a friend, it's about finding someone who's been through the trenches and can offer valuable insight and advice.

Deep Dive: Finding a Mentor

A mentor is someone you trust, admire and respect who will give you honest and invaluable career advice.
Sample questions you might ask a mentor include:

What steps did you take to advance in your career, and are there specific skills or experiences you recommend I focus on?

How do you approach setting career goals, and are there specific milestones you recommend I aim for in my current role and beyond?

How did you build and leverage your professional network throughout your career? Any tips for effective networking?

As a successful professional, how have you managed to maintain a healthy work-life balance, and do you have any advice for finding that balance?

What strategies do you use for continuous professional development? Can you provide feedback on my current performance and suggest areas where I can improve?

Heading

These are just a few. The sky’s the limit as to how much gold you can mine for with a mentor. If they’re female, for example, you may ask them, "Have you faced gender-related challenges in your career, and if so, how did you overcome them? Any advice for navigating gender bias in the workplace?"
If they hold/held a position of senior leadership you might ask, "What leadership skills do you believe are essential for success in our industry today and how can I strengthen these skills?" If they are a self-help junkie, ask, “What strategies do you use for continuous professional development?" You get the picture. As one of the first in her industry to smash through the glass ceiling, many colleagues and team members considered Pat herself to be a mentor.

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Finding a Mentor 
 
 
Sue Nokes 
 
You talked to me about mentors and the importance of mentors. I think it is very important 
to have somebody that you can trust, that you admire and respect, that will give you the 
honest opinion and assessment of your performance.  
 
I've seen a couple of things happen. First of all, we often will ask someone to be our mentor 
because of their position within the organization that you're a part of, whether that's for 
profit in academia or in business. 
 
And often it's not a good choice, and the reason it's not a good choice is because they don't 
see you perform every day. So, I was always getting asked if I would be somebody's mentor. 
And it isn't that you don't want to, it's a matter of, “I really can't help you if I'm not in the 
meetings with you, and I can't see how you interact with others or if I'm not around when 
you're leading your people.” 
 
So, finding a mentor who can truly assess your performance and sees you in your day-to-
day operations is important. Number one. Number two. Finding somebody that will tell you 
when your baby's ugly. So, as you're thinking about your career. Remember, it is yours. You 
own it. 80/20 proposition. 80 percent is your responsibility to grow and develop your skills 
and deliver goods so that the organization provides an environment that's conducive for 
your growth and development. 
 
But don't look for people that are like you. Know yourself. Take an inventory. But understand 
what your gifts are and what your specialties are. And then look for mentors or people that 
you can grow and learn from that cover what I would call your deficits or flat sides of your 
tire so that they're not necessarily who you want to hang out with and then you want to go 
on vacation with, but they are someone that has a skill or a talent that you need to learn 
and develop from.  
 
So that's who you surround yourself with. Don't be intimidated by folks that are smarter 
than you. Learn from them. Surround yourself with excellent talent.

Comrade-in-arms help keep you accountable and can offer much-needed support in the trenches. Plus, success is sweeter when celebrated with those who truly get the hustle.


Pat’s comrade-in-arms were undoubtedly two of her assistant coaches Mickie DeMoss and Holly Warlick, whom she considered as good friends. The three were inseparable, and Pat often relied upon them to keep her grounded and in check.

items.title: Coaches
items.description: Coaches are just that—those who may or may not work for your organization, but have a history in the workplace and can offer encouragement. A coach is there to offer support and point out potential potholes in the career road to avoid, which a work BFF or comrade-in-arms may not necessarily see from their vantage point. Think of them as an encourager or cheerleader with an eye for critical thinking.

items.title: Mentors
items.description:
Last, but certainly not least, are mentors. A mentor isn’t a peer or a coach, they’re someone who has gone before you in your industry—maybe even at your own organization or one similar. They’re not here to be a cheerleader, but rather to pass on experience. Imagine you're facing a workplace decision that feels impossible. Or you’re wondering how to navigate a new technology rollout you haven’t used before, and the team isn’t on board. This is where mentors come in. They've been there, done that, and can help you navigate the twists and turns. 

Mentors can be male or female, and balanced leaders usually have both on their support team. Cross-generational mentors in particular bring a unique perspective that younger generations might readily miss. A mentor might have prior experience in a role or a particular skill set to teach that will help move you forward in your career path. It's not about finding a friend, it's about finding someone who's been through the trenches and can offer valuable insight and advice.

items.paragraph:
A mentor is someone you trust, admire and respect who will give you honest and invaluable career advice.

Sample questions you might ask a mentor include:

items.description: What steps did you take to advance in your career, and are there specific skills or experiences you recommend I focus on?
How do you approach setting career goals, and are there specific milestones you recommend I aim for in my current role and beyond?
How did you build and leverage your professional network throughout your career? Any tips for effective networking?
As a successful professional, how have you managed to maintain a healthy work-life balance, and do you have any advice for finding that balance?
What strategies do you use for continuous professional development? Can you provide feedback on my current performance and suggest areas where I can improve?

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
These are just a few. The sky’s the limit as to how much gold you can mine for with a mentor. If they’re female, for example, you may ask them, "Have you faced gender-related challenges in your career, and if so, how did you overcome them? Any advice for navigating gender bias in the workplace?" 

If they hold/held a position of senior leadership you might ask, "What leadership skills do you believe are essential for success in our industry today and how can I strengthen these skills?" If they are a self-help junkie, ask, “What strategies do you use for continuous professional development?" You get the picture. As one of the first in her industry to smash through the glass ceiling, many colleagues and team members considered Pat herself to be a mentor.

Lesson 4 of 7
Peer Review

Now, mentors aside, let's talk about two words that may make you inwardly cringe: peer review. The beauty of having a tribe is that you now have people you trust in the trenches with you. They can give you not just support but also honest feedback, while a mentor may not witness your daily performance.
Strong female leaders know not to be afraid of criticism or critique but to seek it out in strategic cases. It's not about judgment; it's about growth.

What are some overall areas I can improve on?

What do I do really well?

What is my personal brand? What am I known for?

Are there any relationships I need to improve/work on?

How are my communication skills? Is there anything I need to change?

Heading

Listen to what they say! Resilient leaders learn to see feedback as a tool for improvement, not a red mark on their report card.

Deep Dive: How to Receive Feedback

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

video.transcript_text:
Lesson 12: How to Receive Feedback 
 
Christina Reckard 
 
OK, we’ve talked about mentors and coaches. Now let’s talk about another key component 
of thriving in the workplace – how to receive feedback. If you have a coach or mentor in 
your corner specifically, you want to get as much feedback from them as possible.  
 
Knowing how to receive feedback is a skill most people never master. It’s something too 
many people never seek out to begin with – some people run from feedback altogether! But 
if you’re going to thrive in your career, knowing how to be coachable, how to receive and 
implement feedback from your leader or peers is essential.  
 
First, we’re talking about solicited feedback, or feedback coming from a place you trust. 
We’re not talking about barbs or criticisms made in the heat of an argument or anything on 
social media. Even if it’s unexpected feedback from a colleague you otherwise trust, but 
who surprises you with the timing, if their heart is in the right place, it counts. Ask yourself, 
is this someone I like, trust or respect? If the answer to any of these three is yes, you want 
to be intentional about how you process the feedback.  
 
I remember a time when the executive team I was a part of was tasked with providing peer-
to-peer feedback in order to help us grow as a team. One by one, we each gave and 
received both positive feedback and areas for growth. I found providing positive feedback 
was easier for me than providing negative feedback. I tried to keep that in mind when it was 
my turn to receive feedback so that I could receive it in the constructive way it was 
intended. One key takeaway I received was that I need to be more inquisitive in meetings. 
That piece of feedback sticks with me to this day and helps to keep me mindful when 
participating in meetings.  
 
You may get feedback on a regular basis at your job or you may not. Some people go their 
entire careers without getting feedback, or only get it once a year in their annual review. So 
here are a few tips. 
 
The first step sounds obvious, but we need to listen to the person giving the feedback. 
Those who are practiced know how to accept feedback with grace. They don’t fall apart. 
They don’t lose their cool. Learn how to hold feedback with neutrality and open-
mindedness in the moment in which you receive it.  
 
Don’t interrupt. Don’t get defensive. Remember that feedback is often hard to give, and it 
might be your only chance to hear what they have to say. 
 
The person giving the feedback might deliver it in an emotional or clunky way, and that’s 
OK. They may have a string of faults and inconsistencies themselves, and that’s OK – save

it for another time. You’re not here to argue or talk about their shortcomings, you’re here to 
get feedback on you and how you can grow.  
 
Be mindful of your body language when receiving feedback. Are your arms crossed 
defensively? Are you scowling or slouching? Do you look afraid of what they’re going to 
say?  
 
Remember, you want to exude grace and poise, not defensiveness and hostility. We all 
know people who don’t take feedback well, or who no one wants to approach on a 
particular subject. Don’t let that person be you! 
 
Next, you want to clarify the feedback. Repeat back to them what you heard them say, just 
to make sure that you’re receiving the right message. 
 
Thank them for their feedback. This person is trusting you with the maturity to be 
coachable and learn from whatever is being said. 
 
Then you want to process the feedback. Here’s a tip – feedback can often be hard to 
process in the moment. Sometimes it can take days or even weeks to fully sink in. That’s 
OK! The point is that it sinks in, or whatever element of truth in the feedback can be 
received and help you to grow. Resist the urge to throw out feedback immediately if you 
don’t think it’s valid. 
 
If you don’t understand or aren’t sure quite how to process something, reach out to a friend 
or mentor you trust. Tell them of the feedback you received and that you aren’t sure what 
to make of it. This isn’t to gossip or debate the feedback, but to get more clarity on how you 
can learn from it. It should be a mentor or someone you trust who can give you an honest 
opinion on what was said and how you can learn something productive. 
 
Finally, you want seek out feedback on a regular basis. That’s right – seek it out! Don’t wait 
until your annual review once a year or for your leader to initiate the conversation. Ask for 
feedback on a regular basis. Not only from your leader, but also from other peers you trust.  
 
You want to learn to ask for targeted feedback – rather than saying “Do you have any 
feedback for me?” try asking things like “Do you have any feedback on my communication 
style?” or “Do you have any feedback from me on my design elements?” You’re more likely 
to get feedback on a particular subject if you invite someone to speak up in that specific 
area. 
 
The truth is, how coachable you are – how well you receive feedback overall and can learn 
from it – goes a long way in how others perceive your professionalism and can even affect 
the rise and fall of your career.

Lesson 5 of 7
You Win, I Win

Heading

Finally, but not to be missed, learn to intentionally celebrate the victories of other women in the workplace and have an abundance mindset. Eliminate the scarcity mentality that might propel you to view other women as rivals for a limited number of positions. Other women aren’t competition at work; they can be allies, if you let them. There are several ways to rally around your fellow sisters in the workplace:

Do they know of a good mixer or networking opportunity in your area? Where do they meet other people in your industry? Did you just have a great experience at a recent conference you’d recommend? Share the knowledge!

Share networking strategies

Are you a whiz at design or excel spreadsheets? Know someone who is struggling in an area you can help with, or vice versa? Consider a monthly lunch or skill swap to help educate fellow women in the workplace.

Promote skill development

Did someone just hit a huge milestone or work anniversary? How about a major promotion? Take a moment to help them celebrate! Victories at work are more meaningful when they’re shared.

Celebrate achievements

Maybe someone you know just went through a hard season at work. Or maybe you’re facing a new software rollout or department reorganization and know someone a floor over who went through the same thing. Ask for advice, and also pass along your own wisdom.

Share similar experiences

Look for ways to encourage your organization’s support for women in the workplace, from hiring to mentorship programs or peer group committees.

Champion equal opportunities

Know of a job posting at your organization that’s the perfect fit for a woman you know? Refer her! How about someone who would be a great candidate for a particular committee? Offer the recommendation!

Look for growth opportunities

Give Back

In summary, as you build your tribe and support system at work, be on the lookout for ways to give back. There are people who have helped you get to where you are today, or are mentoring you as a female leader. Take a minute to think about how you can pay it forward with your own talents and skills.

Be the cheerleader someone else needs. Be the resource someone else can count on. Who can you be a reference for, or who needs an introduction? Pat would be the first to reinforce the power of the team in achieving any goal, as opposed to being a lone ranger or individual performer in your career. Remember the old African proverb, “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

video.transcript_text:
Deep Dive: Supporting other Women: An Abundance Mindset 
 
 
Sue Nokes 
 
We tend to want “good news” feedback. We like a lot of feedback as long as they're telling 
me how wonderful I am. And I have found that to be more true of women than men. And 
part of that comes from the way we were cultured. And it is changing generationally, thank 
heavens, but that starts with a time when I was coming up in my career that women weren't 
cultured in the same way. 
 
We did not learn to play on teams like guys did. Little boys had t-ball teams and you would 
put them on a team and you'd prop that little ball up before they could hit a moving target. 
And they learned that it's OK if Johnny hits a home run today and Timmy hits it next week 
because we're all going for ice cream, and we're all going to win and it's a great thing. 
 
Women didn't have that. So, when you went to school, it was about: “How did you look? 
And were you pretty? And were the boys going to like you? Who's going to be on the 
cheerleading squad where you're competing with other women? Who's going to be the 
homecoming queen?” When there's typically one. Then you get into a business 
environment where there aren't that many women. 
 
And if you look at the numbers, and particularly as you get into director level and above 
positions, again, numbers are increasing and it's looking good. And I'm not suggesting we 
put anyone in a position who's not qualified for the position, but there are fewer examples 
and role models to follow. That's part of the issue -- who is around for you to emulate and 
learn from and apply to your leadership style and goals. This lack of opportunities to be 
cultured or to understand the rules of the game, if you will, in a business or an organization 
manifests itself in various ways.  
 
I've watched and studied women in meetings and men in meetings. Men will argue and 
debate and at the end of the debate, smack each other on the back and say, let's go for a 
burger and a beverage. Women leave, and we tend to take it more personally and we take it 
as a personal attack and then won't talk to that person or we will say terrible things about 
that person to others for six months to a year or longer because we haven't learned to 
separate and attack issues and not individuals. It's about, “We're solving a problem. We're 
dealing with an issue. We leave the individual their respect.”  
 
In organizations, it's sometimes tough to not see other women as competition because we 
feel like there are fewer opportunities and that women are only going to get a certain 
percentage of those opportunities. Instead of looking at it as: “What can I do? How do I 
equip myself? How do I give myself the skills and the reputation? And how do I deliver the 
goods -- in other words, get results, so that people see me in that role.”

So, we tend to look throughout organizations, again, in academia, in business, in non-
profits, and we see another person, and we think there's only a handful of us that are going 
to get to the next level, and we tend to then not work together, but we often don't optimize 
each other in our strengths because we see each other as competition.

Look for ways to encourage your organization’s support for women in the workplace, from hiring to mentorship programs or peer group committees.

Know of a job posting at your organization that’s the perfect fit for a woman you know? Refer her! How about someone who would be a great candidate for a particular committee? Offer the recommendation!

items.heading: Give Back
items.paragraph: In summary, as you build your tribe and support system at work, be on the lookout for ways to give back. There are people who have helped you get to where you are today, or are mentoring you as a female leader. Take a minute to think about how you can pay it forward with your own talents and skills.

Be the cheerleader someone else needs. Be the resource someone else can count on. Who can you be a reference for, or who needs an introduction? Pat would be the first to reinforce the power of the team in achieving any goal, as opposed to being a lone ranger or individual performer in your career. Remember the old African proverb, “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

video.transcript_text:
Remembering Pat: Being “Coachable” as a Coach 
 
 
Joan Cronan 
 
You know, when I think of mentorship, I think of Pat and how she helped others and how 
others helped her. But one of the things to be mentored or be received mentorship, you 
have to want it and you have to want to keep learning.  
 
One year we were playing in a regional finals and we lost to a team that we never thought 
we would lose to. I was disappointed. The team was disappointed. I got home before 
sunrise the next morning my phone rang, and it was Pat Summit. And she said, “Joan, it's 
my fault. We lost that game.”  
 
I said, “No Pat, it wasn't your fault. They played really well.”  
 
She said, “No, they ran an offense that I didn't understand.”  
 
Now, this is a coach who has won many championships. This is a coach that's considered 
one of the best coaches in the world. And she's saying, “I didn't understand.”  
 
And you know what she said? “I'm going to learn that offense and I'm never going to have 
somebody beat me with it again.” And she called a male counterpart at that stage, and he 
came in and spent about a week with us. 
 
You know, Pat had to be willing to admit she was wrong and didn't know something. This is 
such a winning coach, but she did it. She was willing to listen to other people and keep 
learning.  
 
And you know what? We never lost to that offense again.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Lesson 1 of 4
Supporting Female Leaders at Your Organization

Summarizing what we've covered...

Now knowing the hidden challenges and stereotypes women face, how can an organization intentionally support the women they manage and employ? Here are eight approaches and principles organizations can use to support female leaders at their own organization.

Summary

Be mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes, and address them when they occur.
Eliminate gender bias in the hiring process.
Make sure performance reviews are wholistic and don’t reward gender-biased attributes.
Offer flexibility and predictability with hours and workspace.
Avoid team-building activities or performance awards that favor one gender.
Ensure benefits are generous and conducive to families.
Have a zero-tolerance sexual harassment policy.
Include both genders on workplace committees.

Be mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes, and address them when they occur.

This is an everyday challenge, but doesn’t have to be a particularly disruptive one. The first step is making sure all employees are educated in common biases and stereotypes and aware that inclusivity of both genders is a priority. The next step is having a policy to address missteps quickly and succinctly. It could be as simple as stopping someone who is a chronic interrupter: “Let’s let Tamara finish her thought.” Or asking a male to take notes instead of volunteering the only female in the room: “Cindy did the recap for us last time. Juan, will you do the honors this time?”
Be especially mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes in meetings. Why? Because workplace culture is inherently learned, and nothing subconsciously sets the tone for interactions quite like team interactions in meetings. Stop both genders from comfortably falling into gender stereotyped roles.
Make sure all employees are educated in common biases and stereotypes and aware that inclusivity of both genders is a priority.

Eliminate gender bias in the hiring process.

Keeping gender bias out of the hiring process can be done in several ways.
Avoiding Gender-Biased Language
The language used in job descriptions can unintentionally discourage women from applying for certain positions, and research has shown that the choice of words and phrases can influence whether women perceive themselves as qualified for a role. To avoid this, organizations should develop clear and gender-neutral job descriptions that focus on qualifications, responsibilities, and skills rather than emphasizing traditionally masculine traits:
Avoid defaulting to one-sided pronouns, such as, “The ideal candidate will have strong organization skills. He will be able to decipher complex situations and make decisions quickly.”
Stay away from using male-oriented words like hunter mentality, maverick, and looking for an alpha-male mentality or someone who can bring home the bacon.
Avoid similarly female-biased descriptions like, “the ideal candidate is cheerful and friendly,” or “sensitive to other’s needs.”
Develop clear and gender-neutral job descriptions that focus on qualifications, responsibilities, and skills rather than emphasizing traditionally masculine traits.
Keeping Gender Out of Applicant Screenings
Blind hiring is an increasingly popular practice that removes identifiable information from resumes and job applications to minimize bias during the initial screening stages. This includes redacting names and other personal details that may indicate the candidate's gender. By evaluating candidates based solely on their skills, experience, and qualifications, it can help ensure that gender is not a factor in the early stages of the hiring process.
Conducting Structured Interviews
Unstructured interviews are more susceptible to bias, as they allow for inconsistencies and personal judgments. Structured interviews, on the other hand, involve asking all candidates the same set of questions in the same order and evaluating their responses against predefined criteria. This ensures each applicant is evaluated fairly, and avoids pitfalls like asking male candidates performance-driven questions while spending the majority of the time asking female applicants about their interpersonal skills, or vice versa.
Diversifying the Hiring Team
Include both sexes in interviews for open roles. This doesn’t always lend itself naturally if the two or three hiring managers are men only (or women only). But if possible, always have someone from the opposite sex sit in the interviews for perspective, even if they aren’t the decision-maker. Why? Women tend to notice things men don’t notice, and vice versa. Men tend to ask different questions and vet employees from a different perspective than women do.
Encouraging Equal Sexes to Apply
Did you interview any men for the open administrative assistant position? Did you interview any women for the open developer or accounting position? Specifically look for ways to add to the diversity of some of your non-diverse work teams, assuming qualifications are met.

Make sure performance reviews are wholistic and don’t reward gender-biased attributes.

Ensure performance reviews take into account a diversity of strengths and don’t only reward traditionally male characteristics. For example, grading someone on the following attributes:
Dominant
Ambitious
Competitive
Confident
Decisive
Independent
Outspoken
Results-driven
Takes charge
Hard-hitting
Assertive
As opposed to more gender-neutral attributes such as:
Subject-matter expertise
Collaboration
Productivity
Communication
Initiative
Problem-solving
Interpersonal skills
Dependability
Attention-to-detail
Creativity and innovation
Conflict resolution

Offer flexibility and predictability with hours and workspace.

Flexibility can come in a variety of forms, but specifically, this includes:
Flexible hours: When possible, offer flexible hours that allow individuals with caregiving responsibilities to work around them as needed.
Predictable schedules: Make sure work schedules are predictable and not subject to wild variations on short notice.
Flexible workspace: If the role permits, flexibility in offering remote, hybrid, or on-site options.

Avoid team-building activities or performance awards that favor one gender.

This can be tricky, and may take an offline examination of your current organization’s activities. (When in doubt, ask a committee of both genders.) For example, does your company plan traditionally masculine events like a retreat at a fly-fishing camp? This is not to say women don’t enjoy fishing—some do—and you can’t make generalizations about all women. But female employees often view masculine-leaning corporate outings, like cigar nights, poker tournaments, or rock-wall climbing, the same way male employees might view a company-sponsored spa getaway, musical, or art class.
Similarly, avoid gender-biased incentives, prizes, and rewards such as box tickets to a professional sporting event, or custom business suit for hitting a sales goal. It may be “tradition” at your organization, but creating a gender-equal workplace may require some new traditions. Consider more gender-neutral activities like an escape room, boating cruise, movie night, outdoor picnic, local tour, or food tasting. In addition, keep in mind team-building events or happy hours after work may be disadvantageous to those with families or to nondrinkers.

Ensure benefits are generous and conducive to families.

Benefits are important and their availability can often shape the careers of female caregivers.  This includes:
Paid maternity leave and spousal leave
Adoption benefits
Ample sick time/time off for caregiving responsibilities
Health insurance
Counseling to combat stress and burnout
Inclusion of on-site facilities such as nursing rooms, childcare, fitness areas etc.
Company events conducive to caregivers
Take, for example, a company with below average health insurance. A female leader was unable to qualify for other independent insurance options and pools because, technically, her employer offered coverage, so she was unable to see herself supporting a family long term on her company’s subpar insurance. A leader at another organization found that the insurance coverage was good, but insurance premiums were too high. She could cover herself, but the premiums weren’t conducive to supporting a family.

Have a zero-tolerance sexual harassment policy.

Anti-harassment policies are now mandatory and sexual harassment is illegal, but make sure employees know it won’t be tolerated on any level. This includes locker-room talk, derogatory slurs, or jokes even without females present. It doesn’t have to become a full-blown incident, but needs to be addressed. Handle any matters with confidentiality and minimal disruption.
This is important: Ensure female employees know that there won’t be social or career implications for bringing sexual harassment issues to an organization’s attention. The last thing any woman wants is to have to speak up because she was propositioned or harassed, then become the center of weeks of unwanted attention while the incident is investigated.

Include both genders on workplace committees.

For example, avoid having six women and two token males on the committee responsible for planning office events, outings, or culture. Aside from stereotyping women into gender roles, this eliminates valuable perspectives from both sides. It also sends the unintentional messages that women are better suited for nonbusiness, extracurricular work, and that the men have more valuable things to do with their time.

Deep Dive: Benefits That Support Female Leaders

When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Heading

In summary, when it comes to creating an environment that supports female leaders, start where you are and do what you can.
While implementing the steps in this lesson may take time and intentionality, the best part is, these policies are good for everyone, not just women. We’ll say it again. Men enjoy flexible hours too! They want to be valued for the variety of skills they bring to the table too, and not just the traditionally masculine ones. And not every male would consider professional football tickets or a mountain bike a sufficiently motivating reward.
You get the idea. By supporting women and attempting to bring balance to the workplace, everyone benefits!

video.transcript_text:
Conclusion: How to Create an Environment that Supports 
Female Leaders  
 
Michelle Marciniak 
OK, hopefully you’ve made it to the end with us and you’ve started to get a much clearer 
picture on how to create an environment that supports strong female leaders. 
To wrap it all up, here are a few basic principles to keep in mind.  
We talked about eliminating gender bias in the hiring process. The first step to supporting 
women is making sure they have an equal opportunity to work at your organization and that 
the metrics used to screen employees are balanced. When in doubt, include a mix of 
genders on your hiring committees – a good practice for any hires, not just female team 
members! 
Next, be mindful of microaggressions and gender stereotypes at your organization and 
begin to think of ways these can be eliminated at your organization. It may be as simple as 
better employee education. It may mean changing some traditions or committees, such as 
asking the women to bring food to the monthly potluck or being in charge of showers and 
other extracurriculars for employees. 
Make sure performance reviews don’t reward gender-biased attributes, such as 
“outspoken, ” “assertive, ” or “takes charge, ” without including qualities such as 
“interpersonal skills, ” “collaboration, ” “dependability,” or “attention-to-detail. ”   
To the best of your ability, offer flexibility with schedule and workspace. You also want to 
make sure you are offering benefits that are flexible and conducive to families. This goes 
without saying. 
Avoid team-building activities or “awards” that favor one gender, such as boxed tickets to a 
sporting event or mountain retreat to a fly-fishing resort. This one is huge! These activities 
and perks weren’t created with women in mind, any more than a night at the symphony or 
spa package as a team building-event would be attractive to most males. There are plenty 
of other gender-neutral activities and rewards to choose from, like escape rooms, game 
nights, vacation credits, or online gift cards.  
Finally, have a zero-tolerance policy on sexual harassment. Most organizations have 
embraced this fully, but make sure employees know it won’t be tolerated on any level. This 
includes locker-room talk, slurs, or jokes even without the opposite sex present. Such

actions contribute to the overall culture and can be insidious whether the actual female is 
present or not. Handle any matters quickly and confidentially. 
These policies are good for everyone, not just for women. And when everyone benefits, the 
team wins! 
So, as you complete this course, take a minute and think about where your organization 
falls. What steps can you take to get better? Which steps can you alone influence, and 
which might you need to suggest to others at your organization? 
Supporting women in leadership is a team effort. And Pat knew how to create winning 
teams.  
So, without further ado, let’s take a closer look.

states_text.text: Summarizing what we've covered... | Now knowing the hidden challenges and stereotypes women face, how can an organization intentionally support the women they manage and employ? Here are eight approaches and principles organizations can use to support female leaders at their own organization.

Summary | Be mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes, and address them when they occur.
Eliminate gender bias in the hiring process.
Make sure performance reviews are wholistic and don’t reward gender-biased attributes.
Offer flexibility and predictability with hours and workspace.
Avoid team-building activities or performance awards that favor one gender.
Ensure benefits are generous and conducive to families.
Have a zero-tolerance sexual harassment policy.
Include both genders on workplace committees.

Be mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes, and address them when they occur. | This is an everyday challenge, but doesn’t have to be a particularly disruptive one. The first step is making sure all employees are educated in common biases and stereotypes and aware that inclusivity of both genders is a priority. The next step is having a policy to address missteps quickly and succinctly. It could be as simple as stopping someone who is a chronic interrupter: “Let’s let Tamara finish her thought.” Or asking a male to take notes instead of volunteering the only female in the room: “Cindy did the recap for us last time. Juan, will you do the honors this time?”
Be especially mindful of microaggressions and stereotypes in meetings. Why? Because workplace culture is inherently learned, and nothing subconsciously sets the tone for interactions quite like team interactions in meetings. Stop both genders from comfortably falling into gender stereotyped roles.
Make sure all employees are educated in common biases and stereotypes and aware that inclusivity of both genders is a priority.

Eliminate gender bias in the hiring process. | Keeping gender bias out of the hiring process can be done in several ways.
Avoiding Gender-Biased Language
The language used in job descriptions can unintentionally discourage women from applying for certain positions, and research has shown that the choice of words and phrases can influence whether women perceive themselves as qualified for a role. To avoid this, organizations should develop clear and gender-neutral job descriptions that focus on qualifications, responsibilities, and skills rather than emphasizing traditionally masculine traits:
Avoid defaulting to one-sided pronouns, such as, “The ideal candidate will have strong organization skills. He will be able to decipher complex situations and make decisions quickly.”
Stay away from using male-oriented words like hunter mentality, maverick, and looking for an alpha-male mentality or someone who can bring home the bacon.
Avoid similarly female-biased descriptions like, “the ideal candidate is cheerful and friendly,” or “sensitive to other’s needs.”
Develop clear and gender-neutral job descriptions that focus on qualifications, responsibilities, and skills rather than emphasizing traditionally masculine traits.
Keeping Gender Out of Applicant Screenings
Blind hiring is an increasingly popular practice that removes identifiable information from resumes and job applications to minimize bias during the initial screening stages. This includes redacting names and other personal details that may indicate the candidate's gender. By evaluating candidates based solely on their skills, experience, and qualifications, it can help ensure that gender is not a factor in the early stages of the hiring process.
Conducting Structured Interviews
Unstructured interviews are more susceptible to bias, as they allow for inconsistencies and personal judgments. Structured interviews, on the other hand, involve asking all candidates the same set of questions in the same order and evaluating their responses against predefined criteria. This ensures each applicant is evaluated fairly, and avoids pitfalls like asking male candidates performance-driven questions while spending the majority of the time asking female applicants about their interpersonal skills, or vice versa.
Diversifying the Hiring Team
Include both sexes in interviews for open roles. This doesn’t always lend itself naturally if the two or three hiring managers are men only (or women only). But if possible, always have someone from the opposite sex sit in the interviews for perspective, even if they aren’t the decision-maker. Why? Women tend to notice things men don’t notice, and vice versa. Men tend to ask different questions and vet employees from a different perspective than women do.
Encouraging Equal Sexes to Apply
Did you interview any men for the open administrative assistant position? Did you interview any women for the open developer or accounting position? Specifically look for ways to add to the diversity of some of your non-diverse work teams, assuming qualifications are met.

Make sure performance reviews are wholistic and don’t reward gender-biased attributes. | Ensure performance reviews take into account a diversity of strengths and don’t only reward traditionally male characteristics. For example, grading someone on the following attributes:
Dominant
Ambitious
Competitive
Confident
Decisive
Independent
Outspoken
Results-driven
Takes charge
Hard-hitting
Assertive
As opposed to more gender-neutral attributes such as:
Subject-matter expertise
Collaboration
Productivity
Communication
Initiative
Problem-solving
Interpersonal skills
Dependability
Attention-to-detail
Creativity and innovation
Conflict resolution

Offer flexibility and predictability with hours and workspace. | Flexibility can come in a variety of forms, but specifically, this includes:
Flexible hours: When possible, offer flexible hours that allow individuals with caregiving responsibilities to work around them as needed.
Predictable schedules: Make sure work schedules are predictable and not subject to wild variations on short notice.
Flexible workspace: If the role permits, flexibility in offering remote, hybrid, or on-site options.

Avoid team-building activities or performance awards that favor one gender. | This can be tricky, and may take an offline examination of your current organization’s activities. (When in doubt, ask a committee of both genders.) For example, does your company plan traditionally masculine events like a retreat at a fly-fishing camp? This is not to say women don’t enjoy fishing—some do—and you can’t make generalizations about all women. But female employees often view masculine-leaning corporate outings, like cigar nights, poker tournaments, or rock-wall climbing, the same way male employees might view a company-sponsored spa getaway, musical, or art class.
Similarly, avoid gender-biased incentives, prizes, and rewards such as box tickets to a professional sporting event, or custom business suit for hitting a sales goal. It may be “tradition” at your organization, but creating a gender-equal workplace may require some new traditions. Consider more gender-neutral activities like an escape room, boating cruise, movie night, outdoor picnic, local tour, or food tasting. In addition, keep in mind team-building events or happy hours after work may be disadvantageous to those with families or to nondrinkers.

Ensure benefits are generous and conducive to families. | Benefits are important and their availability can often shape the careers of female caregivers.  This includes:
Paid maternity leave and spousal leave
Adoption benefits
Ample sick time/time off for caregiving responsibilities
Health insurance
Counseling to combat stress and burnout
Inclusion of on-site facilities such as nursing rooms, childcare, fitness areas etc.
Company events conducive to caregivers
Take, for example, a company with below average health insurance. A female leader was unable to qualify for other independent insurance options and pools because, technically, her employer offered coverage, so she was unable to see herself supporting a family long term on her company’s subpar insurance. A leader at another organization found that the insurance coverage was good, but insurance premiums were too high. She could cover herself, but the premiums weren’t conducive to supporting a family.

Have a zero-tolerance sexual harassment policy. | Anti-harassment policies are now mandatory and sexual harassment is illegal, but make sure employees know it won’t be tolerated on any level. This includes locker-room talk, derogatory slurs, or jokes even without females present. It doesn’t have to become a full-blown incident, but needs to be addressed. Handle any matters with confidentiality and minimal disruption.
This is important: Ensure female employees know that there won’t be social or career implications for bringing sexual harassment issues to an organization’s attention. The last thing any woman wants is to have to speak up because she was propositioned or harassed, then become the center of weeks of unwanted attention while the incident is investigated.

Include both genders on workplace committees. | For example, avoid having six women and two token males on the committee responsible for planning office events, outings, or culture. Aside from stereotyping women into gender roles, this eliminates valuable perspectives from both sides. It also sends the unintentional messages that women are better suited for nonbusiness, extracurricular work, and that the men have more valuable things to do with their time.

items.heading: Deep Dive: Benefits That Support Female Leaders
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
In summary, when it comes to creating an environment that supports female leaders, start where you are and do what you can.

While implementing the steps in this lesson may take time and intentionality, the best part is, these policies are good for everyone, not just women. We’ll say it again. Men enjoy flexible hours too! They want to be valued for the variety of skills they bring to the table too, and not just the traditionally masculine ones. And not every male would consider professional football tickets or a mountain bike a sufficiently motivating reward.

You get the idea. By supporting women and attempting to bring balance to the workplace, everyone benefits!

Deep Dive: Benefits that Attract Female Leaders 
 
Patty Hoppenstedt 
OK, when it comes to supporting female leaders, let’s take a closer look at benefits. There 
are a lot of options out there when it comes to attracting and supporting female team 
members with your benefit program. We’re going to go over a few options in this video.  
We know what benefits you can offer at your organization may differ from business to 
business, and it may not be entirely up to you. The important thing isn’t to implement 
everything, but to start where you are, and do as much as you can. 
The number one benefit employees still say they want, including women, is good 
healthcare. And good healthcare benefits everyone, not just the women, right? 
So, let’s take a look at that for a minute. Healthcare isn’t what it used to be, right? It’s gotten 
a whole lot more nuanced, and a whole lot more expensive. And coverage for a single 
person is drastically different than the monthly coverage for a family of four.  
You may be offering health coverage, but how can you make sure your coverage is truly 
exceptional? Some employers are increasing the amount they pay per employee, that is, 
the employer’s share, to make it more affordable.  
 
You also want to think like a woman when assessing your benefits. Take a close look at the 
contraceptive health, maternity care, and co-pay parts of your plan. Does it cover 
prescriptions? What would the average out-of-pocket cost be to have a child under this 
plan? What is the out-of-pocket maximum for families? Does it cover preventative care like 
mammograms and other annual screenings like osteoporosis or cancer (which also 
benefits men)? 
 
Many plans offer a telehealth option that is extremely popular with working parents – you 
can see a doctor or get a prescription for your child through a quick telehealth screening 
from the comfort of your home without having a lot of time out of office. Our own company 
plan offers this, and it’s become very popular. 
 
In addition to dental and vision, some employers are adding add-ons to their healthcare 
options like fertility and adoption assistance – both of which can be expensive – through 
access to family planning resources.  Some employers are starting to offer pregnancy loss 
leave, menopausal support for challenging health transitions, mental health support –

which again, benefits everyone, not just women – and other supplemental insurances like 
pet insurance, disability insurance, accident or cancer plans, just to name a few. 
You may not be able to implement ALL these features in your current healthcare offering 
but start where you can and do what you can. 
Aside from healthcare, the main thing women say they want is flexibility. This includes both 
flexible working hours and paid time off.  
Again, think like a woman who might have to drop a child off at school or run a family 
member to the doctor’s office in the middle of the day. (Or a man!) How easy is this at your 
organization? What can you do to make it easier? Because it if isn’t the women doing it, it 
would be the men doing it, right? One of the parents has to do it, and America has become 
a nation of dual-income families. Gone are the days when most women stay home and the 
male is the only breadwinner. Studies show most parents work outside the home – 
anywhere from 58-66%.  
So, think about what you can do to offer flexibility to all your employees, not just women. 
This includes flexible hours, options for remote work where appropriate, and generous paid 
time off. At the organization I work for, we recently went to flexible paid time off. The 
employee feedback has been amazing, and the productivity has remained high.  
If you can’t offer something like unlimited time off, studies show women appreciate paid 
holidays that allow them to be off when their kids are off. Most organizations offer the 
major holidays, but this means team members aren’t having to find babysitters for the kids 
on federal holidays like Columbus Day or President’s Day when the schools and childcare 
are closed. Your male and female employees aren’t having to have discussions about 
who’s going to watch the kids in the morning and who’s going to watch them in the 
afternoon because both parents work. Some companies offer generous paid leave around 
Christmas – more than just your standard two days, which helps.  
Childcare is another of the most popular benefits that attract women. Think of how many 
women drop out of the workforce due to childcare costs? If you have a family, you know 
that childcare is so expensive. Some employers offer on-site childcare facilities or offer 
childcare subsidies to help offset the costs of care for parents who work outside the home 
– again, a benefit men will appreciate as much as the women, because it all comes out of 
the household income, right? You may see a common thread here…benefits that are good 
for women usually wind up being beneficial for everyone. 
Finally, it goes without saying that you want to look at your benefits around maternity care 
and parental leave. The average maternity leave in the U.S. is around 10 weeks, which 
includes paid leave, personal leave, and unpaid leave. The FMLA act requires an employer

to offer up to 12 weeks of leave but doesn’t specify that it all be paid. And some women 
can’t afford to take the full 12 weeks without a steady paycheck. It’s no secret that 
European countries like Italy or the Czech Republic offer 5-7 months of paid leave, 
including countries like Sweden, Norway, or the U.K that offer much more. Even China 
offers 14 weeks at 100%.  So, you want to make sure your maternity leave is generous and 
competitive in this area.  
You also want to offer a location for onsite breast pumping for new moms.  Some 
employers off half days or 3-4 day work weeks at the end of 12 weeks for a certain amount 
of time to help ease new moms back into the workforce. And don’t forget to include the 
spouse! Make sure you have a solid parental leave policy that doesn’t leave working 
spouses out of the equation.  
Again, all of this may not be possible at your organization, but do what you can, as much as 
you’re able to offer. The result of retaining more female team members and leaders is well 
worth it in the long run. 
OK, but what if you’re not in charge of benefits at your organization? What can you do to 
ensure an environment that supports female leaders? Plenty!  
First, we talked about microaggressions – and team members are on the front lines of the 
day-to-day grind to make sure your department or group is as gender-neutral and friendly 
as possible. A lot of times unintentional obstacles to females in the workplace aren’t 
systemic, meaning they don’t come down from the organizational level. Many are social in 
the ways we treat each other, support each other and work together. Some of that comes 
down to how we all play together. That’s right – play!  
When your office has any non-business or social activities, are they thought of with women 
in mind?  
Is it a happy hour after work not everyone may be able to attend, but everyone should 
attend? Or a company-sponsored poker or cigar night where women are welcome but…few 
show up? This isn’t a statement on whether women can’t play poker or smoke cigars. Of 
course they can. The key is, do they want to? And is it really the best team-building option, 
whether formal or informal? 
What if your CEO is female and decided to have a spa night, or company sponsored tickets 
to a musical? Would the men find that outing super motivating? Some might, but definitely 
not all, right? What about baby showers that include only the ladies or a golf tournament on 
the weekend that caters more to men?

These things aren’t bad. You just want to think differently when planning social events for 
your department – especially if the goal is team-building. Make sure if someone is being 
celebrated in the office, like a birthday or wedding shower, that everyone is invited to 
attend, and multiple genders help with the planning. The same goes for company events, 
prizes, awards. Movies, escape rooms, food tastings, tour packages, gift cards – you name 
it. The world is bigger than ever when it comes to employee interaction and motivation.  
It takes an entire organization working together to create an environment that is inclusive 
and supportive of both men and women. We all have a part to play!  
So, think about how you can put some of these ideas into practice today.
